articles.appTitle: Getting a passport and other important documents from your country of origin
articles.description: Start with gathering your documents: Prepare all the required documents, such as your passport, birth certificate, educational qualifications, and any…
articles.previewHtml: Start with gathering your documents: Prepare all the required documents, such as your passport, birth certificate, educational qualifications, and any other relevant documents.
articles.gatedHtml:
You should have an original valid passport for at least 6 months after the intended date of departure from Ireland following visits. The passport must have sufficient space for a visa to be inserted, at least two empty pages are required.

When registering, you must present a valid passport from your country of origin to prove your identity. Having a valid passport is also necessary, as immigration stamps are printed on a person’s passport.

Getting a passport and identity documents is also important as formal identification is necessary for many things in Ireland including opening a bank account, applying for a driving licence, applying to study at college or university. Many landlords in Ireland also request proof of identification.

★ Useful Info

Country of origin: The country of a person’s nationality.


Stamp (immigration): An immigration stamps acts as proof of a person’s permission to be in Ireland for longer than 90 days. It indicates some of the rights that a person has when living in Ireland, for example, all Stamp 4 holders are allowed to work or engage in a business or trade in Ireland.

articles.title: Obtain your visa
articles.description: If you are travelling to Ireland and you are not a citizen of the UK, Switzerland, or a country in the European Economic Area (the EU plus Norway…
articles.previewHtml:
If you are travelling to Ireland and you are not a citizen of the UK, Switzerland, or a country in the European Economic Area (the EU plus Norway, Iceland, and Lichtenstein), you may need to apply for a visa.

An Irish visa is a certificate placed on your passport or travel document that allows you to travel to Ireland. You still have to present your passport and documents to immigration control when you arrive at the airport or port, and an immigration officer may still refuse you entry to Ireland.

If you are travelling with children, you have to apply for a visa for your children too.

Do I need a visa?

  • Are a citizen of the EU or the EEA (the EU plus Iceland, Norway, and Lichtenstein) or Switzerland
  • Have a residence card issued by an EEA country or Switzerland because you are the family member of an EEA or Swiss citizen living in a country outside the EEA/Swiss family member’s home country (for example, you live in Germany with your French spouse).
articles.gatedHtml:
• Are a citizen of a country listed in the table below.
AndorraHondurasSamoa
Antigua & BarbudaHong KongSan Marino
ArgentinaIsraelSeychelles
AustraliaJapanSingapore
BahamasKiribatiSolomon Islands
BarbadosLesothoSouth Africa
BelizeMacau (Special Admin. Region)South Korea
BotswanaMalaysiaSwaziland (Eswatini)
BoliviaMaldivesTaiwan
BrazilMexicoTonga
BruneiMonacoTrinidad & Tobago
CanadaNauruTuvalu
ChileNew ZealandUkraine
Costa RicaNicaraguaUnited Arab Emirates
DominicaPanamaUnited Kingdom
El SalvadorParaguayUnited States of America
FijiSaint Kitts & NevisUruguay
GrenadaSaint LuciaVanuatu
GuatemalaSaint Vincent & the GrenadinesVatican City
Guyana

Types of visa

Short stay visas

If you want to come to Ireland for less than 3 months, you should apply for a short stay ‘C’ visa. You should apply for this type of visa if you wish to come to Ireland as a tourist or to visit someone, for a business meeting, or to attend a short course.

You cannot stay for longer than 3 months on a ‘C’ visa. You must leave Ireland and apply for another visa if you wish to return.

Long stay visas

If you want to come to Ireland for more than 3 months, for example to study, for work or to settle permanently in Ireland with family members who live in Ireland, then you can apply for a long stay ‘D’ visa.

If you are granted a long stay ‘D’ visa and wish to remain in the State for longer than 3 months, you must register and get an Irish Residence Permit (IRP).

Re-entry visas

The first visa issued to you is valid for a single entry to the State. If you wish to leave the State for a short period of time, you may need to apply for a re-entry visa – including travel to Northern Ireland.

If you have a valid Irish Residence Permit (IRP) you do not need a re-entry visa when travelling to and from Ireland.

Non-EEA nationals aged under 16 do not have to register for an IRP and do not need a re-entry visa to travel to and from Ireland. They must be accompanied by a parent or guardian who has legal permission to live in Ireland.

Rates

The standard non-refundable visa application processing fees are:

Entry and re-entry visas

A single journey visa costs €60 and will be valid for one entry to the State up to a maximum of 90 days from the date of issue.

A multi journey visa costs €100 and will be valid for multiple entries to the State up to a maximum of 5 years from the date of issue.

Further information and contacts

Information about visas is available from your nearest Irish embassy or consulate.

articles.title: Sell the items you own
articles.description: Making a few more euros just before moving to Ireland could be a logical action. Here is why:
articles.previewHtml:
Making a few more euros just before moving to Ireland could be a logical action. Here is why:

  • The standard domestic electricity supply in Ireland is 230 volts AC. Check your electronic devices’ voltages. Most of them are better off replaced than transported.
  • Shipping furniture and heavy items is costly. And, you will have an uncertainty about your new home’s size. So, think about replacement with new furniture.

Some Irish websites you can find furniture and electronics:
articles.gatedHtml:
Harvey Norman:
https://www.harveynorman.ie/

Woodies:
https://www.woodies.ie/

DID Electrical:
https://www.did.ie/

Power City:
https://www.powercity.ie/

EZ Living Furniture:
https://www.ezlivingfurniture.ie/

Currys PC World:
https://www.currys.ie/

Littlewoods Ireland:
https://www.littlewoodsireland.ie/

How to get rid of your items

Online marketplaces: Websites such as eBay and Craigslist allow you to list items for sale to a global audience, which can be a great way to reach potential buyers in your new country.

Social Media: Platforms like Facebook and Instagram have bought and sell groups where you can post your items for sale.

Consignment shops or second-hand stores: you can take your items to consignment shops or second-hand stores in your area, and they will sell them on your behalf.

Garage Sale: you could hold a garage sale or yard sale in your current area before you move to get rid of items you no longer need.

Professional moving company: If you're hiring a professional moving company, they may be able to help you sell your items or recommend a local service that can assist you.

Specialized Selling: If you have items that are of a specific type, such as antiques or collectibles, you may be able to find specialized buyers or sellers who are interested in those items.

Ultimately, the best option will depend on your specific circumstances and the items you need to sell. It's also recommended that you do your research and compare prices between different platforms.

Eventually, get rid of your unsold items by via charity and with website you can offer your belongings for free. At least, it will be used by for someone rather than abandoned.

articles.title: Arrange your temporary accommodation
articles.description: When relocating to Ireland and looking for temporary accommodation until to find a permanent flat, there are a few options to consider:
articles.previewHtml:
When relocating to Ireland and looking for temporary accommodation until to find a permanent flat, there are a few options to consider:

Hotel or Hostel: Booking a hotel or hostel can be a practical option for short-term stays. This will give you a place to stay while you look for more permanent accommodation.

Serviced flats: Serviced flats can be a suitable option for longer stays. They usually come equipped with a kitchen and other amenities, and can be more cost-effective than staying in a hotel.
articles.gatedHtml:
Vacation rental: Websites like Airbnb or Booking.com have a wide variety of vacation rentals available, from private rooms to entire flats or houses. This can be an adequate option if you're looking for more space and privacy.

Home-sharing: Websites like Spare Room or HouseTrip offer short-term rentals for people searching for a place to stay, and often allow you to rent a room in a shared flat or house.

Corporate housing: Some companies offer corporate housing options for people who are relocating for work. This can be a viable option if your employer is helping to cover the cost of your accommodation.

Relocation agency: Relocation agencies can provide assistance in finding temporary accommodation, as well as helping with other aspects of relocating to Ireland, such as finding a permanent flat, opening a bank account, etc.

★ Tip

There are some agencies operating in Ireland, some popular ones include:

  1. Occu
  2. Corporate Relocations
  3. Caden Grimes
  4. Settle in
  5. OnboardIreland

You may even find your permanent accommodation via a letting agency. Notwithstanding, check “Common Rental Scams” in the accommodation section and beware the risks.

It's important to research different options and compare prices and amenities before deciding. Furthermore, check the location, availability, and duration of the accommodation.

articles.title: Cancel services and subscriptions
articles.description: When a person moves to another country, there are several common subscriptions and automatic payments that they might need to cancel or adjust:
articles.previewHtml:
When a person moves to another country, there are several common subscriptions and automatic payments that they might need to cancel or adjust:

Cable or satellite TV: If you're moving from a country where you have a cable or satellite TV subscription, you'll need to cancel it or find a similar service in your new country.
articles.gatedHtml:
Streaming services: Services like Netflix, Hulu, and Amazon Prime have regional restrictions, and you might have to cancel them or find the equivalent service in your new country.

Internet and phone: If you have a monthly internet or phone plan with your current service provider, you'll need to cancel it or find a new provider in your new country.

Gym or fitness memberships: If you have a gym or fitness membership, you'll need to cancel it or find a new gym in your new location.

Magazine and newspaper subscriptions: If you have subscriptions to magazines or newspapers, you'll need to cancel them or find digital alternatives in your new country.

Automatic payments: Make sure to check your bank statements for any automatic payments you might have, like, for example, recurring subscription boxes or online services.

Insurance policies: If you have insurance policies like car, health or home insurance, you'll need to cancel them or find new providers in your new country.

It's important to check the terms and conditions of each subscription or service to see if you can cancel or transfer your account, and also check if there is an equivalent service in the new country. It's also a good idea to cancel or adjust these subscriptions and payments well in advance of your move to avoid any disruptions or additional fees.

articles.title: Obtain necessary documentation to present on arrival in Ireland
articles.appTitle: Obtain necessary documentation to present on arrival in Ireland
articles.description: When a person arrives in Ireland, they will need to present certain documents to border control to enter the country. Here are some of the common…
articles.previewHtml:
When a person arrives in Ireland, they will need to present certain documents to border control to enter the country. Here are some of the common documents that may be required:

Passport: A valid passport is required for all non-EU citizens travelling to Ireland. Make sure that your passport is valid for at least six months after your intended date of departure from the country.
articles.gatedHtml:
Visa: Depending on the person's nationality and the length of their stay, a visa may be required. It's recommended that you check with the Irish embassy or consulate in your home country to determine if a visa is needed.

Accommodation details: It's advisable to have details of where you will be staying in Ireland, this could be a hotel booking confirmation or a letter from a host if you will be staying with someone.

Financial means: It's advisable to have enough funds to cover your expenses while in Ireland, either in cash or in a credit card.

Travel insurance: It's recommended to have valid travel insurance that covers the duration of your stay in Ireland.

Work permit or proof of employment: If you are moving to Ireland for work, it's recommended to have a valid work permit or proof of employment.

It's important to note that these documents may vary depending on the person's circumstances, and it is always advisable to check with the Irish embassy or consulate in your home country for the most up-to-date information on entry requirements.

articles.title: Protect your credit score
articles.note: Special content for US citizens 🇺🇸
articles.description: As a US citizen moving abroad for work, there are a few steps you can take to protect your credit score:
articles.previewHtml:
As a US citizen moving abroad for work, there are a few steps you can take to protect your credit score:

Keep your credit accounts active: Maintain your current credit accounts, even if you don't use them regularly, to demonstrate that you have a long credit history.

Inform your credit card company: Let your credit card company know that you will be living abroad so that they don't flag any foreign transactions as fraudulent.
articles.gatedHtml:
Use a credit monitoring service: Consider signing up for a credit monitoring service, which will alert you to any changes or suspicious activity on your credit report.

Pay your bills on time: Make sure you continue to make your payments on time, as late payments can have a negative impact on your credit score.

Maintain your US address: Keep your US mailing address current, as this will ensure that you receive any important mail related to your credit accounts.

Get a credit report from US agencies: Obtain a credit report from the major credit reporting agencies in the US to see if there are any errors or inconsistencies that need to be addressed.

Consider a credit freeze: If you're concerned about identity theft or fraud, consider placing a credit freeze on your accounts, which will prevent new accounts from being opened in your name.

By following these steps, you can help protect your credit score while living abroad and ensure that you're able to maintain a good credit history when you return to the US.

articles.title: Bringing money to Ireland
articles.description: Bringing money to a new country can be a daunting task, but it's essential for establishing your life in your new home. As an immigrant coming to…
articles.previewHtml: Bringing money to a new country can be a daunting task, but it's essential for establishing your life in your new home. As an immigrant coming to Ireland, it's important to know the options available for bringing your money safely and securely. Here are some tips on the best ways to bring your money to Ireland.
articles.gatedHtml:
International Wire Transfer

One of the safest ways to transfer money to Ireland is through an international wire transfer. This option is secure, fast, and convenient. You can transfer money from your bank account in your home country to a bank account in Ireland. The process is straightforward and usually takes 1-3 business days. You can contact your bank for assistance with this.

Here are some international wire transfer companies that are considered trustworthy and reliable:

  1. Wise
  2. PayPal
  3. Western Union
  4. MoneyGram
  5. Remitly

It's important to note that the fees and exchange rates can vary among different companies, so it's important to compare the rates and fees before making a transfer. Additionally, some companies may have specific requirements or restrictions, so it's important to review the terms and conditions before choosing a provider.

Support yourself and us! ❤️

Wise is editor’s choice and usually offers the best rates and transaction fees.

It is a popular option and used by millions.

Just sign up with our link and we both get some bonuses* and free transactions.

Traveler's Checks

Traveler's checks are a popular option for bringing money to a new country. They are safe and can be replaced if they are lost or stolen. Traveler's checks are available in various currencies and can be purchased at most banks. However, they may not be accepted everywhere in Ireland, so it's significant to check beforehand.

Credit Cards

Credit cards are widely accepted in Ireland, so it's a good idea to bring one with you. You can use it for everyday expenses like groceries, dining, and shopping. It's important to check with your bank beforehand to ensure that your credit card will work in Ireland and to notify them of your travel plans to avoid fraud alerts.

Debit Cards

Debit cards are another popular option for bringing money to Ireland. They allow you to withdraw cash from ATMs and make purchases at stores. It's significant to check with your bank beforehand to ensure that your debit card will work in Ireland and to notify them of your travel plans to avoid fraud alerts.

Cash

While it's not recommended to carry large amounts of cash when traveling, you can bring cash to Ireland. The maximum amount of cash you can bring into the country is €10,000. It's important to declare any amount over €10,000 to the Irish customs officials.

* Wise changes their bonuses regularly, so it is not possible to say what precisely they offer while you are reading this.

It's important to declare any amount over €10,000 to the Irish customs officials.* Wise changes their bonuses regularly, so it is not possible to say what precisely they offer while you are reading this.
sections: International Wire TransferOne of the safest ways to transfer money to Ireland is through an international wire transfer. This option is secure, fast, and convenient. You can transfer money from your bank account in your home country to a bank account in Ireland. The process is straightforward and usually takes 1-3 business days. You can contact your bank for assistance with this.

  2. Check your passport is valid for the whole period you plan to stay, and renew it now if not.
  3. Gather originals and certified copies of birth certificates, marriage certificates, degrees, vaccination records and police clearance if your permission requires it.
  4. Ask your current bank for six months of statements and your employer for a reference letter; Irish landlords ask for both.
  5. If you drive, check whether your licence is from an EU/EEA state or one of Ireland's recognised states; if it is not, you will have to start from a learner permit. Begin the driver theory test study early if so.
  6. Get a letter from your doctor with your medical history and current prescriptions; Irish GPs will want it.
  7. Book temporary accommodation for at least your first two to four weeks; finding a long-term rental from abroad is very hard.
  8. Read Daft.ie listings to set your rent budget; a Dublin two-bed apartment averaged €2,551 in Q2 2026.
  9. If you are bringing a pet, check the microchip, rabies vaccination and EU pet passport or animal health certificate rules on the Department of Agriculture website; timing matters.
articles.gatedHtml:
One month before you move

  1. Create a basic MyGovID account at mygovid.ie; you will need it to apply for your PPS number on MyWelfare.
  2. Create an account on the Immigration Service Delivery customer portal if you are a non-EEA national, so you can book your registration appointment the day you land.
  3. Cancel or transfer subscriptions, utilities, gym memberships and insurance at home, and set up mail redirection.
  4. Tell your home tax authority you are leaving, and find out whether you must keep filing there (US citizens must).
  5. Arrange how you will move money. Open a euro account with an online bank that accepts a foreign address if your Irish bank account will take weeks.
  6. Check your phone is unlocked; Irish prepaid SIMs need no address.
  7. Print or download proof of your temporary address, your job offer or college acceptance, travel insurance and enough funds for the immigration officer at the border.
  8. Pack documents in hand luggage, never in checked bags.

Arrival week

  1. At passport control, non-EEA nationals get a landing stamp; it tells you to register with immigration within 90 days.
  2. Buy an Irish SIM and a TFI Leap Card (adult card €5 refundable deposit, minimum €5 top-up).
  3. Apply for your PPS number on MyWelfare and book the in-person appointment. Bring your passport and proof of address.
  4. Non-EEA nationals: log into the ISD portal and book your registration appointment at Burgh Quay. Appointments are normally available within two to three weeks and the IRP costs €300.
  5. Start viewing properties. Bring ID, proof of employment and references to every viewing and be ready to decide on the spot.
  6. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have your PPS number, and register your job under Jobs and Pensions to avoid emergency tax.
  7. Find a GP taking new patients near where you will live and ask to join the list.
  8. Get proof of address early: a tenancy agreement, bank statement or official letter dated within three months opens most other doors.

First 90 days

  1. Attend your immigration registration appointment and wait for your IRP card in the post.
  2. Open an Irish bank account with your passport, proof of address and PPS number; you need it for salary and direct debits.
  3. Sign your lease. The deposit is capped at one month's rent plus up to one month's rent in advance. Check the landlord registers the tenancy with the RTB.
  4. Set up electricity and gas in your name, and broadband. Buy a TV licence (€160) if you have a television.
  5. Claim the Rent Tax Credit on myAccount, worth up to €1,000 for a single person and €2,000 for a couple in 2026.
  6. Apply for a GP visit card or medical card if your income is low, and register children under 8 for their free GP visit card.
  7. Decide on private health insurance. If you are over 34, the Health Insurance Authority's lifetime community rating rules give new residents a limited window to take out cover before age loadings apply.
  8. Exchange your driving licence at the NDLS if it is from a recognised state (fee €65), or book your theory test if it is not.
  9. Enrol children in school and crèche, and apply for the National Childcare Scheme if eligible.
  10. Register to vote with your local authority. Non-citizens can vote in local elections.
  11. Tell your embassy your new address.

articles.appTitle: Three months before you move to Ireland
articles.note: Permits, documents, rent budgeting, money, driving, pets and the online accounts to set up early.
articles.description: Three months out is the point where a move to Ireland stops being an idea and becomes a project. The things you do now are the slow ones: immigration…
articles.previewHtml:
Three months out is the point where a move to Ireland stops being an idea and becomes a project. The things you do now are the slow ones: immigration permissions, document gathering, money and the first honest look at what renting will cost. Get these right and the last month before you fly is mostly packing. This guide takes each area in turn, with the official sources you should be reading. Figures are correct as of September 2026.

Sort out your right to live and work

If you hold an EU, EEA, UK or Swiss passport you can simply arrive and start work. Everyone else needs a permission before travelling. The most common routes are the Critical Skills Employment Permit and the General Employment Permit, both applied for through the Department of Enterprise's Employment Permits Online System, usually by your employer. Processing times are published on the department's site and change month to month; check them now and count backwards from your start date. If you are from a visa-required country you must then apply for a long-stay D visa once the permit is granted. Students need a letter of acceptance and proof of funds and, if visa-required, a study visa.
articles.gatedHtml:
Whatever your route, read the Immigration Service Delivery page for your permission type now. It lists exactly what you must show the immigration officer at the airport and what you will need at your registration appointment later.

Gather and certify your documents

Irish offices are strict about originals. Collect the following and keep them together in hand luggage.

DocumentWhy you need it
Passport valid for your whole stayEverything; renew now if it expires within a year
Birth certificate (long form) and marriage certificateImmigration registration for family members, some benefits, schools
Degree and professional certificatesEmployment permits, regulated professions, university enrolment
Police clearance certificateRequired for some permissions and for jobs involving children or vulnerable adults
Employer reference and job offer or contractLandlords, PPS number application, bank account
Six months of bank statementsLandlords, immigration officer, banks
Medical records, prescriptions and vaccination recordsRegistering with a GP, school enrolment
Driving licence and driving recordLicence exchange at the NDLS, car insurance quotes

If any document is not in English or Irish, get a certified translation now. Ask your home country's authorities about apostilles for birth and marriage certificates if you may need them for immigration or citizenship later.

Understand what housing will cost

Rent is the biggest budget line and it is the one people underestimate most. The Daft.ie Rental Report for Q2 2026 puts the average rent for a two-bedroom apartment at €2,551 in Dublin and €2,204 nationwide; the RTB Rent Index for Q1 2026 shows new tenants paying a national average of €1,839, with Dublin City at €2,301, Galway City at €2,004 and Cork City at €1,903. Spend an evening on Daft.ie and MyHome.ie searching the areas near your workplace so you know what your money buys, then read our "Where to live" guides.

Plan for cash up front: a landlord can ask for a deposit of up to one month's rent plus one month's rent in advance, so budget two months' rent on signing, plus the cost of temporary accommodation while you search. Book that temporary place now for your first two to four weeks; short-term rentals in Dublin sell out.

Money, tax and insurance

  • Open a euro account with a bank or fintech that accepts your current address, so you have a card that works on day one. You will open a traditional Irish account later, once you have a PPS number and proof of address.
  • Tell your home tax authority when you are leaving. If you are a US citizen you will keep filing US returns and FBAR reports; see our Paperwork guides.
  • Check whether your home pension can be transferred or must be left in place.
  • Get travel insurance that covers you until you have Irish cover. EU citizens should bring their European Health Insurance Card, which covers necessary care until you are ordinarily resident.
  • If you are over 34, note that the Health Insurance Authority's lifetime community rating rules give new residents a limited window to take out private health insurance without age loadings.

Driving, pets and children

Check now whether your driving licence can be exchanged. Licences from the EU/EEA and from Ireland's recognised states (including the UK, Australia, Canada's larger provinces, Japan, South Korea, South Africa, Switzerland, New Zealand and Taiwan) can be swapped for €65. Others cannot, and you will start from a learner permit and the driver theory test, so book study time. If you are bringing a dog or cat, it needs a microchip, a rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel and either an EU pet passport or an animal health certificate; check the Department of Agriculture's rules for your country of departure. Parents should look up schools near their target areas now and email them, because popular primary schools take applications well ahead of the September intake.

Create your online accounts

Two accounts save weeks later. Create a basic MyGovID account at mygovid.ie; it is how you apply for your PPS number on MyWelfare. Non-EEA nationals should also create an account on the ISD customer portal so that you can book your immigration registration appointment as soon as you land. Neither requires you to be in Ireland.

★ Useful links

  • Immigration Service Delivery
  • Department of Enterprise: employment permits
  • Daft.ie Rental Report Q2 2026
  • Department of Agriculture: pet travel
  • MyGovID

articles.title: Your first week in Ireland
articles.note: Day-by-day plan: landing stamp, SIM and Leap Card, PPS application, IRP booking and house hunting.
articles.description: The first week sets the pace for everything that follows, because two of the slowest processes in Ireland, the PPS number and immigration registration…
articles.previewHtml:
The first week sets the pace for everything that follows, because two of the slowest processes in Ireland, the PPS number and immigration registration, both start with an online booking that you can make on day one. Get those in the queue, get a phone and a travel card, and start the property search, and the rest of the month will run smoothly. This guide is a day-by-day plan; adjust it to your own arrival day. Figures are correct as of September 2026.

Day 1: the airport and the basics

If you are a non-EEA national, the immigration officer will stamp your passport with a landing stamp. Read it: it gives you permission to stay and tells you to register with Immigration Service Delivery within 90 days. Keep every document you showed at the border; you will show them again at registration.

Before you leave the airport, buy an Irish prepaid SIM (no address needed) and a TFI Leap Card. The adult card costs a €5 refundable deposit with a €5 minimum top-up, and inside Dublin the 90-minute fare of €2 covers bus, Luas and DART with a daily cap of €6. Buses from Dublin Airport into the city accept the Leap Card. In Cork, the airport bus and city buses also take Leap.
articles.gatedHtml:
Day 2: apply for your PPS number

You cannot be paid correctly, register with Revenue, open most bank accounts or apply for a GP visit card without a Personal Public Service number, and you can only apply once you are in Ireland. Log into MyWelfare.ie with your MyGovID, fill in the application, upload your documents and book an in-person appointment at a PPS Number Allocation Centre. You need:

  • Your passport (EU citizens can use a national identity card).
  • Proof of address dated within three months. For a new arrival this can be an official letter confirming your address from your hotel, hostel or landlord, or a household bill with a note from the bill holder.
  • Evidence of why you need the number, such as a job offer or a college acceptance letter.

Your number is not issued at the appointment; the Department runs further checks and posts it to you afterwards, and it does not publish a processing time. Take the earliest appointment you can get, anywhere you can reach.

Day 3: book immigration registration

Non-EEA nationals aged 16 and over must register and get an Irish Residence Permit. Log into the ISD customer portal, book an appointment at the registration office at Burgh Quay in Dublin, and gather the documents listed for your permission type. Appointments are normally available within two to three weeks, and the permit costs €300, paid by card. Your IRP card is posted to you after the appointment, so make sure you will have a stable address by then or use your employer's address if they allow it.

Days 3 to 7: find somewhere to live

Start viewing immediately. The rental market moves in hours, not days, and a good listing on Daft.ie can have dozens of enquiries by lunchtime. Set up alerts for your target areas, respond within minutes, and bring a folder to every viewing with:

ItemWhy
Passport or IDLandlords must verify who they are renting to
Employment contract or offer letterProof you can pay
Recent payslips or bank statementsProof of income and savings
Reference from a previous landlordReassurance for the agent
Employer or character referenceUseful if you have never rented before

Know the rules before you hand over money. A deposit cannot exceed one month's rent, and advance rent cannot exceed one month. Never pay a deposit without having viewed the property in person and met the landlord or a licensed agent; read our guide to common rental scams. Once you sign, ask the landlord for confirmation that the tenancy is registered with the RTB.

Also this week

  • Register with Revenue: once you have a PPS number, create a myAccount and register your job under Jobs and Pensions, which stops emergency tax. If your number has not arrived by your first payday you will be taxed at the emergency rate and refunded later.
  • Find a GP: phone practices near your temporary address and ask if they are taking new patients. Many Dublin lists are closed, so expect several calls.
  • Learn the emergency numbers: 112 or 999 for emergencies, and the local GP out-of-hours service for urgent care at night and weekends.
  • Walk the areas you are considering at 8am and 8pm before you commit.
  • Tell your embassy you have arrived if your country asks citizens to register.

What you can and cannot do yet

You can work, sign a lease, use public transport and see a GP as a private patient from day one. You cannot yet open most traditional Irish bank accounts (they want a PPS number and an address), claim the Rent Tax Credit, or exchange your driving licence (the NDLS wants proof of your PPS number and address). All of that follows in the first 90 days.

  • MyWelfare: apply for a PPS number
  • ISD: register your permission for the first time
  • Revenue: starting your first job
  • TFI Leap Card
  • Residential Tenancies Board

articles.description: The 90-day mark is not arbitrary: it is the deadline on the landing stamp for non-EEA nationals to register with immigration, and it is roughly how long…
articles.previewHtml:
The 90-day mark is not arbitrary: it is the deadline on the landing stamp for non-EEA nationals to register with immigration, and it is roughly how long it takes a new arrival to go from a suitcase in a hostel to a settled address, a bank account, a tax record and a GP. This guide groups what needs doing into the three months, in the order that stops one task blocking another. It assumes you have done the first-week tasks (PPS application, immigration booking, property search). Figures are correct as of September 2026.

Month one: register, sign, connect

  1. Attend your PPS appointment. Bring the originals you uploaded. The number is posted to you afterwards; keep the letter, it is your proof of PPS number for the NDLS and banks.
  2. Attend your immigration registration at Burgh Quay, pay the €300 fee and wait for your Irish Residence Permit card in the post. Carry the card once it arrives.
  3. Sign your lease. Check the rent, the deposit (maximum one month), the notice periods and who pays which utilities. Ask for a written inventory with photos.
  4. Open an Irish bank account. Bring your passport, PPS number and proof of address. Give the IBAN to your employer for payroll.
  5. Register with Revenue on myAccount and add your job under Jobs and Pensions. If you were emergency taxed, the refund comes through payroll once you are registered.
  6. Set up utilities. Find the electricity meter number (MPRN) and gas meter number (GPRN) on the meters or the previous bills, then sign up with any supplier; comparison sites list the current offers. Order broadband; installation can take two weeks.
  7. Get an Eircode for your address from the Eircode finder and use it on every form; couriers and the HSE rely on it.
articles.gatedHtml:
Month two: health, money and driving

  1. Register with a GP. Phone practices near home until one accepts you. Private GP visits typically cost in the region of €50 to €80 in Dublin. Children under 8 and adults over 70 get a free GP visit card; others are means-tested, with a weekly net income limit of €418 for a single person living alone (rates set November 2023). Apply at medicalcard.ie.
  2. Decide on health insurance. Public hospital care is available to ordinarily resident people, but waiting lists are long. If you buy private cover, the Health Insurance Authority's comparison tool shows every plan, and new residents over 34 have a limited window before lifetime community rating loadings apply.
  3. Claim the Rent Tax Credit on myAccount: up to €1,000 a year for a single person and €2,000 for a jointly assessed couple in 2026. You will need your landlord's details and the RTB registration number.
  4. Buy a TV licence (€160 a year) if you have a television set; inspectors do call.
  5. Exchange your driving licence at the NDLS if it is from an EU/EEA state or a recognised state. The fee is €65, and you apply online with a verified MyGovID and Public Services Card or in person by appointment. If your licence is not exchangeable, book the driver theory test now; the wait for a driving test later is long.
  6. Apply for a Public Services Card at your Intreo centre; it upgrades your MyGovID to verified, which unlocks online driving licence renewals, Revenue services and more.

Month three: settle in

  1. Children: confirm school places, apply for the National Childcare Scheme subsidy through the NCS portal if you use registered childcare, and register children with a dentist; school-age children get free dental checks in certain classes.
  2. Register to vote through checktheregister.ie. Everyone resident in Ireland can vote in local elections, EU citizens can also vote in European elections, and British citizens can vote in Dáil elections.
  3. Car: if you brought a vehicle, it must be registered and Vehicle Registration Tax paid within 30 days of arrival, then taxed and insured; if you buy one, check the NCT status and motor tax. Read our Transportation guides.
  4. Pets: license your dog with your local authority and register the microchip to your Irish address.
  5. Employment rights: check your payslip shows PRSI class A; this builds your entitlement to Irish social insurance benefits.
  6. Pension: ask HR about the company scheme. Automatic enrolment into the state-backed MyFutureFund scheme began in 2026 for employees without a workplace pension.
  7. Community: join a sports club, a parkrun or a meetup. Irish social life runs through clubs and it is the fastest way to stop feeling like a visitor.

The 90-day tracker

TaskTargetCostDepends on
PPS number receivedWeek 3 to 6FreeAppointment attended
IRP card receivedWeek 4 to 8€300Registration appointment
Lease signed and RTB registeredWeek 2 to 6Deposit plus one monthReferences, funds
Bank account openWeek 4 to 8Free or small monthly feePPS number, address
Revenue registered, emergency tax refundedWeek 4 to 8FreePPS number
GP registeredWeek 4 to 10Free to joinAddress
Driving licence exchangedWeek 8 to 12€65PPS number, proof of address
Rent Tax Credit claimedWeek 8 to 12Free, worth up to €1,000Lease, RTB number

Watch out for

  • Do not let the 90-day registration deadline slip; if you cannot get an appointment in time, keep the booking confirmation as evidence that you tried.
  • Keep every letter with your name and address; each one is proof of address for the next form.
  • Rent increases once you are in a tenancy are capped at 2% a year or inflation, whichever is lower; if your landlord asks for more, contact the RTB or Threshold.

articles.title: Critical Skills Employment Permit: who qualifies and how to apply
articles.appTitle: Critical Skills Employment Permit: who qualifies and how to apply
articles.note: 2026 CSEP salary thresholds, occupations list, €1,000 fee, processing dates, family rights and Stamp 4 route.
articles.description: The Critical Skills Employment Permit (CSEP) is Ireland's flagship work permit for skilled non-EEA professionals. It is the fastest route to a Stamp 4…
articles.previewHtml:
The Critical Skills Employment Permit (CSEP) is Ireland's flagship work permit for skilled non-EEA professionals. It is the fastest route to a Stamp 4 permission, it lets your spouse or partner work without their own permit, and it skips the labour market needs test that slows down other permit types. This guide sets out the 2026 rules so you can check whether you qualify before you accept a job offer.

Who qualifies

You need a job offer from an employer registered in Ireland (not a recruitment agency) for at least 2 years. There are then two ways in. The first is a role on the Critical Skills Occupations List (CSOL) paying at least €40,904 a year. The second is any role that is not on the Ineligible Occupations List, paying at least €68,911. Both thresholds took effect on 1 March 2026, up from €38,000 and €64,000. If you graduated within the 12 months before you apply and the job is on the CSOL, a reduced threshold of €36,848 applies. Public sector critical skills roles follow the relevant pay agreement instead. Roles under €68,911 need a degree or higher; roles above it can rely on relevant experience.
articles.gatedHtml:
RouteMinimum annual salary (from 1 March 2026)Other conditions
Occupation on the Critical Skills Occupations List€40,904Degree or higher; 2-year job offer
CSOL role, qualified in the last 12 months€36,848Recognised qualification; 2-year job offer
Any eligible occupation (not on the Ineligible list)€68,911Degree or sufficient experience; 2-year job offer

Remuneration for the threshold means basic salary plus health insurance paid by the employer. Bonuses, overtime and allowances do not count.

Which occupations are on the list

The CSOL is published by the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (DETE) and reviewed periodically. As of September 2026 it covers roles in medicine, ICT, sciences, engineering, finance and business, including:

  • Programmers, software developers, web developers, IT business analysts, IT project managers and ICT directors
  • Civil, structural, mechanical, electrical, electronics, chemical and design engineers, plus site managers and project engineers
  • Medical practitioners, registered nurses and midwives, pharmacists, radiographers, physiotherapists, occupational therapists and speech and language therapists
  • Chemical, biological and physical scientists in manufacturing and biotech, and medical laboratory scientists
  • Chartered and certified accountants, tax specialists and data analytics consultants

Always download the current list from enterprise.gov.ie before you apply, because roles are added and removed after each review.

Fee, processing time and how to apply

Either you or your employer can submit the application through the Employment Permits Online portal. The fee is €1,000, and 90% is refunded if the application is refused or withdrawn. Your employer cannot deduct the fee from your pay. No labour market needs test is needed, so the employer does not have to advertise the role first. If refused, you can ask for a review within 28 days.

Processing is in date order. On 11 September 2026 DETE was working on CSEP applications received on 3 September 2026, so a complete application was taking roughly a week or two. Renewals and other categories were further behind, with renewal applications from 22 June 2026 being processed on the same date. Check the live processing dates page before you resign from your current job.

ItemFigure (September 2026)
Application fee€1,000 (90% refunded if refused)
Permit duration2 years
Current processing (new CSEP)Applications received 3 September 2026 being processed on 11 September 2026
IRP registration fee after arrival€300
Minimum time with first employer9 months

After you arrive: registration and changing jobs

The permit is not a residence permission on its own. Within 90 days of arrival you must register with Immigration Service Delivery and pay €300 for an Irish Residence Permit, which will show Stamp 1. Since the Employment Permits Act 2024 came into force on 2 September 2024, you must stay with your first employer for at least 9 months unless you are made redundant or the employment relationship changes fundamentally. After that you can move to a new employer with a fresh CSEP application.

Family reunification

CSEP holders can apply for immediate family reunification for a spouse, de facto partner and dependent children, without a waiting period. Once in Ireland, your spouse or partner registers for a Stamp 1G permission, which allows them to take any job without an employment permit. Time on Stamp 1G counts as reckonable residence for citizenship. Other dependants can apply for a Dependant, Partner or Spouse Employment Permit, which is free.

The path to Stamp 4 and citizenship

The permit is issued for 2 years. After 21 months of working on it you can apply directly to the Department of Justice for Stamp 4, which lets you work for any employer or run a business without a permit. No support letter from DETE has been required since 30 November 2023. Stamp 4 is granted for 2 years and is renewable. After 5 years of reckonable residence (with 1 continuous year immediately before applying) you can apply for naturalisation. Note that a bill proposed in September 2026 would extend the residence requirement to 8 years; it has not been enacted, so check the current rules when you are close to applying.

articles.title: General Employment Permit explained
articles.note: GEP salary floors from March 2026, labour market needs test, fees, duration, renewals and changing employer.
articles.description: The General Employment Permit (GEP) is the route for non-EEA workers whose job is not on the Critical Skills Occupations List but is not on the…
articles.previewHtml:
The General Employment Permit (GEP) is the route for non-EEA workers whose job is not on the Critical Skills Occupations List but is not on the Ineligible Occupations List either. It covers everything from chefs and healthcare assistants to construction workers and mid-level office roles. The trade-off is more paperwork: a labour market needs test, a lower salary floor, and a permit that ties you to one employer. Here is how it works in 2026.

Salary threshold

From 1 March 2026 the standard minimum salary for a GEP is €36,605 a year, up from €34,000. Lower thresholds apply in a few sectors and for recent graduates. Remuneration means basic pay plus employer-paid health insurance; board and accommodation can be included only if agreed in writing. The Government's December 2025 roadmap ties future increases to the national average earnings index, with further adjustments phased in through 2030, so expect the figure to rise again.
articles.gatedHtml:
CategoryMinimum salary (from 1 March 2026)
Standard General Employment Permit€36,605
Graduate of an Irish third-level institution within the last 12 months€34,009
Horticulture workers, meat processors, healthcare assistants and home support workers€32,691 (at least €16.12 per hour)
Salary at which the labour market needs test is waived€68,911

The labour market needs test

Before applying, your employer must show that no suitable Irish or EEA candidate was available. The role must be advertised on the Department of Social Protection's employment services and the EURES network, plus on an additional online platform. The test is not needed when:

  • The role is on the Critical Skills Occupations List
  • The salary is €68,911 or more
  • Enterprise Ireland or IDA Ireland has recommended the application
  • The job is a carer for a person with an established dependency
  • You are a permit holder made redundant within the last 6 months

The employer must also satisfy the 50:50 rule: at least half of its employees must be EEA nationals. Start-ups less than 2 years old backed by Enterprise Ireland or IDA Ireland, and companies where you would be the sole employee, can be exempt.

Fees and duration

Either you or the employer can apply through Employment Permits Online, and 90% of the fee is refunded if the application is refused or withdrawn. The employer cannot recoup the fee from your wages.

PermitDurationFee
New permit6 months or less€500
New permitMore than 6 months, up to 24 months€1,000
Renewal6 months or less€750
RenewalMore than 6 months, up to 36 months€1,500

A first GEP is issued for up to 24 months. It can then be renewed for up to a further 3 years. After 5 years of residence on employment permits you can apply to the Department of Justice for long-term residency, which grants a 5-year Stamp 4 without a permit. Processing is in strict date order: on 11 September 2026 DETE was processing new GEP applications received on 6 August 2026, about 5 weeks, while renewals were at 22 June 2026, closer to 12 weeks. Apply for renewal well before your permit runs out.

Registration and family

A permit is not a residence permission. Within 90 days of arriving you must register with Immigration Service Delivery and pay €300 for an Irish Residence Permit showing Stamp 1. Unlike the Critical Skills permit, a GEP does not give your spouse or partner a right to work: they are not eligible for the free Dependant, Partner or Spouse Employment Permit and would need their own permit. Family reunification is possible but only after you have been working here for 12 months and meet the income rules set by ISD.

Changing employer and losing your job

Under the Employment Permits Act 2024, in force since 2 September 2024, first-time permit holders must remain with their initial employer for 9 months. After that you can move, but the new employer must apply for a new GEP and the labour market needs test applies again unless an exemption fits. You can leave earlier if you are made redundant or if unforeseen circumstances fundamentally change the employment relationship. If you are made redundant, notify DETE within 4 weeks; you then have 6 months to find a new job and the needs test is waived for that application. Doctors on rotation in the public health system and transfers of undertakings are also treated as exceptions.

articles.title: Irish immigration stamps explained: Stamp 0 to Stamp 6
articles.appTitle: Irish immigration stamps explained: Stamp 0 to Stamp 6
articles.note: What every Irish stamp allows for work and study, and which ones count towards citizenship.
articles.description: Every non-EEA resident in Ireland holds an immigration permission that is recorded as a "stamp" on their Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card. The stamp…
articles.previewHtml:
Every non-EEA resident in Ireland holds an immigration permission that is recorded as a "stamp" on their Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card. The stamp number tells you what you can do: whether you can work, study or run a business, and whether the time counts towards citizenship. Reading the wrong stamp can cost you a job offer or years of reckonable residence, so it is worth knowing them all. The descriptions below follow the Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) definitions as published in September 2026.

The full list at a glance

StampWho gets itWork allowed?Counts for citizenship?
Stamp 0Retirees, dependent elderly relatives, visiting academicsNoNo
Stamp 1Employment permit holders, business owners, working holiday makersYes, per permit or ISD letterYes
Stamp 1ATrainee accountantsOnly the training contractNo
Stamp 1GThird Level Graduate Programme; spouses and partners of CSEP holders and hosted researchersYes, no permit neededYes
Stamp 1HDoctors on a 2-year Multi-Site General Employment PermitYes, in public hospitalsYes
Stamp 2Full-time students on ILEP coursesCasual: 20 hours per week in term, 40 in holidaysNo
Stamp 2AStudents on non-ILEP courses, semester abroad, private secondary schoolNoNo
Stamp 3Non-working spouses and dependants, volunteers, ministers of religionNoYes
Stamp 4Spouses of Irish citizens, CSEP holders after 21 months, refugees, long-term residents, investorsYes, any employer or self-employmentYes

Stamp 0: temporary and self-funded

Stamp 0 is for people of independent means, such as retirees, dependent adult relatives of residents, or visiting academics. You cannot work, claim benefits or use publicly funded services, and you must hold private health insurance. Crucially, Stamp 0 time does not count as reckonable residence for naturalisation, and it does not count towards long-term residency either.

Stamps 1, 1A, 1G and 1H: working permissions

Stamp 1 is the standard work stamp. You get it when you hold a General or Critical Skills Employment Permit, or a letter from ISD saying you may work without one. Working Holiday Authorisation holders also get Stamp 1, but that version cannot be renewed or changed. Stamp 1 is reckonable for citizenship. Stamp 1A is limited to full-time paid accountancy training and is not reckonable.

Stamp 1G has two uses. articles.note: Routes to Stamp 4, the 5-year long-term residency scheme, fees and the naturalisation timeline.
articles.description: Stamp 4 is the permission most non-EEA residents in Ireland are working towards. It cuts the link between your right to live here and a single employer…
articles.previewHtml:
Stamp 4 is the permission most non-EEA residents in Ireland are working towards. It cuts the link between your right to live here and a single employer, lets you set up a business, and keeps the citizenship clock running. This guide explains the main routes to Stamp 4, what the permission allows, how the long-term residency scheme works after 5 years on employment permits, and how the timeline runs on to naturalisation. Figures are correct for September 2026.

What Stamp 4 gives you

With Stamp 4 you can take up any job without an employment permit, work in a profession subject to the rules of the relevant professional body, and establish or run a business or be self-employed. You may access state services and benefits in line with your entitlements, and your time on Stamp 4 is fully reckonable for citizenship. Stamp 4 is granted for a set period, usually 1 to 3 years depending on the route, and must be renewed online before it expires. Each renewal costs the standard €300 IRP fee unless you are exempt, for example as the spouse of an Irish citizen.
articles.gatedHtml:
Routes to Stamp 4

RouteWhen you can applyInitial Stamp 4 duration
Critical Skills Employment Permit holderAfter 21 months working on the permit2 years, renewable
Long-term residency (any employment permits)After 60 months on Stamp 1 or Stamp 4 based on permits5 years
Spouse or civil partner of an Irish citizenOn approval of the application, if living together in IrelandSet by ISD, renewable
Stamp 1G holder (graduate or CSEP spouse)After 5 years on Stamp 1GSet by ISD
Refugee status or subsidiary protectionOn grant of status3 years, renewable
Parent of an Irish citizen childOn approval, subject to conditionsSet by ISD
Immigrant Investor Programme (closed to new applicants since 2023)Existing approvals onlySet by ISD

The Critical Skills route is the quickest for most skilled workers: the permit runs for 2 years and after 21 months you apply directly to Immigration Service Delivery for Stamp 4, with no support letter from the Department of Enterprise needed since 30 November 2023. General Employment Permit holders do not get this shortcut and rely on the long-term residency scheme instead.

Long-term residency after 5 years

The Long Term Residency scheme is for people who have completed at least 60 months of legal residence in Ireland on the strength of employment permits issued by the Department of Enterprise. If approved, you receive a Stamp 4 valid for 5 years, which lets you work without a further permit. The key rules as published by ISD are:

  • Residence is calculated from the stamps in your passport and the validity dates on your expired IRP cards, not from the dates on the permits themselves. Any gap without a stamp or valid card is not counted.
  • Only Stamp 1 granted on the basis of a work permit, and Stamp 4 granted to Critical Skills (formerly Green Card) holders, qualify. A mix of the two adding up to 60 months is fine.
  • Stamp 0, Stamp 1A, Stamp 1 under the Atypical Working Scheme, contract for services permits, Stamp 4 under the investor or start-up entrepreneur programmes, and Stamp 1 granted by the Minister for Justice to work without a permit do not count.
  • You must be of good character, must not have been an undue burden on the State and must not have breached your previous conditions.

Apply by post to the Domestic Residence and Permissions Division. If approved you are asked to pay a €500 fee within 28 days of the approval letter; miss that window and the file is closed. You then register the new permission online and pay the €300 IRP fee on top. There is no appeal against a refusal, but you can re-apply at any time. As of September 2026 ISD warns of high volumes and delays in acknowledging applications, so apply as soon as you pass 60 months and keep your existing permit renewed in the meantime.

The naturalisation timeline

Stamp 4 is not permanent residence, and it does not remove the need to renew. Most people treat it as the last stop before citizenship. Under the current Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act you need 5 years of reckonable residence in the previous 9, including 1 continuous year immediately before applying (3 years if you are married to or in a civil partnership with an Irish citizen). Time on Stamps 1, 1G, 1H, 3, 4 and 5 counts; time on Stamps 0, 1A, 2 and 2A does not.

StepCost or time (2026)
Naturalisation application fee€175
Median time to decision (Department of Justice, 2024 and 2025)About 8 months
Certificate fee, standard adult€950 (€200 for minors and widowed spouses of Irish citizens; nil for refugees and stateless applicants)
Citizenship ceremonyInvited after payment; 19 ceremonies were held in 2025 up to November

Be aware that in September 2026 the Government approved priority drafting of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship (Amendment) Bill 2026, which proposes raising the residence requirement to 8 years and adding language and civics tests. It has not been enacted, and how it would treat pending applications is not yet settled. If you are close to 5 years, check the current law and consider applying early.

  • Citizens Information: naturalisation

articles.note: Who qualifies via an Irish parent or grandparent, documents, €278 fee, 12-month wait and first passport.
articles.description: If you have an Irish-born parent or grandparent, you may already be entitled to Irish citizenship, and with it an EU passport, without ever living in…
articles.previewHtml:
If you have an Irish-born parent or grandparent, you may already be entitled to Irish citizenship, and with it an EU passport, without ever living in Ireland. The mechanism for most people is the Foreign Births Register (FBR), run by the Department of Foreign Affairs. This guide explains who qualifies, what documents you need, what it costs, how long it takes and what happens afterwards, with figures as published by the Department in September 2026.

Who is automatically a citizen

You are an Irish citizen from birth, with no application needed, if one of your parents was an Irish citizen at the time of your birth and was born on the island of Ireland. In that case you skip the FBR entirely and apply straight for a passport, using your own birth certificate and your parent's Irish birth certificate as proof.

Who qualifies through the Foreign Births Register

If you were born outside Ireland, you can become an Irish citizen by registering on the FBR if either:

  • One of your grandparents was born in Ireland, or
  • One of your parents was an Irish citizen at the time of your birth but was not born in Ireland, for example because they had themselves registered on the FBR or naturalised before you were born.
articles.gatedHtml:
Timing matters. Citizenship through the FBR takes effect from the date of registration, not from birth. That means if your parent registered on the FBR only after you were born, you cannot claim through them; you would need to rely on an Irish-born grandparent instead. It also means that if you register now and later have children, they will be entitled to register too, but only if you were on the register before they were born. Expectant parents should say so clearly on the application, and the Department advises contacting its customer service hub if the birth may come before the application is processed.

Documents you will need

The application is started online, then printed, signed in front of an approved witness and posted with original civil documents. The witness can be, for example, a solicitor, notary, peace commissioner, doctor, teacher, accountant, engineer, vet, bank manager or elected representative. As a guide, an adult applying through an Irish-born grandparent needs:

PersonDocuments (originals unless stated)
You, the applicantSigned and witnessed application form; civil birth certificate showing parents' details; marriage certificate or change of name document if applicable; certified copy of current photo ID; 2 separate original proofs of address; 4 colour photographs, 2 of them witnessed
Your Irish citizen parentCivil birth certificate showing their parents' details; marriage certificate or change of name document if applicable; certified copy of current photo ID, or civil death certificate if deceased
Your Irish-born grandparentCivil birth certificate showing their parents' details; marriage certificate or change of name document if applicable; certified copy of current photo ID, or civil death certificate if deceased

Church records and photocopies are not accepted in place of civil certificates. Irish civil birth, marriage and death records can be ordered from the General Register Office or through the HSE's civil registration service if you do not hold them. Incomplete applications are returned, and all originals are sent back to you at the end of the process.

Fees and processing time

ApplicantRegistration and certificatePostage and handlingTotal
Aged 18 or over€270€8 (non-refundable)€278
Under 18€145€8 (non-refundable)€153

Payment is made online when you submit the form. Applications are processed in strict date order and, as of September 2026, the Department says a completed FBR application takes approximately 12 months. Post is not acknowledged, so send your documents by recorded delivery. If more documentation is needed the Department will contact you, and the clock only really starts once the file is complete.

After registration: your first Irish passport

Once your name is entered on the register you are an Irish citizen and receive an FBR certificate. You can then apply for a passport through Passport Online, which accepts first-time adult applications from almost anywhere in the world. A standard 32-page adult passport costs €75. First-time applications cannot be expedited because every document is verified, and processing only begins once your supporting documents, including the FBR certificate, arrive, so allow several weeks on top of the online turnaround. Check the Passport Service's current turnaround times page before booking travel.

Other routes for people with Irish links

If your Irish connection is more distant than a grandparent, the FBR is not open to you, but the Minister for Justice can grant naturalisation on the basis of "Irish associations", usually meaning descent or adoption, at their discretion. People born on the island of Ireland before 1 January 2005 are Irish citizens automatically; those born later depend on their parents' status at the time of birth. Northern Ireland-born people are entitled to Irish citizenship on the same basis as anyone born in the Republic.

articles.appTitle: IRP appointments and current processing times
articles.note: First-time registration at Burgh Quay, online renewal, €300 fee, current waits and the 12-week grace rule.
articles.description: Your Irish Residence Permit (IRP) is the card that proves you are legally in Ireland, and almost every non-EEA resident staying longer than 90 days needs…
articles.previewHtml:
Your Irish Residence Permit (IRP) is the card that proves you are legally in Ireland, and almost every non-EEA resident staying longer than 90 days needs one. Getting the first card means an in-person appointment; keeping it means renewing online before it expires. Both stages have queues, and the waits change from month to month. This guide explains how the system works in September 2026, what it costs, and what your rights are if your card runs out while you wait.

Who must register and by when

If you are not a citizen of the EEA, the UK or Switzerland and you intend to stay in Ireland for more than 90 days, you must register your permission with Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) within 90 days of arrival. That covers workers, students, family members and anyone else granted a residence permission. Children under 16 do not need to register. ISD says that if you cannot get an appointment inside the 90 days your permission will not be cancelled and you will not be asked to leave, so the important thing is to have a booking.
articles.gatedHtml:
First-time registration: Dublin or anywhere else

Until early 2025, people living outside Dublin registered at their local Garda immigration office. That ended on 13 January 2025, when responsibility for all first-time registrations nationwide transferred to ISD. Wherever you live in the Republic, your first registration now happens in person at the ISD Registration Office, 13-14 Burgh Quay, Dublin 2. You book through your own ISD customer portal account, which anyone aged 16 or over must create with their own email address; you can set it up before you travel and book once you arrive. There is no fee to book, and no third party can get you a slot faster.

ItemFigure (September 2026)
Registration deadlineWithin 90 days of arrival
Where to register for the first timeISD Registration Office, Burgh Quay, Dublin (all counties)
Typical wait for a first-time appointmentNormally within 2 to 3 weeks (Citizens Information, page updated 18 August 2026)
Fee€300 per registration or renewal
Card delivery after a successful appointmentBy post, within about 10 working days (ISD)

Bring your passport, proof of your permission (for example your employment permit or college letter), proof of address and, where relevant, proof of private health insurance or of your relationship to the person you are joining. The fee is paid only when your registration is completed at the counter.

What it costs and who is exempt

The standard fee is €300 each time you register or renew. You pay nothing if you are under 18, have refugee status or subsidiary protection, have leave to remain under section 49 of the International Protection Act 2015, are resident on the basis of marriage to an Irish citizen, are the family member of an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or are a recognised victim of domestic abuse. On top of this, employment permit holders will already have paid their permit fee to the Department of Enterprise, so budget for both.

Renewing online

Renewals are done entirely online through the ISD portal: complete the form, upload scans of your passport photo page, both sides of your current IRP and the documents for your permission, pay the fee and note the reference number emailed to you. You can apply from 12 weeks before your current card expires, and no earlier. The new card is posted to you.

Processing times are published live on the ISD website and have moved a lot in 2026. In its notice of 30 June 2026, ISD said extra staff had brought certain renewal categories down to 6 to 8 weeks from application, with no category exceeding 16 weeks. Citizens Information, in its page updated 18 August 2026, still warned that some categories were taking more than 17 weeks. The safe assumption is 2 to 4 months, so apply on the first day the 12-week window opens.

If your card expires while you wait

Do not panic. Provided you applied to renew before your old card expired, you keep the conditions of your previous permission for up to 12 weeks after its expiry while ISD decides. articles.title: Ireland immigration in numbers: the latest statistics
articles.appTitle: Ireland immigration in numbers: the latest statistics
articles.note: CSO April 2026 migration estimates, 2025 permits by nationality and sector, and 2025 citizenship grants.
articles.description: Ireland's population passed 5.5 million in 2026, and migration is the main reason. If you are planning a move, the official numbers tell you a lot: who…
articles.previewHtml:
Ireland's population passed 5.5 million in 2026, and migration is the main reason. If you are planning a move, the official numbers tell you a lot: who is arriving, which nationalities are getting work permits, which sectors are hiring, and how many people are becoming citizens each year. This article pulls together the most recent releases from the Central Statistics Office (CSO), the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment and the Department of Justice, with the year each figure refers to.

Population and migration flows

The CSO's Population and Migration Estimates for April 2026, published on 24 August 2026, put the usually resident population at 5,525,600, up 66,900 or 1.2% in a year. Immigration fell for the second year running but remains high by historical standards, and net migration stayed strongly positive.

Indicator (year to April)20252026
Immigrants125,300110,600 (-12%)
Emigrants65,60062,500 (-5%)
Net migration59,70048,100
Natural increase (births minus deaths)n/a18,800
Total population changen/a+66,900 (+1.2%)
articles.gatedHtml:
Of the 110,600 people who arrived in the year to April 2026, 30,200 were returning Irish citizens (down 4%), 20,700 were other EU citizens (down 18%), 4,300 were UK citizens (down 12%) and 55,500 came from the rest of the world (down 13%). Immigrants are young: 53% (58,300) were aged 25 to 44 and 19% were children under 15. On the way out, 35,400 of the 62,500 emigrants were Irish citizens, a reminder that the country has two-way traffic. The CSO also notes that the population aged 0 to 14 fell below one million for the first time since 2014, while those aged 65 and over reached 891,100, or 16.1% of the total.

Employment permits: who is coming to work

The Department of Enterprise publishes permit statistics monthly, with annual tables released each January. Its 2025 tables, published on 2 January 2026, show 31,044 permits issued in 2025 and 3,432 refused. That is a drop of about 21% from the record 39,390 issued in 2024, driven mainly by a fall in health and ICT permits. India remains far ahead of every other source country.

NationalityPermits issued 2025Refused 2025
India9,947807
Philippines3,398335
Brazil3,381522
China1,922215
Pakistan1,453186
South Africa1,240209
United States1,03980
Zimbabwe831138
Nigeria726156
Sri Lanka63168
All nationalities31,0443,432

Indian nationals took roughly one permit in three. For comparison, in 2024 the top five were India (13,566), Brazil (4,553), the Philippines (4,049), China (1,962) and Pakistan (1,742), so the Philippines overtook Brazil in 2025 while both fell.

Which sectors hire permit holders

The sector tables for 2025 show health and social work still on top despite a sharp fall, with hospitality, ICT, construction and other services making up the rest of the top five.

SectorPermits issued 20252024
Health and social work7,94812,501
Accommodation and food services3,499n/a
Information and communication3,6306,788
Construction2,031n/a
Other service activities2,087n/a
Agriculture, forestry and fishing1,9152,990
Financial and insurance1,424n/a
Transport and storage1,363n/a

Healthcare assistants, care workers and home carers alone accounted for more than 12% of all permits in 2025. In 2024, just over half of new permits were Critical Skills permits, with an average salary of €58,746 for those roles. Monthly figures for 2026 are on the Department's statistics page and are worth checking if you are targeting a specific sector.

Citizenship and naturalisation

Naturalisation has accelerated sharply. The Department of Justice reports that it received 40,479 citizenship applications in 2025, granted 26,400 and refused 377. That follows more than 30,000 decisions in 2024, itself a record, and around 20,000 in 2023. The median processing time to a decision was about 8 months in both 2024 and 2025, down from 15 months in 2023 and 19 months in 2022. Ceremonies, where certificates are handed over, numbered 24 in 2024 and 19 in 2025 up to November.

What the numbers mean for you

  • Competition for permits is highest from India, the Philippines and Brazil, but refusal rates are modest across the board: about 1 in 10 applications overall in 2025.
  • Health, hospitality, ICT and construction are the sectors most used to sponsoring non-EEA staff, which usually means smoother HR processes.
  • Immigration is falling from its 2024 peak, which in a housing-constrained market may ease rental competition slightly, though the population is still growing by over 1% a year.
  • Citizenship decisions are now measured in months rather than years, so the 5-year residence clock is the real bottleneck, not the queue.

  • European Migration Network Ireland
