articles.title: Obtain Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card
articles.description: The Irish Residence Permit (IRP), formerly known as GNIB card, is a document that proves a non-European Union (EU) national's right to live and work in…
articles.previewHtml:
The Irish Residence Permit (IRP), formerly known as GNIB card, is a document that proves a non-European Union (EU) national's right to live and work in Ireland. It is a requirement for non-EU nationals who plan to stay in Ireland for more than 90 days.

Why is an IRP Card Necessary in Ireland?

The IRP Card serves as a form of identification for non-EU nationals in Ireland and is needed for various purposes, such as opening a bank account, accessing healthcare, or enrolling in school. It also provides evidence of a person's immigration status in Ireland and allows them to work and live in the country legally.

Who requires an Irish Residence Permit (IRP)?

As you are a non-EU/EEA and non-Swiss citizen, and you want to stay in Ireland for any reason for longer than 90 days, you must apply for immigration permission and, if successful, then register.
articles.gatedHtml:
If your registration is successful, you will be issued with an IRP.

To register, you must:

  • be a non-EU/EEA and non-Swiss national
  • be aged 16 or older
  • go to a registration office in-person
  • If you want to stay in Ireland past the expiry date on your IRP, you must apply to extend your immigration permission and renew your registration. If successful, you will be given a new IRP.

An IRP costs €300 per person every time you register and renew.

You may also have to pay for a new IRP if your current card is lost or stolen.

How to apply for an IRP Card in Ireland?

To get an Irish Residence Permit, you must be allowed to be in Ireland in the first place. Once you receive your Ireland visa, you can travel to Ireland, where you’ll be required to pass through Border Control and request for permission to stay. If the immigration officers at the Border Control allow you to enter, they will put a stamp on your passport which shows how long you can stay in Ireland for.

Every non-EU/EEA national is only allowed a maximum stay of 90 days if they have not received an Irish residence permit. So, before the days stated on your passport stamp are up, you must make an Ireland Residence Permit appointment.

★ Important info

  • The Ireland visa is simply a pre-entry requirement. Both visas only allow the holder to stay in Ireland for a maximum of 90 days.

However, to be able to apply for an Ireland residence permit, you must have an Irish long stay (D) visa. You cannot apply for residency with a short stay (C) visa.

Where you submit your application for an Irish residence permit depends on your place of residence. As such:

If you live in Dublin, you must schedule an online appointment and show up in person to register at the Burgh Quay Registration Office.

If you live outside Dublin, you must contact your nearest Garda station (registration office) for an appointment and show up in person.

How long it takes to obtain an IRP Card?

If you are a Dublin resident and apply online, you will receive your IRP card within approximately 10 working days of processing your application. If you are attending a registration office outside of Dublin, the Immigration Officer will advise you how you will receive your Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card.

The Irish Residence Permit registration process

The process for obtaining an Irish Residence Permit (IRP) involves a visit to a registration appointment. During this appointment, an immigration officer will examine your documents and immigration status (e.g., work authorization). They will then compile your information and place a stamp on your card.

The IRP stamp in your card will indicate the activities you are authorized to engage in while in Ireland, including work or study.

★ Useful links

  • The process and required documents will vary according to the stamp you will apply.
  • Follow this page to get the most recent information:

https://www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-register-your-immigration-permission-for-the-first-time/

articles.title: Open bank account
articles.description: If you're moving to Ireland and want to open a bank account, there are several steps you can follow:
articles.previewHtml:
If you're moving to Ireland and want to open a bank account, there are several steps you can follow:

Research the different banks operating in Ireland: Some of the largest banks in Ireland include AIB, Bank of Ireland, Permanent TSB. There are some fresh digital-only financial institutions, such as Revolut and N26, that are vying with conventional banks. Most banks in Ireland impose transaction fees or administrative charges on their current accounts.

Check if you meet the eligibility criteria: Most banks in Ireland require that you have a valid form of identification, proof of address, and proof of income. You may also need to provide proof of your eligibility to reside and work in Ireland.

Gather the necessary documentation: You'll need to bring along your passport or national ID card, proof of address (such as a utility bill), proof of income (such as a recent payslip), and any other documents that may be required by the bank you choose.
articles.gatedHtml:
Decide a type of account: Most banks offer a range of accounts, including current accounts, savings accounts, and credit card accounts. Consider your specific needs and select the account that is best for you.

Open the account: You can typically open a bank account by visiting a branch of the bank you've selected. During your visit, you'll need to provide the necessary documentation and fill out any required forms. If you’ve selected an online banking, you can do open the account online. N26 opens your account in 8 minutes.

Activate your account: After your account is opened, you'll receive an ATM card or debit card, as well as other information about how to activate and use your account.

★ Tip

  • Note that different banks may have different requirements, so it's a good idea to check with the specific bank you're interested in before making a visit. Compare current account fees and benefits with Bonkers.ie. Find the account that’s right for you.

Editor’s Choice

If you don't require in-person access to a bank branch, don't need to deposit checks, and don't plan to deposit cash, a free account with Revolut or N26 would suffice, and they both offer their services at no cost.

If you believe you'll need to deposit both cash and checks, consider having both an account with EBS and one with N26 or Revolut. Keep in mind that you won't receive a checkbook from either account. Both accounts are free to maintain.

The EBS account can be used for withdrawing funds at ATMs, depositing cash, and checks. You can use the N26 or Revolut debit card for transactions such as Apple Pay, Google Pay, and free purchases made in currencies besides the euro. Your salary can be deposited into either bank, and you can transfer money between them as needed.

Additionally, having multiple bank accounts reduces the risk of having no access to funds in the event of IT issues with your bank or card provider.

Note: EBS is a subsidiary of AIB group, and they announced in January 2022 that they were undergoing “a number of strategic changes that build on the current proposition.” It is possible that EBS may eventually close current accounts and focus solely on mortgages.

articles.title: The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion for US expats
articles.appTitle: The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion for U.S. Expats
articles.note: Special content for US citizens 🇺🇸
articles.description: As you are a US citizen, you must file both your US taxes and your Republic of Ireland taxes, but may claim the Foreign Earned Income exclusion.
articles.previewHtml:
As you are a US citizen, you must file both your US taxes and your Republic of Ireland taxes, but may claim the Foreign Earned Income exclusion.

The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE) can be a lifesaver for U.S. expats looking to reduce their tax burden. It allows eligible individuals to exclude all or part of their foreign earned income from U.S. taxes.

However, it's important to understand the details before claiming the FEIE:

  • The FEIE can lead to substantial savings on your U.S. taxes if utilized properly.
  • It's not a one-size-fits-all solution, as certain foreign income may or may not be excluded.
  • Eligibility for the FEIE is not automatic, you need to meet specific criteria and file Form 2555.
  • The FEIE is just one of the many tax relief options available to you. Consult a Tax Advisor to determine the best option for your situation.

Which foreign earnings are eligible for exclusion with the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE)?

The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion can be a great way to lower your U.S. tax burden when you work abroad, but it only covers certain types of income. Earned income such as salaries, wages, bonuses, commissions, and self-employment income are eligible for exclusion, but passive income like interest and dividends are not. To be considered foreign earned income, the income must be earned outside the United States.
articles.gatedHtml:
Who is eligible for the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion?

To be eligible for the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion, you must have lived abroad for a specified duration within the tax year. If you have recently relocated to a foreign country or returned to the U.S. during the year, you may still qualify for partial-year exclusions.

Expats who meet either of the following criteria may qualify for the FEIE:

  • Employment outside the U.S. by a U.S. or non-U.S. employer
  • Self-employment or partnership work outside the U.S.
  • Satisfaction of either the Bona Fide Residency Test or Physical Presence Test


Please note, employees of the U.S. government are not eligible for the foreign income exclusion. However, those employed by private companies under contract with the government may still be qualified.

Meet the Bona Fide Residency Test

To meet the requirements for the Bona Fide Residency Test, you need to show a stronger connection to your foreign country of residence compared to the US. This means you must reside there uninterrupted for a full tax year, intending to continue to reside there even after returning to the US temporarily. To qualify, you must:

  • Be a US citizen or resident alien of a country with a tax treaty with the US.
  • Have active income sources such as salary or self-employment income. Passive income like pensions or dividends are not eligible.
  • Spend more than a year working abroad.
  • Have a permanent place of work in your foreign country of residence.

Even if you haven't met the Bona Fide Residency Test for a full tax year, you may still be eligible for partial-year exclusions if you've lived abroad for a full tax year in the past.

Meet the Physical Presence Test

To meet the Physical Presence Test, you need to show that you have been physically residing outside the U.S. for 330 complete days within a 12-month period. Keep in mind that a full day is calculated as 24 hours starting from midnight, and you need to be present in the foreign country for the entire 24 hours.

How much of my foreign income can be excluded?

The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion allows eligible U.S. expats to exclude a portion of their foreign earned income from U.S. taxes. The maximum exclusion amount is adjusted annually for inflation and in 2022, it was $108,700, and it was increased to $112,000 in 2023. If you incurred housing costs, you may be able to exclude more. If you and your spouse both meet either the Bona Fide Residency Test or the Physical Presence Test, both of you can claim the FEIE individually.

Foreign Earned Income Exclusion vs. Foreign Tax Credit

It is crucial to make a well-informed decision when deciding between the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion and the Foreign Tax Credit. Changing your choice from the exclusion to the credit and back to the exclusion again within a five-year period will not be possible without a complicated and costly process with the IRS. Working with an experienced expat tax advisor can provide valuable guidance in making this decision.

Choosing the Foreign Tax Credit and filing Form 1116 may be a more favorable option if:

  • You are paying foreign taxes at a rate that is higher than your U.S. tax rate
  • You want to participate in an individual retirement account (IRA)
  • You are eligible for certain family-related credits based on non-excluded income
  • You intend to exclude or minimize taxes on passive or investment income.

Common issues faced by American expatriates with the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion and Form 2555

Many American expats face similar questions and challenges when it comes to filing for the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE). Here are the most frequent issues encountered with the FEIE:

Not filing Form 2555: Some expats believe that the FEIE will automatically be included in their tax filing if they qualify. However, it is necessary to file Form 2555 to claim the FEIE.

Being a government employee: Regrettably, U.S. government employees are not eligible to claim the foreign income exclusion.

Incorrect calculation of the FEIE: If you miscalculate the FEIE, you may not receive the correct amount of exclusion, leading to inaccuracies in your tax filing.

Claiming the FEIE instead of the Foreign Tax Credit (FTC): For instance, if you are retired abroad and your income is solely from investments and passive sources, claiming the FTC may be more beneficial.

Inadequate tracking of time: To pass the Bona Fide Residency or Physical Presence tests, it's essential to keep an accurate record of your time spent abroad. Even a minor deviation from the required hours could impact your eligibility for the FEIE.

Lack of active income for the year: If your income is solely from investments or passive sources while living abroad, you won't qualify for the FEIE.

Neglecting to pay U.S. self-employment taxes: Even if you're claiming the FEIE, you're still required to pay U.S. self-employment taxes.

Last Words

In conclusion, the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion and Form 2555 can be complex and challenging for U.S. expats. Whether it's determining eligibility, navigating the calculation, completing the form, or keeping up with changes in tax law, many expats face significant hurdles when claiming the FEIE. For this reason, many expats choose to work with professional tax advisors to help them through the process, and to ensure that they are maximizing their tax savings while staying compliant with all relevant regulations.

As you are a US citizen, you must file both your US taxes and your Republic of Ireland taxes, but may claim the Foreign Earned Income exclusion.

The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE) can be a lifesaver for U.S. expats looking to reduce their tax burden. It allows eligible individuals to exclude all or part of their foreign earned income from U.S. taxes.

However, it's important to understand the details before claiming the FEIE:

The FEIE can lead to substantial savings on your U.S. taxes if utilized properly.It's not a one-size-fits-all solution, as certain foreign income may or may not be excluded.Eligibility for the FEIE is not automatic, you need to meet specific criteria and file Form 2555.The FEIE is just one of the many tax relief options available to you. Consult a Tax Advisor to determine the best option for your situation.

Which foreign earnings are eligible for exclusion with the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE)?

The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion can be a great way to lower your U.S. tax burden when you work abroad, but it only covers certain types of income. Earned income such as salaries, wages, bonuses, commissions, and self-employment income are eligible for exclusion, but passive income like interest and dividends are not. To be considered foreign earned income, the income must be earned outside the United States.

Who is eligible for the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion?

To be eligible for the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion, you must have lived abroad for a specified duration within the tax year. If you have recently relocated to a foreign country or returned to the U.S. during the year, you may still qualify for partial-year exclusions.Expats who meet either of the following criteria may qualify for the FEIE:

Employment outside the U.S. by a U.S. or non-U.S. employerSelf-employment or partnership work outside the U.S.Satisfaction of either the Bona Fide Residency Test or Physical Presence Test

Please note, employees of the U.S. government are not eligible for the foreign income exclusion. However, those employed by private companies under contract with the government may still be qualified.

Meet the Bona Fide Residency Test

To meet the requirements for the Bona Fide Residency Test, you need to show a stronger connection to your foreign country of residence compared to the US. This means you must reside there uninterrupted for a full tax year, intending to continue to reside there even after returning to the US temporarily. To qualify, you must:

Be a US citizen or resident alien of a country with a tax treaty with the US.Have active income sources such as salary or self-employment income. Passive income like pensions or dividends are not eligible.Spend more than a year working abroad.Have a permanent place of work in your foreign country of residence.

Even if you haven't met the Bona Fide Residency Test for a full tax year, you may still be eligible for partial-year exclusions if you've lived abroad for a full tax year in the past.

Meet the Physical Presence Test

To meet the Physical Presence Test, you need to show that you have been physically residing outside the U.S. for 330 complete days within a 12-month period. Keep in mind that a full day is calculated as 24 hours starting from midnight, and you need to be present in the foreign country for the entire 24 hours.

How much of my foreign income can be excluded?

The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion allows eligible U.S. expats to exclude a portion of their foreign earned income from U.S. taxes. The maximum exclusion amount is adjusted annually for inflation and in 2022, it was $108,700, and it was increased to $112,000 in 2023. If you incurred housing costs, you may be able to exclude more. If you and your spouse both meet either the Bona Fide Residency Test or the Physical Presence Test, both of you can claim the FEIE individually.

Foreign Earned Income Exclusion vs. Foreign Tax Credit

It is crucial to make a well-informed decision when deciding between the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion and the Foreign Tax Credit. Changing your choice from the exclusion to the credit and back to the exclusion again within a five-year period will not be possible without a complicated and costly process with the IRS. Working with an experienced expat tax advisor can provide valuable guidance in making this decision.

Choosing the Foreign Tax Credit and filing Form 1116 may be a more favorable option if:

You are paying foreign taxes at a rate that is higher than your U.S. tax rateYou want to participate in an individual retirement account (IRA)You are eligible for certain family-related credits based on non-excluded incomeYou intend to exclude or minimize taxes on passive or investment income.

Common issues faced by American expatriates with the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion and Form 2555

Many American expats face similar questions and challenges when it comes to filing for the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE). Here are the most frequent issues encountered with the FEIE:

Not filing Form 2555: Some expats believe that the FEIE will automatically be included in their tax filing if they qualify. However, it is necessary to file Form 2555 to claim the FEIE.

Being a government employee: Regrettably, U.S. government employees are not eligible to claim the foreign income exclusion.

Incorrect calculation of the FEIE: If you miscalculate the FEIE, you may not receive the correct amount of exclusion, leading to inaccuracies in your tax filing.

Claiming the FEIE instead of the Foreign Tax Credit (FTC): For instance, if you are retired abroad and your income is solely from investments and passive sources, claiming the FTC may be more beneficial.

Inadequate tracking of time: To pass the Bona Fide Residency or Physical Presence tests, it's essential to keep an accurate record of your time spent abroad. Even a minor deviation from the required hours could impact your eligibility for the FEIE.

Lack of active income for the year: If your income is solely from investments or passive sources while living abroad, you won't qualify for the FEIE.

Neglecting to pay U.S. self-employment taxes: Even if you're claiming the FEIE, you're still required to pay U.S. self-employment taxes.

Last Words

In conclusion, the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion and Form 2555 can be complex and challenging for U.S. expats. Whether it's determining eligibility, navigating the calculation, completing the form, or keeping up with changes in tax law, many expats face significant hurdles when claiming the FEIE. For this reason, many expats choose to work with professional tax advisors to help them through the process, and to ensure that they are maximizing their tax savings while staying compliant with all relevant regulations.

articles.description: As a US citizen or green card holder living abroad, you have an obligation to report your foreign financial accounts to the U.S. government. The Foreign…
articles.previewHtml: As a US citizen or green card holder living abroad, you have an obligation to report your foreign financial accounts to the U.S. government. The Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts Report (FBAR) is a way for the government to track these foreign accounts and ensure that U.S. taxpayers are reporting their foreign income and paying the appropriate taxes. Failing to file an FBAR can result in severe penalties, so it’s important to understand your FBAR obligation if you’re a U.S. expat.
articles.gatedHtml:
What is an FBAR?

The FBAR is an annual report that is required for any U.S. person who has a financial interest in, or signature authority over, foreign financial accounts with an aggregate value of $10,000 or more at any time during the calendar year. The FBAR is filed with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and must be filed by June 30 of the year following the calendar year for which the report is required. For example, if you had foreign financial accounts with a total value of $10,000 or more during the calendar year 2022, your FBAR for that year must be filed by June 30, 2023.

What types of accounts must be reported on the FBAR?

The FBAR must include any foreign financial accounts that you have a financial interest in or signature authority over. This includes, but is not limited to, foreign bank accounts, investment accounts, mutual funds, and life insurance policies with cash value. It’s important to note that the FBAR is not a tax form, but rather a report of your foreign financial accounts to the U.S. government.

Who must file an FBAR?

U.S. citizens, U.S. residents, and entities (such as corporations and partnerships) that are formed in the U.S. or under U.S. law must file an FBAR if they have a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts with an aggregate value of $10,000 or more at any time during the calendar year. This includes U.S. expats living abroad and U.S. residents with foreign financial accounts.

What happens if I don’t file an FBAR?

Failing to file an FBAR can result in severe penalties. If the failure to file is considered non-willful, you could face a fine of up to $10,000 per year. If the failure to file is considered willful, you could face a fine of up to $100,000 or 50% of the account balance, whichever is greater, per year. In some cases, you could also face criminal penalties, including imprisonment.

How do I file an FBAR?

The FBAR can be filed electronically through the BSA E-Filing System website. The process is straightforward and simple, and the website provides step-by-step instructions to help you complete the form. In addition, you may need to file additional forms, such as Form 8938, if you have a foreign financial asset with a value that exceeds the threshold established by the U.S. government.

In conclusion, understanding your FBAR obligation is crucial if you’re a U.S. expat. Failing to file an FBAR can result in severe penalties, so it’s important to ensure that you’re reporting your foreign financial accounts accurately and on time. If you require any further assistance about the FBAR or your tax obligations as a U.S. expat, it’s a good idea to speak with a tax professional.

https://bsaefiling.fincen.treas.gov/main.html

articles.title: Proof of address
articles.description: Moving to a new country can come with many challenges, including the process of proving your residence. One of the biggest hurdles faced by those…
articles.previewHtml: Moving to a new country can come with many challenges, including the process of proving your residence. One of the biggest hurdles faced by those settling in Ireland is demonstrating their Irish residential address to meet the stringent requirements of local banks. Here are a few strategies to help simplify this process.
articles.gatedHtml:
One option is to request your employer provide an employment confirmation letter that includes your current Irish address. This letter should be printed on the company's official letterhead, making it a credible and trustworthy form of proof.

Another option is to sign up for health insurance as soon as you arrive in Ireland, or even before you arrive if you already have an Irish address to receive your mail. Once you become a member, the insurance company will send you a membership letter, which serves as evidence of your Irish address.

Furthermore, any document which includes your address from government office like PPS approval or statement letter from Revenue.ie is acceptable.

By taking these steps, you can increase your chances of providing acceptable proof of your Irish residential address to banks and other organizations.
articles.plainText:
Moving to a new country can come with many challenges, including the process of proving your residence. One of the biggest hurdles faced by those settling in Ireland is demonstrating their Irish residential address to meet the stringent requirements of local banks. Here are a few strategies to help simplify this process.

One option is to request your employer provide an employment confirmation letter that includes your current Irish address. This letter should be printed on the company's official letterhead, making it a credible and trustworthy form of proof.

Another option is to sign up for health insurance as soon as you arrive in Ireland, or even before you arrive if you already have an Irish address to receive your mail. Once you become a member, the insurance company will send you a membership letter, which serves as evidence of your Irish address.

Furthermore, any document which includes your address from government office like PPS approval or statement letter from Revenue.ie is acceptable.

By taking these steps, you can increase your chances of providing acceptable proof of your Irish residential address to banks and other organizations.

articles.title: How long does a PPS number take?
articles.appTitle: How long does a PPS number take?
articles.note: The MyWelfare process, documents, realistic timelines in 2026 and what you can do while you wait.
articles.description: Your Personal Public Service (PPS) number is the key that opens almost every other door in Ireland: payroll, Revenue, the public health system, a bank…
articles.previewHtml:
Your Personal Public Service (PPS) number is the key that opens almost every other door in Ireland: payroll, Revenue, the public health system, a bank account, a driving licence. So the first question most new arrivals ask is how long it takes. The honest answer is that the Department of Social Protection does not publish a processing time, and the total wait is made up of two parts you can influence and one you cannot. This guide explains the process step by step, what documents you need, how long each stage tends to take as of September 2026, and what you can get on with while you wait.

The three stages of the wait

StageWhat happensHow long
1. Online applicationYou apply on MyWelfare.ie with a MyGovID, upload documents and choose an appointment slotAbout 20 minutes, once you are in Ireland
2. In-person appointmentYou attend a PPS Number Allocation Centre with your original documents so staff can verify your identityDepends on slot availability at your chosen centre; days to several weeks at busy centres
3. Post-appointment checks and letterThe Department completes further checks and posts your number to your addressNo official timeframe published; relocation guides in 2026 report a few weeks in most cases
articles.gatedHtml:
The Department's own wording is worth quoting: "During the in-person appointment, your application will not be processed immediately. If approved, your PPS number will be sent to you via post at a later date." Plan on the whole process taking several weeks from arrival, and treat anything faster as a bonus.

Step 1: apply online on MyWelfare

You must be aged 18 or over and physically in Ireland (or Northern Ireland) to apply as a resident. You cannot apply in advance from abroad on the grounds that you are about to move. Create a basic MyGovID account if you have not already, log into MyWelfare.ie, choose "Apply for a PPS number", and fill in the form. You will be asked why you need the number; acceptable reasons include taking up employment, registering for a course, applying for or exchanging a driving licence, accessing public health services and registering the birth of a child. You then pick a location, date and time for your appointment. If you are applying for a child as well, you can do both in one application, and the child must also attend.

Step 2: the documents you need

Bring originals to the appointment; uploads alone are not enough. You need proof of identity, proof of address and proof of the reason you need the number.

Proof of identityProof of address (dated within 3 months)Reason for the number
Non-EU citizens: current passport or 1951 travel documentHousehold utility billJob offer or employment contract
EU/EEA citizens: current passport or national identity cardBank statementLetter of acceptance from a school or college
UK citizens: current passport, or birth certificate plus full driving licenceProperty lease or tenancy agreementLetter from a government body or a specified body asking for it
Irish citizens: passport, or Irish/UK driving licenceOfficial letter from a government department, or confirmation of address from a hotel, hostel, landlord or school; if staying with friends, their bill plus a signed noteEvidence of a driving licence application, a birth registration, or similar

Other documents that help staff confirm your identity, if you have them: a medical card, a European Health Insurance Card, a debit card with a statement, a student card, or a Revenue document.

Step 3: after the appointment

The officer verifies your documents and photographs you, and your application goes for further checks. The number is posted to the address you gave, so use an address where you will still be receiving mail in a few weeks; a friend's or your employer's address is fine if they agree. Once you have it, it is yours for life. There is no card at this stage; if you later want a Public Services Card, that is a separate application at an Intreo centre and it upgrades your MyGovID to verified.

What you can do while you wait

  • Start work. You do not need the number to start a job. Give it to your employer when it arrives. Until then you will be on emergency tax, which is refunded through payroll once Revenue has your details.
  • Register with Revenue as soon as the number arrives. Create a myAccount and register the job under Jobs and Pensions; this is what triggers your tax credits and the emergency tax refund.
  • Rent a home. Landlords do not need your PPS number to sign a lease.
  • Open a fintech account. Several online banks accept a passport and a foreign address; traditional Irish banks will generally want the PPS number.
  • Book immigration registration. The IRP process is separate and does not wait for the PPS number.
  • See a GP privately and buy a Leap Card, a SIM and a TV licence.

Special cases

People who arrived from Ukraine under the Temporary Protection Directive should not apply online; the Department asks them to go directly to a PPS Number Allocation Centre, where a dedicated arrangement applies. People living outside Ireland who need a number for an Irish matter (for example probate or Revenue) can apply online or by post, but this route is not available to people who intend to move here. Children born in Ireland get a number automatically when the birth is registered. If you think you may already have a number from an earlier stay, contact Client Identity Services on 0818 927 999 before applying, because you cannot be issued a second one.

★ Useful links

  • Revenue: starting your first job
  • MyGovID

articles.title: Salary after tax in Ireland: what you actually take home
articles.appTitle: Salary after tax in Ireland: what you actually take home
articles.note: How income tax, USC and PRSI reduce your gross pay in 2026, with worked examples for €35k, €50k and €80k.
articles.description: The salary in your job offer is a gross figure. Before it reaches your bank account, three separate deductions come off it: income tax, the Universal…
articles.previewHtml:
The salary in your job offer is a gross figure. Before it reaches your bank account, three separate deductions come off it: income tax, the Universal Social Charge (USC) and Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI). Newcomers often overestimate their net pay because they only budget for income tax, or underestimate it because they have heard Ireland's 40% rate and assume it applies to everything. This guide walks through the three deductions using the 2026 rates and gives you worked examples for three common salaries. All figures apply to the 2026 tax year as set out in Budget 2026 (announced in October 2025).

Deduction 1: income tax

Ireland has two income tax rates. For a single person in 2026 the first €44,000 of income is taxed at 20% and everything above that at 40%. Married couples and civil partners get a wider standard rate band: €53,000 for one income, or up to €88,000 where both partners earn (a maximum of €44,000 per person). Single parents who qualify for the Single Person Child Carer Credit get €48,000.
articles.gatedHtml:
Once the tax is calculated, tax credits are subtracted from it euro for euro. Almost every employee gets two: the Personal Tax Credit of €2,000 and the Employee (PAYE) Tax Credit of €2,000. Together they wipe out the first €4,000 of tax, which is why a single person pays no income tax at all on the first €20,000 of earnings. Renters can add the Rent Tax Credit of up to €1,000, and there are further credits for carers, single parents and some medical expenses.

Deduction 2: USC

USC is a separate charge on gross income and no tax credits reduce it. If you earn €13,000 or less in the year you are exempt. Above that, the whole of your income is charged in bands: 0.5% on the first €12,012, 2% from €12,013 to €28,700, 3% from €28,701 to €70,044 and 8% on anything above €70,044. Budget 2026 widened the 2% band from €27,382 to €28,700 so that a full-time minimum wage worker stays out of the 3% band.

Deduction 3: PRSI

PRSI is Ireland's social insurance contribution and it funds the State Pension, Jobseeker's Benefit, Maternity Benefit, Illness Benefit and other payments. Most private and public sector employees are in Class A. The employee rate is 4.2% of gross pay from 1 January 2026, rising to 4.35% from 1 October 2026. If you earn €352 or less in a week you pay nothing, and a tapered credit of up to €12 a week softens the charge for anyone earning between €352.01 and €424 a week. Your employer pays a separate, larger contribution on top of your salary that never appears in your deductions.

Worked examples for 2026

The table below assumes a single employee with only the personal and employee credits, paid evenly through the year, and uses the 4.2% PRSI rate that applies from January to September 2026. Because the rate rises to 4.35% in October, the annual PRSI figure will be roughly €13 higher on €35,000, €19 higher on €50,000 and €30 higher on €80,000 across the full year. Figures are rounded to the nearest euro.

Gross salaryIncome taxUSCPRSI (4.2%)Annual netMonthly net
€35,000€3,000€583€1,470€29,947€2,496
€50,000€7,200€1,033€2,100€39,667€3,306
€80,000€19,200€2,431€3,360€55,009€4,584

Look at how the €35,000 case works. Income tax is 20% of €35,000, which is €7,000, minus €4,000 in credits, leaving €3,000. USC is 0.5% of €12,012 (€60) plus 2% of the next €16,688 (€334) plus 3% of the final €6,300 (€189), a total of €583. PRSI is 4.2% of €35,000, or €1,470. The overall deduction rate is a little over 14%.

At €50,000 the first €44,000 is taxed at 20% (€8,800) and the remaining €6,000 at 40% (€2,400), less €4,000 in credits, so €7,200. At €80,000 the 40% rate applies to €36,000 of income and the 8% USC rate kicks in on the slice above €70,044. Even so, the effective deduction rate on €80,000 is about 31%, not 40%. The 40% is a marginal rate that only applies to the top slice of income, although the marginal rate including USC and PRSI on that slice is 52.2%.

Things that change the numbers

Pension contributions through payroll reduce your income tax (though not USC or PRSI) and are worth considering once you have settled in. If you rent, claiming the Rent Tax Credit adds up to €1,000 a year to your net pay. If you start work part way through the year, your tax credits and standard rate band for the full year are still available, so you may pay very little tax in your first months or receive a refund the following January. Married couples can transfer part of their band and credits between them. articles.plainText:
The salary in your job offer is a gross figure. Before it reaches your bank account, three separate deductions come off it: income tax, the Universal Social Charge (USC) and Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI). Newcomers often overestimate their net pay because they only budget for income tax, or underestimate it because they have heard Ireland's 40% rate and assume it applies to everything. This guide walks through the three deductions using the 2026 rates and gives you worked examples for three common salaries. All figures apply to the 2026 tax year as set out in Budget 2026 (announced in October 2025).

Deduction 1: income tax

Ireland has two income tax rates. For a single person in 2026 the first €44,000 of income is taxed at 20% and everything above that at 40%. Married couples and civil partners get a wider standard rate band: €53,000 for one income, or up to €88,000 where both partners earn (a maximum of €44,000 per person). Single parents who qualify for the Single Person Child Carer Credit get €48,000.

Once the tax is calculated, tax credits are subtracted from it euro for euro. Almost every employee gets two: the Personal Tax Credit of €2,000 and the Employee (PAYE) Tax Credit of €2,000. Together they wipe out the first €4,000 of tax, which is why a single person pays no income tax at all on the first €20,000 of earnings. Renters can add the Rent Tax Credit of up to €1,000, and there are further credits for carers, single parents and some medical expenses.

Deduction 2: USC

USC is a separate charge on gross income and no tax credits reduce it. If you earn €13,000 or less in the year you are exempt. Above that, the whole of your income is charged in bands: 0.5% on the first €12,012, 2% from €12,013 to €28,700, 3% from €28,701 to €70,044 and 8% on anything above €70,044. Budget 2026 widened the 2% band from €27,382 to €28,700 so that a full-time minimum wage worker stays out of the 3% band.

Deduction 3: PRSI

PRSI is Ireland's social insurance contribution and it funds the State Pension, Jobseeker's Benefit, Maternity Benefit, Illness Benefit and other payments. Most private and public sector employees are in Class A. The employee rate is 4.2% of gross pay from 1 January 2026, rising to 4.35% from 1 October 2026. If you earn €352 or less in a week you pay nothing, and a tapered credit of up to €12 a week softens the charge for anyone earning between €352.01 and €424 a week. Your employer pays a separate, larger contribution on top of your salary that never appears in your deductions.

Worked examples for 2026

The table below assumes a single employee with only the personal and employee credits, paid evenly through the year, and uses the 4.2% PRSI rate that applies from January to September 2026. Because the rate rises to 4.35% in October, the annual PRSI figure will be roughly €13 higher on €35,000, €19 higher on €50,000 and €30 higher on €80,000 across the full year. Figures are rounded to the nearest euro.

Gross salaryIncome taxUSCPRSI (4.2%)Annual netMonthly net€35,000€3,000€583€1,470€29,947€2,496€50,000€7,200€1,033€2,100€39,667€3,306€80,000€19,200€2,431€3,360€55,009€4,584

Look at how the €35,000 case works. Income tax is 20% of €35,000, which is €7,000, minus €4,000 in credits, leaving €3,000. articles.title: Minimum wage in Ireland 2026
articles.note: The €14.15 rate, youth rates, lawful deductions, typical hours and where the living wage plan stands.
articles.description: Ireland has one of the higher statutory minimum wages in the EU, and it is reviewed every year on the advice of the Low Pay Commission. If you are…
articles.previewHtml:
Ireland has one of the higher statutory minimum wages in the EU, and it is reviewed every year on the advice of the Low Pay Commission. If you are arriving to work in hospitality, retail, care, cleaning, agriculture or an entry-level role, the minimum wage sets the floor for what an employer may legally pay you. This guide covers the 2026 rate, the lower rates for young workers, what an employer may and may not deduct, the hours you can expect, and where the Government's living wage plan stands.

The 2026 rate

From 1 January 2026 the National Minimum Wage for an experienced adult worker is €14.15 per hour, up 65 cent from €13.50 in 2025. On a standard 39-hour week that is €551.85 gross, or roughly €28,700 a year. The 2026 Budget widened the 2% USC band to exactly €28,700 so that someone on the full-time minimum wage does not tip into the 3% band. In July 2026 the Low Pay Commission recommended a further increase of 79 cent for 2027; the rate for 2027 will be confirmed in Budget 2027 in October 2026.

The rate applies to almost all employees, including part-time, casual, agency and temporary staff, regardless of nationality or immigration status. It does not apply to close relatives of the employer (a spouse, parent or child, for example) or to registered craft apprentices, whose pay is set under their apprenticeship terms.
articles.gatedHtml:
Sub-minimum rates for under 20s

Younger workers may legally be paid a percentage of the adult rate. The percentages are fixed in law, so the youth rates move automatically whenever the main rate changes.

WorkerShare of adult rateHourly rate 2026
Aged 20 and over100%€14.15
Aged 1990%€12.74
Aged 1880%€11.32
Under 1870%€9.91

Many employers pay the full adult rate to everyone, but they are not obliged to. If you are 18 or 19 and receive an offer, check which rate is being used. Sectoral Employment Orders and Employment Regulation Orders set higher legal minimums in construction, security, contract cleaning and some other sectors, so the €14.15 figure is a floor rather than the going rate in those industries.

What counts and what can be deducted

Your basic pay, shift premiums, piece rates and commission all count towards the minimum wage. Overtime premiums, tips, service charges, expenses and most allowances do not. Since the Payment of Wages (Amendment) (Tips and Gratuities) Act 2022, electronic tips and service charges must be passed on to staff and may not be used to top up pay to the minimum.

An employer may take a fixed amount off your pay for board and lodging that they provide, but only within limits set by the Department of Enterprise. From 1 January 2026 the maximum that can be counted is €1.27 per hour worked for meals and €33.42 per week (or €4.77 per day) for accommodation, whatever the food or room actually costs the employer. Deductions for uniforms, training, breakages or till shortages are only lawful if they are in your contract or you have agreed in writing, and they must be fair and proportionate. Any other deduction that pushes your hourly pay below the minimum wage is illegal.

Hours, breaks and payslips

Full-time work in Ireland is typically 37 to 40 hours a week, and the Organisation of Working Time Act caps the average at 48 hours over a reference period. You are entitled to a 15-minute break after 4.5 hours and a 30-minute break after 6 hours, and to at least 11 hours' rest between shifts. Sunday work must attract a premium, extra time off or a rate that already takes Sunday work into account. Every employee is entitled to a written statement of core terms within 5 days of starting, and to a payslip showing gross pay and each deduction. Employees on the minimum wage build up paid annual leave in the normal way (8% of hours worked, up to 4 weeks) and are entitled to statutory sick pay, which is 70% of normal pay up to €110 a day for 5 days in 2026.

The living wage plan

In 2022 the Government committed to replacing the minimum wage with a national living wage set at 60% of the median hourly wage. The original target date was 2026. In 2025, after lobbying from small businesses over rising costs, the timeline was pushed back and the target is now to reach 60% of median earnings by 2029, with the minimum wage rising in steps each January until then. This is separate from the voluntary Living Wage Technical Group figure, which is a research-based estimate of what a single adult needs to live on and is €15.40 per hour for 2025/26. Employers are not obliged to pay that figure, but many larger companies and public bodies use it as a benchmark.

If you are underpaid

You can ask your employer for a written statement of your average hourly pay for any period in the previous 12 months, and they must supply it within 4 weeks. If the statement shows you were paid below the minimum, you can bring a complaint to the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) within 6 months, and the WRC inspectorate can also investigate employers directly. It is unlawful for an employer to penalise you for asking about your pay or making a complaint.

  • Department of Enterprise: National Minimum Wage
  • Low Pay Commission
  • Living Wage Technical Group

articles.title: PAYE explained for newcomers
articles.note: How Irish payroll tax works, why emergency tax happens, how to read a payslip and when refunds arrive.
articles.description: If you are employed in Ireland, you almost never send money to the tax office yourself. Instead your employer calculates the tax on each payslip and pays…
articles.previewHtml:
If you are employed in Ireland, you almost never send money to the tax office yourself. Instead your employer calculates the tax on each payslip and pays it over to Revenue on your behalf. That system is called Pay As You Earn, or PAYE. It is efficient once it is set up correctly, but a newcomer who does not understand how it works can lose a large slice of their first few pay packets to emergency tax. This guide explains the mechanics, what each line on your payslip means, and when money comes back to you.

How the system works

Everything in PAYE hinges on a document you never see: the Revenue Payroll Notification (RPN). When your employer registers you as a new starter, their payroll software asks Revenue for an RPN in your name. The RPN tells the employer your tax credits, the width of your standard rate band, your USC rates and whether any of these should be applied on a cumulative basis or week by week. Revenue in turn builds the RPN from what it knows about you: your PPS number, your other jobs, your marital status and any credits you have claimed in myAccount.
articles.gatedHtml:
Since 2019 Irish payroll has operated in real time. Every time you are paid, your employer reports the pay and deductions to Revenue on or before payday. That is why you can log in to myAccount and see your year-to-date pay within days. It also means mistakes are corrected quickly: update your details with Revenue and a new RPN normally reaches your employer before the next pay run.

Cumulative basis versus week 1 basis

The normal method is the cumulative basis. Your annual credits and rate band are spread across the year, and each payday the payroll looks at your total pay and total tax so far. If you started in June, the credits for January to May are still available, so you may pay almost no tax until you have used them up. The alternative is the week 1 or month 1 basis, where each payslip is calculated in isolation. Revenue applies week 1 when it is unsure of your circumstances, for example when you have moved between jobs and the old employer has not yet reported your final pay. It is not a penalty, but it can leave you overpaid, which is settled when you file a return after year end.

Emergency tax

Emergency tax applies when the employer cannot get an RPN for you. There are two versions, and the difference is big.

SituationIncome tax chargedUSC charged
PPS number given, but job not registered with RevenueWeeks 1 to 4: 20% up to the single rate band cut-off (€44,000 a year, or €846 a week) and 40% above, with no credits. Week 5 onwards: 40% on everything.8% on all pay
No PPS number given to employer40% on everything from the first payslip8% on all pay

On a €3,000 monthly salary the emergency deductions in month 2 onwards can exceed €1,400. Avoiding this takes two steps: get a PPS number before or immediately after arrival, and register your job in myAccount if your employer has not done it for you (the article on Revenue myAccount in this section walks through the steps). Emergency tax is always refunded once your RPN is in place, usually through your next payslip on the cumulative basis.

Reading an Irish payslip

Payslip layouts vary, but the same lines appear on nearly all of them.

  • Gross pay: your salary for the period before any deductions, including overtime and bonuses.
  • PAYE or Income tax: the tax calculated from your rate band and credits. Some payslips show the credit and cut-off point used.
  • USC: the Universal Social Charge, shown separately because it has its own bands.
  • PRSI EE: your own social insurance contribution, 4.2% in Class A until 30 September 2026 and 4.35% from 1 October 2026. PRSI ER is the employer's contribution and is shown for information only.
  • Pension: any contribution to an occupational or auto-enrolment (My Future Fund) scheme.
  • Insurable weeks: the number of PRSI weeks credited in the period, which matters for your future benefit entitlements.
  • Net pay: what is transferred to your bank account.

The year-to-date columns are the ones to watch. If they reset unexpectedly, or if the tax credit figure is zero, it usually means an RPN problem.

When you get a refund

Refunds arrive in three ways. First, through payroll: when a missing RPN arrives or you claim a new credit mid-year, the cumulative calculation gives back any overpayment in the next pay run. Second, if you leave a job and are out of work for more than 4 weeks, you can claim a refund of tax already paid through myAccount. Third, after the year ends, Revenue publishes a Preliminary End of Year Statement in myAccount every January. If you file an income tax return (Form 12 online), you receive a Statement of Liability, and any overpayment is transferred to your bank account, usually within a few days. You can go back 4 years, so in 2026 you can still claim for 2022 onwards.

Most people leave money on the table by not claiming credits: rent, medical expenses (20% of GP, consultant and prescription costs), the remote working relief and flat-rate expenses for certain trades all go through the same return. Set a reminder each January.

articles.title: Tax credits, USC and PRSI explained
articles.appTitle: Tax credits, USC and PRSI explained
articles.note: The 2026 credits you can claim, USC bands, PRSI classes and the benefits your contributions unlock.
articles.description: Three separate sets of rules decide how much of your Irish salary you keep. Tax credits cut your income tax bill directly. USC is a second charge on the…
articles.previewHtml:
Three separate sets of rules decide how much of your Irish salary you keep. Tax credits cut your income tax bill directly. USC is a second charge on the same income with its own bands. PRSI is social insurance that buys you cover for unemployment, illness, maternity and retirement. The three are often lumped together as "tax", but they behave differently, and knowing which is which helps you claim what you are owed and understand what you are paying for. All figures below are for the 2026 tax year.

Tax credits: money off your tax bill

A tax credit is not a deduction from income. It is subtracted from the tax you would otherwise pay, so a €2,000 credit is worth exactly €2,000 to everyone who has enough tax to use it. The credits below are the ones most newcomers can claim.

Credit (2026)AmountWho gets it
Personal Tax Credit, single€2,000Every single person, automatically
Personal Tax Credit, married or civil partners€4,000Jointly assessed couples
Employee (PAYE) Tax Credit€2,000Anyone taxed under PAYE, automatically
Earned Income Credit€2,000Self-employed and proprietary directors (instead of the Employee credit)
Single Person Child Carer Credit€1,900A single parent with a qualifying child living with them; also widens the 20% band to €48,000
Rent Tax Credit€1,000 single, €2,000 couplePrivate tenants paying rent for their home; must be claimed
Home Carer Credit€1,950A married person caring at home for a child or dependent relative
articles.gatedHtml:
The personal and employee credits together mean a single employee pays no income tax on the first €20,000 of earnings. The Rent Tax Credit is worth 20% of rent paid up to the maximum, and Budget 2026 extended it unchanged until the end of 2028. It is not applied automatically: claim it in myAccount for the current year (which adjusts your payslips) or in your tax return for a past year. Landlords must be registered with the Residential Tenancies Board and you need their name and the RTB registration number. Other common claims are medical expenses at 20%, tuition fees, the remote working relief on 30% of electricity, heat and broadband, and flat-rate expenses for many occupations including nurses, teachers and hospitality workers.

USC: the second income charge

The Universal Social Charge was introduced in 2011 and has never been fully removed. No credits reduce it. If your total income for the year is €13,000 or less you are fully exempt. Once you pass that figure, all your income is charged, in the bands below.

Income slice (2026)USC rate
First €12,0120.5%
€12,013 to €28,7002%
€28,701 to €70,0443%
Above €70,0448%

Two reduced-rate rules are worth knowing. If you are aged 70 or over, or you hold a full medical card, and your total income is €60,000 or less, you pay a maximum of 2% on anything above €12,012. Self-employed people pay an extra 3% surcharge on income over €100,000, making 11% on that slice. USC applies to employment income, benefit in kind, rental income and self-employed profits, but not to Department of Social Protection payments.

PRSI: what you pay

Pay Related Social Insurance is collected through payroll alongside tax. Almost all employees aged 16 to 70 in private industry, and most public servants recruited since 1995, are in Class A. Rates are rising a little each year until 2028 under the Government's plan to fund the State Pension.

Class A employee PRSIValue
Rate from 1 January 20264.2% of gross pay
Rate from 1 October 20264.35% of gross pay
Weekly earnings at or below €352No employee PRSI (employer still pays)
Weekly earnings €352.01 to €424Tapered credit of up to €12 a week reduces the charge
Employer contribution11.25% (11.40% from 1 October 2026); 9% (9.15% from 1 October 2026) on pay of €552 a week or less

The other classes you may meet are Class S for self-employed people (4.2%, rising to 4.35%, on all income, with a minimum annual contribution), Class J for people earning under €38 a week or working past 70 (occupational injuries cover only), and Class M for people with no liability, such as those under 16. Your PRSI class appears on every payslip.

PRSI: what it entitles you to

Each week you pay Class A PRSI you earn one paid contribution. Benefits are unlocked once you have enough contributions, and a few depend on recent contributions rather than lifetime totals.

  • Jobseeker's Benefit and the new Jobseeker's Pay-Related Benefit: after 104 paid contributions, if you lose your job.
  • Illness Benefit: after 104 paid contributions and 39 in the relevant year, once statutory sick pay from your employer ends.
  • Maternity, Paternity and Parent's Benefit: 39 contributions in the 12 months before your leave, or in the relevant tax year.
  • Treatment Benefit: free dental exams, scale and polish, eye tests and hearing aid grants after a qualifying period of contributions.
  • State Pension (Contributory): paid from age 66 to people with at least 520 paid contributions (10 years).
  • Invalidity Pension, Carer's Benefit, Widow's or Surviving Civil Partner's Pension and the Occupational Injuries scheme.

Contributions you paid in another EU or EEA country, the UK or a country with a bilateral agreement with Ireland can be combined with Irish contributions to qualify for many of these benefits, so keep your social security records from home. You can check your Irish contribution record at any time on MyWelfare.ie once you have a verified MyGovID.

articles.plainText:
Three separate sets of rules decide how much of your Irish salary you keep. Tax credits cut your income tax bill directly. USC is a second charge on the same income with its own bands. PRSI is social insurance that buys you cover for unemployment, illness, maternity and retirement. The three are often lumped together as "tax", but they behave differently, and knowing which is which helps you claim what you are owed and understand what you are paying for. All figures below are for the 2026 tax year.

Tax credits: money off your tax bill

A tax credit is not a deduction from income. It is subtracted from the tax you would otherwise pay, so a €2,000 credit is worth exactly €2,000 to everyone who has enough tax to use it. The credits below are the ones most newcomers can claim.

Credit (2026)AmountWho gets itPersonal Tax Credit, single€2,000Every single person, automaticallyPersonal Tax Credit, married or civil partners€4,000Jointly assessed couplesEmployee (PAYE) Tax Credit€2,000Anyone taxed under PAYE, automaticallyEarned Income Credit€2,000Self-employed and proprietary directors (instead of the Employee credit)Single Person Child Carer Credit€1,900A single parent with a qualifying child living with them; also widens the 20% band to €48,000Rent Tax Credit€1,000 single, €2,000 couplePrivate tenants paying rent for their home; must be claimedHome Carer Credit€1,950A married person caring at home for a child or dependent relative

The personal and employee credits together mean a single employee pays no income tax on the first €20,000 of earnings. The Rent Tax Credit is worth 20% of rent paid up to the maximum, and Budget 2026 extended it unchanged until the end of 2028. It is not applied automatically: claim it in myAccount for the current year (which adjusts your payslips) or in your tax return for a past year. Landlords must be registered with the Residential Tenancies Board and you need their name and the RTB registration number. Other common claims are medical expenses at 20%, tuition fees, the remote working relief on 30% of electricity, heat and broadband, and flat-rate expenses for many occupations including nurses, teachers and hospitality workers.

USC: the second income charge

The Universal Social Charge was introduced in 2011 and has never been fully removed. No credits reduce it. If your total income for the year is €13,000 or less you are fully exempt. Once you pass that figure, all your income is charged, in the bands below.

Income slice (2026)USC rateFirst €12,0120.5%€12,013 to €28,7002%€28,701 to €70,0443%Above €70,0448%

Two reduced-rate rules are worth knowing. If you are aged 70 or over, or you hold a full medical card, and your total income is €60,000 or less, you pay a maximum of 2% on anything above €12,012. Self-employed people pay an extra 3% surcharge on income over €100,000, making 11% on that slice. USC applies to employment income, benefit in kind, rental income and self-employed profits, but not to Department of Social Protection payments.

Pay Related Social Insurance is collected through payroll alongside tax. Almost all employees aged 16 to 70 in private industry, and most public servants recruited since 1995, are in Class A. Rates are rising a little each year until 2028 under the Government's plan to fund the State Pension.

The other classes you may meet are Class S for self-employed people (4.2%, rising to 4.35%, on all income, with a minimum annual contribution), Class J for people earning under €38 a week or working past 70 (occupational injuries cover only), and Class M for people with no liability, such as those under 16. Your PRSI class appears on every payslip.

Each week you pay Class A PRSI you earn one paid contribution. Benefits are unlocked once you have enough contributions, and a few depend on recent contributions rather than lifetime totals.

articles.title: How to find a job in Ireland from abroad
articles.appTitle: How to find a job in Ireland from abroad
articles.note: Job boards, sectors hiring in 2026, Irish CV format, employment permit thresholds and recruitment agencies.
articles.description: Ireland has close to full employment, with unemployment hovering around 4 to 5% through 2025 and 2026, and many employers are used to hiring from…
articles.previewHtml:
Ireland has close to full employment, with unemployment hovering around 4 to 5% through 2025 and 2026, and many employers are used to hiring from overseas. That does not mean the search is easy from a distance. Recruiters filter hard on right-to-work status, CV format and time zone, and the best roles often go through agencies or referrals rather than public listings. This guide sets out where to look, which sectors are hiring, how to present yourself in the Irish format, and how employment permit sponsorship works if you are not an EU, EEA, Swiss or UK citizen.

Where the jobs are advertised

Most Irish vacancies appear on a small number of boards, and it is worth setting alerts on all of them.

SiteBest for
IrishJobs.ieThe largest general board; strong on office, finance and tech roles
Jobs.ieRetail, hospitality, warehousing, healthcare and entry-level
LinkedInTech, pharma, multinational and senior hires; most recruiters source here
Indeed.ieAggregator covering almost everything, useful for salary ranges
JobsIreland.ieThe State employment service; free to employers, so many SME and public roles
PublicJobs.ieCivil and public service competitions
EURESEU portal where Irish employers advertise specifically to candidates abroad
articles.gatedHtml:
Company career pages matter more in Ireland than in many countries because so much employment is concentrated in large multinationals. Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, Salesforce, Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson, Accenture and the big four accountancy firms all run their own applicant systems and rarely rely on boards alone.

Sectors that are hiring

Demand in 2026 is strongest in the areas the Critical Skills Occupations List targets: software engineering, data and cyber security, cloud and infrastructure, accountancy and financial services, pharma and medical device manufacturing, engineering (civil, electrical, mechanical and process), and healthcare across nurses, doctors, radiographers and allied professions. Construction is short of quantity surveyors, site engineers and trades. Outside the permit lists, hospitality, retail, logistics, childcare and care work consistently have vacancies and take on newcomers quickly, though usually at or near the minimum wage of €14.15 an hour. Dublin holds the largest share of jobs, but Cork (pharma, tech), Galway (medical devices), Limerick (manufacturing, engineering) and Waterford are all significant and cheaper to live in.

The Irish CV format

Irish CVs are short and plain. Two pages is standard, three is tolerated for senior roles, and one is fine for graduates. Do not include a photo, your date of birth, marital status, nationality or a full address; a city and country is enough. Lead with a three or four line profile, then work history in reverse order with dated achievements rather than duties, then education, then skills and languages. Spell out qualifications that may be unfamiliar with a one-line equivalent. Write a short cover letter for every application, and state your right-to-work position clearly in the first paragraph, for example "EU citizen, relocating to Dublin in March" or "Would require Critical Skills Employment Permit sponsorship". Recruiters would rather know now than find out at offer stage. Give a phone number with the international dialling code and mention your availability for interviews in Irish time. Check your LinkedIn profile matches your CV, because it will be read alongside it.

Employment permits and sponsorship

Citizens of the EU, EEA, Switzerland and the UK do not need permission to work. Everyone else needs an employment permit, which the employer or you apply for from the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, or a separate immigration permission such as a spouse of an Irish citizen or a Stamp 1G graduate. The two permits that matter for most people are below. Salary thresholds rose on 1 March 2026 and are scheduled to rise again in 2027 and 2028.

PermitMinimum salary from 1 March 2026Key points
Critical Skills Employment Permit€40,904 for occupations on the Critical Skills list with a relevant degree; €68,911 for most other occupationsNo labour market test; family can join immediately and work; eligible for Stamp 4 after 2 years
General Employment Permit€36,605 (€32,691 for healthcare assistants, home carers, horticulture and meat processing)Employer must usually advertise the job for 28 days first (labour market needs test); a 50:50 rule requires at least half the workforce to be EEA nationals

Lower thresholds apply to recent graduates of Irish and other recognised institutions. Employers who sponsor regularly include hospitals, the HSE, nursing homes, tech multinationals, pharma manufacturers and large construction firms. Smaller companies are often unfamiliar with the process, so it helps to be able to explain it. The permit is tied to the employer, and processing times in 2026 have run at several weeks for Trusted Partner employers and longer for standard applications, so build that into your timeline.

Recruitment agencies and networking

Agencies fill a large share of professional roles in Ireland and are free for candidates. CPL, Morgan McKinley, Hays, Sigmar, Brightwater, Lincoln, Robert Walters and FRS Recruitment cover most sectors; nursing and medical staff should look at the specialist agencies that recruit directly for the HSE and private hospitals. Register with two or three, be honest about your start date and permit position, and keep in touch. Professional bodies (Engineers Ireland, Chartered Accountants Ireland, the Nursing and Midwifery Board) also list vacancies and can tell you whether your qualification needs recognition before you can practise. Finally, join the online groups for your nationality in Ireland: many people find their first role, or at least a realistic salary benchmark, through those communities.

★ Useful links

  • Department of Enterprise: employment permits
  • Citizens Information: Critical Skills Employment Permit
  • JobsIreland (State employment service)
  • EURES European job portal
  • Critical Skills Occupations List

articles.title: Register with Revenue myAccount and avoid emergency tax
articles.appTitle: Register with Revenue myAccount and avoid emergency tax
articles.note: Step-by-step myAccount registration, adding your job, how the RPN works and what to check on your first payslip.
articles.description: myAccount is Revenue's online service for employees. It is where you register a new job, claim tax credits, check what your employer has reported, and…
articles.previewHtml:
myAccount is Revenue's online service for employees. It is where you register a new job, claim tax credits, check what your employer has reported, and file your annual return. For a newcomer it is also the single most effective tool for avoiding emergency tax, because it lets you tell Revenue about your job even before your employer's payroll catches up. This guide lists what you need, walks through registration and job set-up step by step, and explains the Revenue Payroll Notification that ties it all together.

What you need before you start

ItemWhere it comes fromWhy it matters
PPS numberDepartment of Social Protection, via MyWelfare.ieWithout it your employer must deduct 40% tax and 8% USC on all pay from day one
Employer registration numberAsk HR or payroll; it is on your contract or a colleague's payslipIdentifies the employer when you register the job yourself
Start date and expected payYour contract or offer letterUsed to allocate credits and rate band across the year
Irish mobile number and emailAny providerNeeded for two-factor authentication on every login
Photo ID and proof of address (for instant verification)Passport or IRP card; a utility bill or bank letterLets Revenue verify you immediately rather than by post
articles.gatedHtml:
The PPS number is the critical piece. Apply for it as soon as you have an address in Ireland (there is a separate guide in the Paperwork section). If you already have a PPS number from an earlier stay, it is still valid; do not apply for a new one.

Step 1: register for myAccount

  1. Go to revenue.ie and choose "myAccount", then "Register now".
  2. Enter your PPS number, date of birth, name, address, mobile number and email.
  3. Choose a verification route. If you have a verified MyGovID (the account you may already have created for your PPS number application) you can sign in with it instantly. Otherwise Revenue can verify you online against information it holds, or it posts a temporary password to your address within a few working days.
  4. Log in, set your own password and complete two-factor authentication.

Register even if you have not started work yet. An existing account means you can act the moment your first payslip looks wrong.

Step 2: register your job

Most employers register new starters with Revenue through their payroll software before the first payday, and if yours does, the job will already appear under "PAYE Services" in myAccount. If it does not, add it yourself:

  1. In myAccount open PAYE Services and choose Update Job or Pension Details.
  2. Select "Add job" and enter the employer registration number, your start date and how often you are paid.
  3. Confirm whether this is your only employment. If you also have a second job or a pension, you can split your credits and rate band between them here.
  4. Submit. Revenue creates or updates your record and makes a new Revenue Payroll Notification (RPN) available to the employer straight away.

The RPN is what stops emergency tax. Your employer's payroll requests it electronically each pay run; it carries your annual credits (normally the Personal and Employee credits, €2,000 each in 2026), your standard rate band (€44,000 for a single person), your USC bands and whether calculations are cumulative or on a week 1 basis. Until an RPN exists, the payroll has nothing to go on and must apply emergency rates: 20% then 40% with no credits if it has your PPS number, or 40% on everything if it does not, plus 8% USC in both cases.

Step 3: check the first payslip

Once you have been paid, log in and open Manage Your Tax 2026. It shows the credits and rate band allocated to your job. Compare it with your payslip: the tax credit for the period should be visible (about €333 a month for a single employee) and the deductions should look like roughly 14% of gross on €35,000, not 40%. If emergency tax was applied, do nothing except confirm the RPN has now issued; the cumulative calculation on your next payslip repays the excess automatically. If several weeks pass with no correction, ring Revenue's PAYE helpline or use the "My Enquiries" service inside myAccount.

Step 4: claim your credits and keep it updated

While you are in Manage Your Tax, claim anything you are entitled to so it flows into your payslips immediately: the Rent Tax Credit (up to €1,000 for a single person in 2026), the remote working relief, flat-rate expenses for your occupation, and if you are married or in a civil partnership, tell Revenue so the joint assessment options are opened. Update your address when you move. In January each year, open the Preliminary End of Year Statement and file your return to receive the Statement of Liability and any refund due. Also consider registering for the Revenue app or enabling notifications, since Revenue communicates through the My Documents inbox rather than by post.

If you are self-employed or have a second job

Sole traders and contractors register for income tax through Revenue Online Service (ROS) rather than myAccount, and pay preliminary tax each October. If you are both employed and self-employed, you can use both. If you have two PAYE jobs, allocate your credits and rate band between them in myAccount, otherwise the second employer will receive an RPN with nothing left and deduct 40%.

★ Useful links

  • Revenue: register for myAccount
  • Revenue: starting your first job
  • Revenue: emergency tax
  • MyWelfare: apply for a PPS number
  • MyGovID

categories.name: Cost of living
categories.tagline: What Ireland really costs: rent, bills, budgets by city

articles.title: Cost of living in Ireland in 2026
articles.appTitle: Cost of living in Ireland in 2026
articles.note: Verified 2026 figures for rent, groceries, energy, transport, childcare and healthcare, with sample monthly budgets.
articles.description: Ireland is one of the more expensive countries in Europe to live in, and rent is the reason. Almost everything else, from groceries to public transport…
articles.previewHtml:
Ireland is one of the more expensive countries in Europe to live in, and rent is the reason. Almost everything else, from groceries to public transport, sits close to the western European average. If you are about to relocate, the useful question is not "is Ireland expensive?" but "what will my month actually cost?". This guide pulls the latest official figures together so you can build a realistic budget before you sign a lease or accept a salary.

Rent: the number that decides everything

The Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) Rent Index for Q1 2026 puts the national standardised average rent for a new tenancy at €1,839 a month, up 9.1% in a year. Existing tenants pay far less, on average €1,513, because annual rent increases are capped nationwide (at 2% or inflation, whichever is lower, since March 2026). As a newcomer you will be paying the new-tenancy price. In Dublin the same index shows €2,335 for a new tenancy, against €1,806 in the commuter counties of Meath, Kildare and Wicklow and €1,432 everywhere else.

Daft.ie's Q2 2026 report, which tracks advertised (asking) rents, puts a two-bedroom apartment at €2,204 nationally and €2,634 in Dublin. A double room in a shared house averaged €806 nationwide in Q1 2026. Supply is the real problem: Daft counted just under 2,400 homes to rent across the whole country in early August 2026, compared with more than 4,300 before the pandemic. Budget for a deposit of one month's rent plus the first month up front.
articles.gatedHtml:
Groceries, energy and broadband

The CSO's Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% in the year to August 2026, but staple food prices were actually falling by late summer (butter, cheddar and milk were all cheaper than a year earlier). The most recent CSO Household Budget Survey (2022 to 2023) recorded average household food spending of €161 a week. Comparison sites put a single person's weekly shop at roughly €60 to €80, so allow €260 to €350 a month if you cook at home and shop at Lidl, Aldi, Dunnes or Tesco.

Energy is where Ireland stings. The average annual electricity bill was around €1,805 in July 2026 and the average gas bill about €1,429 (Selectra, based on typical usage), so a house with both pays roughly €270 a month. Standard unit rates are 35 to 38 cent per kWh, among the highest in the EU, and switching supplier every year can save several hundred euro. Home broadband runs from about €25 to €60 a month and a SIM-only mobile plan from €10 to €15.

Transport

Public transport is cheap by European standards. In Dublin the TFI 90-minute Leap fare is €2 across bus, Luas and DART, with a daily cap of €6. A monthly Dublin Bus and Luas TaxSaver ticket is €96, or under €60 a month if you commit to an annual ticket through your employer (which is also paid before tax). Cork introduced the same 90-minute fare in July 2026 at €1.70, and Bus Éireann city singles in Galway and Limerick are €1.50 with a Leap card. Owning a car is expensive: motor tax, insurance, and fuel add up quickly, and insurance quotes for new arrivals without an Irish claims history are high.

Childcare and healthcare

Childcare is the second biggest cost for families. From September 2026 the government capped fees for Core Funding creches: for 45 hours a week the maximum charge is €280, and after the universal National Childcare Scheme subsidy of €96.30 you pay at most €183.70 a week, roughly €796 a month. Income-assessed subsidies bring this down further for many families. Children aged 3 to 5 get two free ECCE preschool years (3 hours a day, 38 weeks).

Healthcare is a mix of public and private. A GP visit costs €50 to €70 unless you hold a medical card or GP visit card (all children under 8 and everyone over 70 qualify for free GP care). Public hospital inpatient charges were abolished in 2023, but attending an emergency department without a GP referral costs €100. The Drugs Payment Scheme caps your family's prescription spend at €80 a month and is open to anyone ordinarily resident. Private health insurance is optional but common; the Health Insurance Authority put the average adult premium at €1,902 a year in March 2026.
