The national minimum wage rose to €14.15 an hour on 1 January 2026. The CSO puts average weekly earnings at €1,046.88 in Q2 2026 (preliminary), about €54,400 a year. A single person pays 20% income tax on the first €44,000 and 40% above that, plus USC and 4.2% PRSI, but the €2,000 personal and €2,000 employee tax credits mean roughly the first €20,000 is income-tax free. Renters can also claim a €1,000 rent tax credit.

articles.plainText:
Ireland is one of the more expensive countries in Europe to live in, and rent is the reason. Almost everything else, from groceries to public transport, sits close to the western European average. If you are about to relocate, the useful question is not "is Ireland expensive?" but "what will my month actually cost?". This guide pulls the latest official figures together so you can build a realistic budget before you sign a lease or accept a salary.

Rent: the number that decides everything

The Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) Rent Index for Q1 2026 puts the national standardised average rent for a new tenancy at €1,839 a month, up 9.1% in a year. As a newcomer you will be paying the new-tenancy price. In Dublin the same index shows €2,335 for a new tenancy, against €1,806 in the commuter counties of Meath, Kildare and Wicklow and €1,432 everywhere else.

A double room in a shared house averaged €806 nationwide in Q1 2026. The average annual electricity bill was around €1,805 in July 2026 and the average gas bill about €1,429 (Selectra, based on typical usage), so a house with both pays roughly €270 a month. Standard unit rates are 35 to 38 cent per kWh, among the highest in the EU, and switching supplier every year can save several hundred euro. Public transport is cheap by European standards. In Dublin the TFI 90-minute Leap fare is €2 across bus, Luas and DART, with a daily cap of €6. Childcare is the second biggest cost for families. articles.title: Cost of living in Dublin
articles.note: What Dublin really costs in 2026: rent by area, house prices, transport, bills and a single person's monthly budget.
articles.description: Dublin is where most people moving to Ireland land first, and it is comfortably the most expensive place in the country to live. The premium is almost…
articles.previewHtml:
Dublin is where most people moving to Ireland land first, and it is comfortably the most expensive place in the country to live. The premium is almost entirely housing: once you have a roof over your head, a pint, a bus fare or a weekly shop costs about the same as in Cork or Galway. This guide gives you the latest 2026 figures so you can judge whether a Dublin salary offer actually stretches far enough.

Rent in Dublin in 2026

The RTB Rent Index for Q1 2026 puts the standardised average rent for a new tenancy in County Dublin at €2,335 a month, 7.8% higher than a year earlier. Sitting tenants pay an average of €1,960, but as a newcomer you will pay the new-tenancy rate. Within the county, Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown is dearest at €2,629, followed by Dublin City at €2,301, Fingal at €2,269 and South Dublin at €2,267.

Daft.ie's advertised rents show what you will actually see in listings. In Q1 2026 a one-bedroom apartment in Dublin averaged €2,012, a two-bed €2,609 and a three-bed house €3,162. By Q2 2026 the two-bed figure had crept up to €2,634, with annual inflation slowing to 6.5%. A double room in a shared house in the city centre averaged €1,002, which is why so many professionals in their twenties and thirties still house-share.

Supply is tight: Daft counted fewer than 1,150 homes to rent in Dublin in early August 2026, down 18% on the year. Start searching before you arrive, have your documents ready (proof of employment, references, ID) and expect to pay a deposit plus the first month in advance. Once you are in, annual increases are capped nationwide at 2% or inflation, whichever is lower, under the rules in force since March 2026.

Buying instead of renting

If you plan to stay, the Daft.ie House Price Report for Q2 2026 puts an average three-bed semi in Dublin at €580,000, with listed prices up 3% in a year. The CSO's median price paid in the 12 months to June 2026 was €396,000 nationally and €682,334 in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown, the most expensive local authority in the State. Non-Irish citizens can buy freely, but lenders generally want to see 6 to 12 months of Irish payslips.

Getting around

Transport is one of Dublin's bargains. The TFI 90-minute Leap fare is €2 for any combination of Dublin Bus, Luas, DART and commuter rail in the short-hop zone, capped at €6 a day. A monthly Bus and Luas TaxSaver ticket is €96, and an annual ticket covering bus, Luas, DART and commuter rail costs €960, bought through your employer before tax. Dublin Bikes membership is inexpensive and the city is flat, so many people cycle. A car is optional in most of the city and parking in the centre is scarce and expensive.

Everyday costs

Groceries cost the same in Dublin as anywhere in Ireland. Allow €260 to €350 a month for one person and around €700 for a family of four, based on the CSO Household Budget Survey average of €161 a week per household. Electricity for an apartment runs roughly €100 to €150 a month at 2026 unit rates of 35 to 38 cent per kWh; a house with gas heating should budget about €270 a month for both, based on average annual bills of €1,805 for electricity and €1,429 for gas. Broadband is €25 to €60 and a SIM-only mobile plan €10 to €15.

Eating and drinking out is where Dublin does feel pricey. The average pint across Dublin pubs was about €7 in 2026 (Pint Tracker's county average was €6.96), with local pubs in Stoneybatter, Phibsborough or Rathmines closer to €5 to €6 and Temple Bar and hotel bars charging €7 to €9. The national average for a pint of stout passed €6 for the first time in March 2026.

A single person's monthly budget

ItemShared house, double roomOne-bed apartment
Rent€918€2,012
Bills share / electricity€80€150
Broadband and mobile€30€55
Groceries€300€300
Public transport€96€96
Health allowance (GP, prescriptions)€40€40
Total before going outabout €1,460about €2,650

Set that against pay. Average weekly earnings in Ireland were €1,046.88 in Q2 2026 (CSO, preliminary), and Dublin salaries in tech, finance and pharma run well above that. A single person on €55,000 takes home roughly €3,500 a month after income tax, USC and PRSI at 2026 rates, so a one-bed alone is doable but leaves little slack; house-sharing or a commuter-town rental is how most new arrivals make Dublin work in year one.

articles.title: Cost of living in Cork
articles.note: Cork rents, house prices, bus fares and bills in 2026, compared with Dublin, plus sample monthly budgets.
articles.description: Cork is Ireland's second city and the obvious alternative to Dublin if you work in pharma, medtech or tech. Apple, Pfizer, Stryker and dozens of others…
articles.previewHtml:
Cork is Ireland's second city and the obvious alternative to Dublin if you work in pharma, medtech or tech. Apple, Pfizer, Stryker and dozens of others have large sites in and around the city, and salaries in those sectors are close to Dublin levels. Living costs are not. Rent in Cork is meaningfully lower than in the capital, and almost everything else costs the same, which is why so many relocating families choose it. Here is what your money buys in 2026.

Rent in Cork in 2026

The RTB Rent Index for Q1 2026 puts the standardised average new-tenancy rent in Cork City at €1,903 a month and across County Cork at €1,678. That is about €430 a month below Dublin City (€2,301) and €650 below County Dublin. The catch is momentum: Cork City rents were up 16.3% on Q1 2025, the fastest growth of any city in the index, and Daft.ie recorded a further 12% annual rise in Q2 2026.
articles.gatedHtml:
Daft.ie's advertised figures show what listings look like. In Q1 2026 a one-bed apartment in Cork City averaged €1,806, a two-bed €2,126 (rising to €2,168 by Q2 2026) and a three-bed house €2,516. A double room in a shared house was €757. Popular areas for newcomers are Douglas, Ballincollig, Blackrock and Glanmire for families, and the city centre, Sunday's Well and Wilton for singles and couples. The county figure (€1,660 for a two-bed in Q1 2026) covers towns such as Midleton, Carrigaline and Cobh, all within commuting range.

Buying a home

Cork is where the maths of buying starts to work for a couple on two professional salaries. The Daft.ie House Price Report for Q2 2026 puts a three-bed semi in Cork City at €439,000, up 5.1% in a year, against €580,000 in Dublin. The CSO's Residential Property Price Index shows prices in the South-West region (Cork and Kerry) rising 3.7% in the 12 months to June 2026. Local Property Tax on a €400,000 home is €333 a year at the basic rate, before the council's local adjustment.

Transport

Cork joined the TFI 90-minute fare scheme on 20 July 2026: any Bus Éireann city journey, including transfers, costs €1.70 with a Leap card (85 cent for students and young adults), and Leap fare capping limits what you can spend in a day or week. The city is compact and walkable, but bus frequency drops sharply in the suburbs and many people still drive. If you commute by car, budget for motor tax, insurance (expensive for new arrivals with no Irish driving history) and fuel, and expect city-centre parking to be scarce. Cork Airport, ten minutes from the centre, has direct flights to most of Europe, which keeps trips home cheap.

Groceries, energy and other bills

Supermarket prices are national, so a single person spends about €260 to €350 a month on groceries and a family of four around €700 (the CSO Household Budget Survey average is €161 a week per household). The English Market in the city centre is excellent for fresh produce but not a budget option. Electricity and gas cost the same as everywhere else in Ireland: average annual bills were around €1,805 for electricity and €1,429 for gas in July 2026, so a three-bed house with both should budget roughly €270 a month, and an apartment on electricity alone €100 to €150. Broadband is €25 to €60 and mobile €10 to €15.

Healthcare and childcare are national too: a GP visit costs €50 to €70, the Drugs Payment Scheme caps prescriptions at €80 a month per family, and from September 2026 full-time creche fees in Core Funding services are capped at €183.70 a week after the universal subsidy, before any income-based subsidy.

Compared with the same lifestyle in Dublin, a single person saves roughly €250 a month in Cork and a family about €700, almost all of it on rent. With average Irish weekly earnings at €1,046.88 in Q2 2026 (CSO), and Cork's big employers paying above that, the city offers the best balance of salary and cost in the country, provided you can find somewhere to live before the next rent rise.

articles.title: Cost of living in Galway
articles.note: Galway's 2026 rents, house prices, transport and bills, with budgets for singles and families and a city comparison.
articles.description: Galway is the smallest of Ireland's main cities and, for many people, the most likeable: a compact medieval centre, the sea at Salthill, a big student…
articles.previewHtml:
Galway is the smallest of Ireland's main cities and, for many people, the most likeable: a compact medieval centre, the sea at Salthill, a big student population and a medtech cluster (Medtronic, Boston Scientific and many smaller firms) that provides well-paid work. The trade-off is housing. Galway has the tightest rental market outside Dublin, and in 2026 its rents are rising faster than anywhere else in the country. Here is what to expect.

Rent in Galway in 2026

The RTB Rent Index for Q1 2026 shows the standardised average rent for a new tenancy in Galway City at €2,004 a month, the first time the city has passed €2,000, and €1,718 across County Galway. That makes Galway City the most expensive city in Ireland after Dublin (€2,301). Daft.ie's Q2 2026 report recorded market rents in Galway City up 13% year-on-year, the highest rate of any city, with a two-bed apartment averaging €2,336, slightly above Cork and Limerick.
articles.gatedHtml:
Daft's Q1 2026 asking rents give the fuller picture: a one-bed apartment in the city averaged €1,547, a two-bed €2,290, a three-bed house €2,492 and a double room in a shared house €773. Because the University of Galway and ATU enrol tens of thousands of students, competition is fiercest in late August and September; if you can time your arrival for the spring, do. Popular areas include Salthill and Knocknacarra to the west, Renmore and Roscam to the east, and Oranmore, Athenry and Moycullen if you have a car. Rents in County Galway towns (a two-bed at €1,533 in Q1 2026) are noticeably lower.

Buying a home

The Daft.ie House Price Report for Q2 2026 puts the average three-bed semi in Galway City at €626,000, up 4.4% in a year and higher than Dublin's €580,000, reflecting a very small stock of family homes in the city itself. articles.description: Limerick is the city that relocation guides used to skip, and that is exactly why it deserves a look. It has a university (UL), a growing tech and…
articles.previewHtml:
Limerick is the city that relocation guides used to skip, and that is exactly why it deserves a look. It has a university (UL), a growing tech and financial-services base (Analog Devices, Johnson and Johnson, Northern Trust, Dell), Shannon Airport twenty minutes away and the cheapest house prices of any Irish city. Rent, however, has been climbing steeply since 2024, so the old "Limerick is cheap" reputation needs updating. Here are the 2026 figures.

Rent in Limerick in 2026

The RTB Rent Index for Q1 2026 puts the standardised average rent for a new tenancy in Limerick City at €1,921 a month and across County Limerick at €1,744. Limerick City has now overtaken Cork City (€1,903) and sits just behind Galway (€2,004). The RTB notes that new-tenancy rents in Limerick City have risen by €410 a month since Q1 2024, and that the gap between what new and sitting tenants pay is the widest in the country at 52.3%, or €660 a month. In other words, existing tenants have a great deal and newcomers do not.
articles.gatedHtml:
Daft.ie's asking rents for Q1 2026 show a one-bed apartment in Limerick City at €1,800, a two-bed at €2,187 (rising to €2,244 by Q2 2026, up 11% in a year), a three-bed house at €2,563 and a double room in a shared house at €687, the cheapest room rate of the four main cities. Castletroy and Annacotty are popular with UL staff and families, Raheen and Dooradoyle for the hospital and industrial estate, and the city centre and Ennis Road for people who want to walk to work. Towns in County Limerick and across the river in Clare (Shannon, Ennis) are cheaper still.

Property type (Daft.ie Q1 2026 asking rents)Limerick CityCork CityGalway CityDublin
Studio€1,075€1,198€1,174not listed
One-bed apartment€1,800€1,806€1,547€2,012
Two-bed apartment€2,187€2,126€2,290€2,609
Three-bed house€2,563€2,516€2,492€3,162
Double room, shared house€687€757€773€918 (North City)

Buying: Limerick's real advantage

The gap opens up when you buy. The Daft.ie House Price Report for Q2 2026 puts the average three-bed semi in Limerick City at €379,000, up just 1.9% in a year, compared with €439,000 in Cork, €580,000 in Dublin and €626,000 in Galway. The CSO's Residential Property Price Index shows the Mid-West region (Limerick, Clare and Tipperary) up 5.6% in the 12 months to June 2026, but from a low base. A couple on two average salaries (CSO average weekly earnings were €1,046.88 in Q2 2026) can realistically buy a family home in Limerick within a few years of arriving, which is not true of Dublin or Galway. Local Property Tax on a €379,000 home is €333 a year at the basic rate.

Transport

Bus Éireann city services cost €1.50 a single with a Leap card (75 cent for students and young adults), and Limerick is part of the national TFI network. The city is flat and compact, and the Shannon riverside paths make cycling pleasant. Most people who work at the industrial estates in Raheen or the National Technology Park in Castletroy drive, and traffic is lighter than in Cork or Galway. Shannon Airport has direct flights to the UK, mainland Europe and the US, and the train to Dublin Heuston takes about two hours. If you drive, budget for motor tax, insurance and fuel; insurance quotes for new arrivals without an Irish claims history are high everywhere in Ireland.

Groceries, energy and bills

Supermarket prices do not vary by city. Allow €260 to €350 a month for one person and about €700 for a family of four, based on the CSO Household Budget Survey average of €161 a week per household. The Milk Market on Saturdays is Limerick's best food market. Energy costs the same as elsewhere: average annual bills were about €1,805 for electricity and €1,429 for gas in July 2026, so roughly €270 a month for a house with both and €100 to €150 for an apartment on electricity alone. Many older houses in the county are on oil heating, at about €1,270 per 1,000 litres in August 2026. Broadband runs €25 to €60 and a SIM-only mobile plan €10 to €15.

Healthcare and childcare are national: a GP visit costs €50 to €70, the Drugs Payment Scheme caps prescriptions at €80 a month per family, and from September 2026 full-time creche fees in Core Funding services are capped at €183.70 a week after the universal subsidy.

A monthly budget for Limerick

ItemSingle person, one-bedCouple with one child, three-bed house
Rent€1,800€2,563
Energy€130€270
Broadband and mobile€55€80
Groceries€300€550
Transport (bus)€60€120
Childcare€0€796
Health allowance€40€80
Total before leisureabout €2,385about €4,460

On rent alone, Limerick no longer undercuts Cork, and one-bed apartments are as dear as Cork's. Where it wins is on shared rooms, house prices and commute times, and on the simple fact that your salary in a multinational here is close to what you would earn in Dublin while your mortgage would be a third smaller.

articles.description: Where you live in Ireland matters more to your budget than almost any other decision. A new tenancy in Dublin costs more than double one in Leitrim, and…
articles.previewHtml:
Where you live in Ireland matters more to your budget than almost any other decision. A new tenancy in Dublin costs more than double one in Leitrim, and the commuter counties around the capital are now dearer than Cork or Galway. This guide gives you the latest official rent figures for every county, explains the two main sources and what they measure, and shows how the figures differ between a new lease and an existing one.

Two sources, two different numbers

The RTB Rent Index is the official series, compiled by the Residential Tenancies Board with the ESRI from actual registered tenancies. Its "standardised average rent" adjusts for the mix of property types, so it is the best like-for-like comparison between counties. It publishes separate figures for new tenancies (what you will pay as a newcomer) and existing tenancies (what sitting tenants pay, which is much lower because annual increases are capped). The latest edition is Q1 2026, published in September 2026.
articles.gatedHtml:
The Daft.ie Rental Report uses asking rents on advertised listings, so it runs a quarter ahead of the RTB and tends to be higher, because only new lettings are advertised and landlords list at the top of the range. Its latest edition is Q2 2026. Both are worth checking; the RTB tells you the average, Daft tells you what you will actually see on your phone.

Headline figures for 2026

The RTB's national standardised average rent for a new tenancy was €1,839 a month in Q1 2026, up 9.1% in a year, while existing tenancies averaged €1,513 (up 4.2%). Dublin was €2,335 for new tenancies, the Greater Dublin Area counties (Meath, Kildare, Wicklow) €1,806 and the rest of the country €1,432. Ten counties recorded annual increases of at least 10%. Daft.ie's Q2 2026 report put a two-bed apartment at €2,204 nationally, with rents rising 1.4% in the quarter, a slowdown from a record 4.4% in Q1.

Average rent by county

Sources: RTB Rent Index Q1 2026 (standardised average rent in new tenancies, rounded to the nearest euro) and Daft.ie Rental Report Q1 2026 (average asking rent for a two-bedroom apartment). For Cork, Galway, Limerick and Waterford the Daft figures are split between the city and the rest of the county.

The five cities

Cities are dearer than the counties around them. The RTB Q1 2026 figures for new tenancies are Dublin City €2,301, Galway City €2,004, Limerick City €1,921 and Cork City €1,903. Within Dublin, Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown was highest at €2,629 and South Dublin lowest at €2,267. Daft.ie's Q2 2026 asking rents for a two-bed apartment were €2,634 in Dublin, €2,336 in Galway, €2,244 in Limerick and €2,168 in Cork, with annual growth of 6.5% in Dublin but 11% to 13% in the other three. Rent growth is now fastest outside the capital.

How to read the table when you are budgeting

Take the RTB new-tenancy figure as your realistic floor for a decent one- or two-bed, and the Daft figure as what a two-bed will be advertised at. If you are moving with a family and need a three-bed house, add roughly 15% to 25% to the Daft two-bed figure; in Q1 2026 a three-bed house averaged €3,162 in Dublin, €2,468 across the other four cities and €2,080 in the rest of Leinster. If you are single and happy to share, a double room averaged €806 nationwide and €1,002 in Dublin city centre.

Two further points. First, rent controls have applied to the whole country since June 2025, and since 1 March 2026 annual increases are capped nationwide at 2% or inflation, whichever is lower, so the premium you pay is at the start. Second, the counties nearest Dublin (Kildare, Wicklow, Meath, Louth) are only 15% to 25% cheaper than the capital, while the train or bus commute can be an hour or more. Counties such as Westmeath, Carlow and Laois, one stop further out, are where the savings become substantial.

  • Citizens Information: renting a home
  • CSO price statistics

articles.description: Ireland and the UK share a language, a Common Travel Area that lets citizens of each live and work freely in the other, and a lot of the same shops. What…
articles.previewHtml:
Ireland and the UK share a language, a Common Travel Area that lets citizens of each live and work freely in the other, and a lot of the same shops. What they do not share is a cost structure. Ireland pays more, taxes differently, charges you to see a doctor and has a far tighter housing market. Here is how the two compare on the numbers that matter in 2026, in each country's own currency.

Rent and housing

Ireland's rental market is smaller, tighter and dearer relative to income. The RTB Rent Index puts the average new tenancy at €1,839 a month nationally and €2,335 in Dublin in Q1 2026, and Daft.ie counted fewer than 2,400 homes to rent in the entire country in August 2026. The UK's ONS puts the average private rent at £1,383 a month in May 2026, with London at £2,294 and the North East at about £770. In practice London and Dublin cost similar amounts for a one-bed in a good area, while every other UK city is markedly cheaper than Cork, Galway or Limerick, where the RTB average new tenancy was €1,903 to €2,004. Rent control also differs: since March 2026 Ireland caps annual increases nationwide at 2% or inflation, whichever is lower, while England has no rent caps.
articles.gatedHtml:
Buying is similar in the two capitals and cheaper in Ireland's regions than in southern England. The CSO's national median price paid was €396,000 in the 12 months to June 2026; Daft.ie puts a three-bed semi at €580,000 in Dublin, €439,000 in Cork and €379,000 in Limerick.

Income tax and take-home pay

Ireland has a lower entry point into the higher rate but more generous credits at the bottom. A single person pays 20% on the first €44,000 and 40% above that, plus USC (0.5% to 8%) and 4.2% PRSI, with €4,000 of tax credits. In the UK you pay nothing on the first £12,570, 20% up to £50,270, 40% up to £125,140 and 45% above, plus 8% National Insurance on earnings between £242 and £967 a week. Broadly, low and middle earners keep a similar share of their pay in both countries, while high earners keep a little more in the UK because Ireland's 40% band starts so much earlier and USC adds up to 8% on top. Ireland has no council tax; homeowners pay Local Property Tax instead (€333 a year on a €400,000 home at the basic rate), against an average Band D council tax of £2,392 in England in 2026/27, which tenants pay too.

Healthcare

This is the biggest practical difference. The NHS is free at the point of use for residents, with a £9.90 prescription charge in England (free in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland). Ireland's public system is free for inpatient hospital care, but you pay €50 to €70 to see a GP unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card (all children under 8 and adults over 70 do), €100 to attend an emergency department without a referral, and up to €80 a month for prescriptions under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Waiting lists for public consultants are long, so about half the population carries private health insurance at an average of €1,902 a year per adult (Health Insurance Authority, March 2026). Budget €100 to €200 a month for healthcare in Ireland that would cost you nothing in the UK.

Childcare and schools

The UK has moved faster on childcare. Since September 2025, working parents in England get 30 funded hours a week (38 weeks a year) from nine months to school age; families who do not qualify pay an average of £189 a week for a part-time under-two place (Coram, 2026). Ireland caps creche fees instead: from September 2026 a full-time place in a Core Funding service costs at most €183.70 a week after the universal subsidy, and less again with income-assessed subsidies, plus two free preschool years from age 3. State schools are free in both countries.

Wages and everyday prices

Irish wages are higher in nominal terms. The minimum wage is €14.15 against the UK's £12.71, and CSO average weekly earnings were €1,046.88 in Q2 2026 (about €54,400 a year). Groceries cost a little more in Ireland, and energy noticeably more: Irish electricity is 35 to 38 cent per kWh and the average annual bill about €1,805. Public transport is cheaper in Ireland: a Dublin 90-minute fare is €2 and a monthly bus and Luas ticket €96.

Which is cheaper?

For a single professional, Dublin and London cost about the same and both are hard on renters; Dublin wins on transport and loses on healthcare and energy. For a family, the UK's free GP care and funded childcare hours make a real difference, but Ireland's regional cities give you a house you can afford on two ordinary salaries, which is increasingly rare in southern England. For anyone from outside the Common Travel Area, Ireland's EU membership is an advantage no cost table captures.

articles.title: Ireland vs the Netherlands and Germany for expats
articles.appTitle: Ireland vs the Netherlands and Germany for expats
articles.note: How Ireland compares with the Netherlands and Germany on rent, tax, the 30% ruling, health insurance and childcare.
articles.description: Ireland, the Netherlands and Germany compete for the same people: English-speaking tech, pharma, finance and engineering professionals who can pick where…
articles.previewHtml:
Ireland, the Netherlands and Germany compete for the same people: English-speaking tech, pharma, finance and engineering professionals who can pick where in the EU to build a career. All three are safe, well-paid and expensive, but they distribute the cost very differently. Ireland charges you at the estate agent, the Netherlands at the tax office and Germany, comparatively, at neither. Here is how they line up in 2026 if you are choosing between Dublin, Amsterdam and Berlin or Munich.

Rent: Ireland is the outlier

Ireland has the tightest housing market of the three. The RTB's average new tenancy was €1,839 a month nationally and €2,335 in Dublin in Q1 2026, with a Dublin one-bed advertised at around €2,012 (Daft.ie). The Netherlands is close behind in the cities: Pararius reports free-sector rents averaging €20.94 per square metre nationally in Q2 2026 and €28.69 per square metre in Amsterdam, which puts a typical 60-square-metre Amsterdam apartment at roughly €1,700 and a larger one well above €2,000. Germany is cheaper almost everywhere: the HousingAnywhere index for Q1 2026 puts a one-bed at about €1,590 in Berlin and €1,815 in Munich, and around €814 as a national average. Tenant protections are strongest in Germany, where unlimited leases are the norm, and weakest in Ireland, where competition for viewings is intense.
articles.gatedHtml:
Income tax and social charges

Headline rates flatter Ireland and mislead about the Netherlands. In Ireland a single person pays 20% up to €44,000, then 40%, plus USC of up to 8% and 4.2% PRSI, offset by €4,000 of credits. The Netherlands charges 35.75% on the first €38,883 (of which 27.65 points are social security premiums), 37.56% to €78,426 and 49.5% above, with general and labour tax credits softening the bottom. Germany starts at 0% up to a €12,348 allowance, then rises on a curve from 14% to 42% at €69,878, with 45% at very high incomes, plus social contributions of roughly 20% of gross pay for pension, health, unemployment and care insurance (matched by your employer).

The Netherlands has one weapon the others lack: the 30% ruling, which lets qualifying recruits from abroad receive 30% of salary tax-free for five years if they earn at least €48,013 in 2026. On an €80,000 salary that is worth roughly €9,800 a year and closes most of the gap with Ireland. Ireland's equivalent, SARP, only applies to intra-company transfers above €100,000. Germany has no expat tax break.

Item (2026)IrelandNetherlandsGermany
Capital-city rent, one-bedabout €2,012 Dublin (Daft Q1 2026)€28.69 per sq m Amsterdam (Pararius Q2 2026)about €1,590 Berlin (HousingAnywhere Q1 2026)
National average rent€1,839 new tenancy (RTB Q1 2026)€20.94 per sq m free sectorabout €814 one-bed
Minimum wage€14.15 an hour€14.99 an hour (from July 2026)€13.90 an hour
Higher tax rate starts40% at €44,00049.5% at €78,42642% at €69,878
Expat tax reliefSARP (limited)30% ruling (from €48,013 salary)None
Health coverPublic; GP €50 to €70; private cover avg €1,902 a yearMandatory insurance avg €159.30 a month plus €385 deductibleStatutory insurance about 17.5% of gross (half paid by employer)
Full-time childcareMax €183.70 a week after universal subsidySubsidised up to €11.23 an hour; up to 96% refunded for lower incomesFree in Berlin (meals about €23 a month); varies by state

Healthcare

The Dutch and German systems are insurance-based and, once you are enrolled, comprehensive. In the Netherlands you must buy basic insurance from a private insurer at an average of €159.30 a month in 2026, pay the first €385 of most non-GP care each year, and can claim a healthcare allowance (zorgtoeslag) on a modest income. In Germany, statutory insurance costs 14.6% of gross salary plus an average 2.9% supplementary rate, split with your employer, and covers your non-working spouse and children for free. Ireland's public system is free for hospital stays but charges €50 to €70 per GP visit and up to €80 a month for prescriptions, and public waiting lists push about half the population into private insurance at an average €1,902 a year. For a family with young children, Germany is clearly the cheapest of the three to get sick in.

Childcare and family costs

Germany wins again for families, at least in Berlin, where daycare is free from age one apart from a small meals contribution; other states charge, typically on a sliding income scale. The Netherlands subsidises daycare through the kinderopvangtoeslag up to €11.23 an hour in 2026, refunding up to 96% for lower earners, though many Amsterdam creches charge above the cap. Ireland's new fee cap of €183.70 a week (about €796 a month) for a full-time place is a big improvement on the €1,000-plus monthly bills of a few years ago, and income-assessed subsidies reduce it further. All three offer free state schooling; Ireland's is in English.

Wages and the bottom line

Ireland pays the highest salaries in nominal terms: the minimum wage is €14.15, CSO average weekly earnings were €1,046.88 in Q2 2026, and multinational salaries in Dublin are generally above Amsterdam and Berlin equivalents for the same role. Against that, Dublin rent will eat roughly a third to a half of a single person's net pay, and there is no tax break to soften year one. The Netherlands gives you the 30% ruling, a functioning cycling city and rents almost as bad as Dublin's. Germany gives you the lowest rents, the cheapest childcare and healthcare, and a language barrier plus a heavier tax wedge on middle incomes. If you are single, in tech and want the highest gross salary in an English-speaking EU country, Ireland is hard to beat; if you are moving with children on a middle income, look seriously at Germany.

  • Revenue: Irish tax rates and bands

articles.title: How to rent accommodation in Ireland
articles.appTitle: How to Rent Accommodation in Ireland
articles.description: Renting accommodation in Ireland can be a challenging process, but with the right tips, you can make it a smooth experience. Whether you're a student, a…
articles.previewHtml:
Renting accommodation in Ireland can be a challenging process, but with the right tips, you can make it a smooth experience. Whether you're a student, a professional, finding a place to call home in Ireland can be a daunting task. But with the right resources and a clear understanding of the process, you can find a suitable place to rent that fits your needs and budget.

We will go through all these in-depth in the next steps but, here is the summary to help you rent accommodation in Ireland:
articles.gatedHtml:
Determine your budget: Determine how much you can afford to spend on rent each month, and keep in mind other expenses such as utilities, internet, and transportation.

Research the areas you want to live in: Take the time to research different areas in Ireland to determine where you would like to live. Consider factors such as proximity to work, public transportation, and the availability of amenities such as shops and restaurants.

Use online resources: Take advantage of the numerous online resources available for finding rental properties in Ireland. Websites such as Daft.ie and MyHome.ie are popular.

Set an alert for the new adverts: Websites such as Daft.ie and MyHome.ie have a notification feature when a new house available to rent on the market. Make sure you set an alarm and get the new adverts to email. It is crucial being proactive seeker in a very competitive market.

Contact a letting agent: If you are having difficulty finding a suitable property, consider contacting a letting agent. They have access to a wide range of properties and can assist you in finding the right place for you.

Prepare necessary documents: Before you start looking for a rental property, make sure you have all the necessary documents ready. You will need a valid form of identification, proof of income, and references from your previous landlord or employer.

View properties in person: Once you have found some properties you are interested in, arrange to view them in person. This will give you a better idea of what the property is like and help you make a more informed decision.

Sign the lease: Once you have agreed on the rent and other terms, sign the lease. Make sure you understand all the terms and conditions before signing.

Renting accommodation in Ireland can be a challenge, but with the right approach, you can find a suitable place to call home. Keep these tips in mind, and you will be well on your way to finding the perfect rental property in Ireland.

articles.title: Determine your budget
articles.description: When renting accommodation in Ireland, it's important to be prepared for a few upfront costs. Here are a few key things to keep in mind:
articles.previewHtml: When renting accommodation in Ireland, it's important to be prepared for a few upfront costs. Here are a few key things to keep in mind:
articles.gatedHtml:
Rent: Rent is usually paid on a monthly basis, and you'll need to pay your first month's rent upfront. Be sure to budget accordingly and have enough funds available.

Deposit: You'll likely be required to pay a deposit before moving in, which is typically equivalent to one or two months' worth of rent. Make sure you have enough funds to cover this expense.

Utilities: As a tenant, you'll typically be responsible for paying utilities such as electricity, gas, and water. Make sure to factor this into your budget when deciding how much rent you can afford to pay. Some rental properties may include a fixed amount for utilities in the monthly rent, while others may require you to set up and pay for these services yourself.
articles.plainText:

Deposit: You'll likely be required to pay a deposit before moving in, which is typically equivalent to one or two months' worth of rent. Make sure you have enough funds to cover this expense.

Utilities: As a tenant, you'll typically be responsible for paying utilities such as electricity, gas, and water. Make sure to factor this into your budget when deciding how much rent you can afford to pay. Some rental properties may include a fixed amount for utilities in the monthly rent, while others may require you to set up and pay for these services yourself.

articles.title: Research the area you want to live in
articles.appTitle: Research the area you want to live in
articles.description: Before making any decisions on where to live in Ireland, it is crucial to conduct thorough research on the areas you're interested in. Take the time to…
articles.previewHtml: Before making any decisions on where to live in Ireland, it is crucial to conduct thorough research on the areas you're interested in. Take the time to explore different neighborhoods, get to know the local communities, and find out what amenities and services are nearby.
articles.gatedHtml:
Consider factors such as transportation, access to shops, parks, and other essential services. Seek information about the safety of the area and any other concerns that may be relevant to you. With all this information, you will be in a better position to make an informed decision on the best place to call home in Ireland.

Is Ireland safe?

Ireland is recognized as a highly safe country, ranking as one of the top-10 safest in the world according to the 2022 Global Peace Index. However, Dublin, being the largest city in Ireland with a metropolitan population nearly double the size of the next largest city, Belfast, may require a different approach in terms of safety. How a great message should be?

When sending a message to a landlord to inquire about a rental property, it's important to include certain information in order to make a good impression and increase your chances of securing the property. A good message to a landlord should include the following elements:

Introduction: Start by introducing yourself and why you're interested in the property.

Reason for the move: Provide a brief explanation of why you're looking to move, such as a change in job or lifestyle.

Occupants: Mention the number of people who will be living in the property and their relationship to you.

Budget: Indicate your budget and any relevant information about your income, such as employment status or salary.

Move-in date: Specify the date you are looking to move in and how long you are hoping to rent for.

References: Offer to provide references, including previous landlords or employers, if necessary.

Contact information: Provide your contact information, including a phone number and email address.

By including these elements in your message, you can demonstrate your professionalism and reliability to the landlord and increase your chances of securing the property.

articles.title: Prepare necessary documents
articles.description: When applying for an apartment or a house rental in Ireland, the following documents are usually required:
articles.previewHtml:
When applying for an apartment or a house rental in Ireland, the following documents are usually required:

Identification: A government-issued ID such as a passport or a driver's license.
articles.gatedHtml:
Proof of income: You will need to provide proof of income, such as a recent pay stub, a letter of employment or a tax return, to show that you have a steady source of income to pay the rent.

Renting history: Landlords will often ask for proof of your renting history, such as references from previous landlords or proof of payments from your previous rental.

Bank statements: You may be asked to provide recent bank statements to demonstrate that you have a stable financial situation and the means to pay the rent.

Guarantor: In some cases, a landlord may require a guarantor, who is a person who agrees to pay the rent if you are unable to do so. A guarantor will need to provide proof of income, as well as identification.

It is important to note that the requirements may vary between landlords and letting agencies. It is always best to ask in advance what specific documentation is needed to avoid any confusion or delays in the rental application process.

articles.title: View properties in person
articles.description: When viewing properties in person before renting in Ireland, there are several factors to consider:
articles.previewHtml:
When viewing properties in person before renting in Ireland, there are several factors to consider:

Location: Is the property located in a convenient and desirable area, near public transportation, amenities, and other necessities?
articles.gatedHtml:
Condition of the property: Is the property well-maintained and in good condition? Are there any noticeable repairs or upgrades that need to be made?

Space and layout: Does the property have enough space for your needs, both in terms of the living area and storage? Is the layout functional and suitable for your lifestyle?

Amenities: What kind of amenities are included in the property and surrounding area? Are they adequate and in good condition?

Cost: Is the cost of rent within your budget, and does it include any additional expenses such as utilities or parking?

Landlord/management: What is the reputation of the landlord or management company, and what is their track record in maintaining the property and addressing tenant concerns?

Safety and security: Is the property safe and secure, with good locks, proper lighting, and well-maintained common areas?

It's important to take the time to carefully evaluate these factors before making a final decision to rent a property in Ireland.

articles.description: When signing a lease for a rental property in Ireland, it's important to consider the following factors:
articles.previewHtml:
When signing a lease for a rental property in Ireland, it's important to consider the following factors:

Rent and security deposit: Make sure you fully understand the amount of rent you will be paying each month, as well as any security deposit required.

Lease term: Make sure you are comfortable with the length of the lease and whether it is a fixed-term or rolling lease.
articles.gatedHtml:
Maintenance and repair responsibilities: Make sure you understand who is responsible for any maintenance or repairs that need to be carried out.

Restrictions and conditions: Make sure you understand any restrictions or conditions that apply to the use of the property, such as restrictions on subletting or making alterations.

Utilities and services: Make sure you understand what utilities and services are included in the rent, such as electricity, or internet.

Termination clause: Make sure you understand the terms under which either you or the landlord can end the lease, and the notice period required.

Insurance: Make sure you understand whether you need to take out insurance to protect your personal belongings and if so, who will be responsible for the cost.

It is important to carefully read and fully understand all the terms and conditions of the lease before signing, and if you need any clarification, seek advice from a legal professional.

articles.title: Tenancy Rights
articles.description: Tenancy rights are the rights and protections granted to tenants under the law. In Ireland, the rights of tenants are defined by the Residential…
articles.previewHtml:
Tenancy rights are the rights and protections granted to tenants under the law. In Ireland, the rights of tenants are defined by the Residential Tenancies Act 2004 and subsequent amendments. As a tenant, it is important to understand these rights and how they affect your living situation. This article provides an overview of some key tenancy rights in Ireland.

Right to a written tenancy agreement: In Ireland, all tenancy agreements must be in writing and signed by both the landlord and the tenant. This agreement should outline the terms of the tenancy, including the rental amount, the length of the tenancy, and any other relevant terms.
articles.gatedHtml:
Right to privacy: Tenants have the right to privacy and quiet enjoyment of their rental property. This means that landlords cannot enter the property without permission, unless it is an emergency, or in accordance with the terms of the tenancy agreement.

Right to rent control: Rent control is an important aspect of tenancy rights in Ireland. The Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) sets the maximum amount of rent that can be charged for a property, and landlords cannot charge more than this amount. Tenants have the right to challenge any rent increases that they believe are excessive.

Right to repair and maintenance: Landlords are responsible for keeping the rental property in good condition, and for making any necessary repairs. Tenants have the right to request repairs and to expect the landlord to carry them out in a timely manner.

Right to termination: Tenants have the right to terminate a tenancy agreement if they are unhappy with their living situation or if their circumstances have changed. However, they must give the landlord the appropriate notice, as outlined in the tenancy agreement.

Right to security of tenure: In Ireland, tenants have the right to security of tenure, which means that they cannot be evicted from their property without just cause. Landlords must follow a specific process in order to legally evict a tenant, which involves obtaining a court order.

In conclusion, tenants in Ireland have a number of rights and protections under the law. These rights are designed to ensure that tenants can live in their rental properties in a safe and comfortable manner, and to protect their rights as tenants. It is important to be aware of these rights and to assert them if necessary, in order to have a positive rental experience.

Discover your rights as a tenant in Ireland through the Residential Tenancies Board. Get informed on your responsibilities and obligations.

articles.title: Common Rental Scams
articles.description: Rental scams can happen anywhere and can affect anyone looking to rent a property. In Ireland, some common rental scams include:
articles.previewHtml:
Rental scams can happen anywhere and can affect anyone looking to rent a property. In Ireland, some common rental scams include:

False advertising: Some scammers post fake ads for rental properties, either with made-up information or stolen photos, and ask for a deposit or rental fee in advance. When you show up to the property, you'll realize it's not available, and you've lost your money.
articles.gatedHtml:
Fake landlords: Some scammers pose as landlords and ask for a deposit or rent upfront before you even see the property. They might also ask for sensitive information such as your passport or ID.

Phishing: Scammers send emails that appear to be from real estate agents, landlords, or property management companies, asking for sensitive information such as your bank account details or credit card number.

Rental deposit scams: Scammers claim to be property owners and ask for a deposit in advance. After you send the money, you'll never hear from them again.

To protect yourself from these scams, it's important to be cautious and do your due diligence when looking for a rental property in Ireland. Always visit the property in person, check the credentials of the landlord or agent, and never send money without seeing the property first. It's also a good idea to research the market rates for similar properties to avoid overpriced listings.

articles.title: Irish housing standards
articles.description: Housing in Ireland, like in any other country, can vary greatly in terms of quality and safety. If you're considering a rental property in Ireland, it's…
articles.previewHtml:
Housing in Ireland, like in any other country, can vary greatly in terms of quality and safety. If you're considering a rental property in Ireland, it's important to be aware of some common issues that may arise.

Homes built in the 1990s or 2000s may have problems such as missing insulation, ungrounded electrical systems, and open attics that are exposed to the elements. Additionally, the low water pressure in Dublin means that many homes have storage tanks for the upstairs bathroom that are open on top, potentially harboring dead animals.
articles.gatedHtml:
When looking at floor plans, it's important to note that “HP” stands for “hot press,” which is essentially a closet with a poorly insulated water heater that may be used for drying clothes or as a linen cupboard. Additionally, many homes in Ireland still have an immersion switch, which can increase your electric bill by up to €100 per month and require you to schedule showers in advance.

It's also important to be mindful of the safety of the water supply in your rental property. Avoid drinking from any tap except for the one in the kitchen, and make sure that you're aware of any potential health hazards.

Latest standards introduced by government in last years

In Ireland, the standard of housing varies greatly, ranging from older, traditional properties to new, modern buildings. However, all properties must adhere to certain safety standards and building regulations, as set out by the government. These regulations cover a range of areas, including heating, electrical safety, fire safety, and structural integrity.

In terms of energy efficiency, the government has set minimum standards for new buildings, as well as a target for all homes to have a BER (Building Energy Rating) of A3 by 2030. This rating system assesses the energy efficiency of a building, considering factors such as insulation, heating, and ventilation.

Additionally, the government has introduced the "Better Energy Warmer Homes" scheme, which provides financial support for low-income households to improve the energy efficiency of their homes.

Overall, the standard of housing in Ireland has improved greatly in recent years, but there is still much room for improvement, particularly in terms of energy efficiency. The government is committed to improving the standard of housing in Ireland, and is implementing various initiatives to achieve this goal.

articles.title: Best areas to live in Dublin for families
articles.appTitle: Best areas to live in Dublin for families
articles.note: Family suburbs north and south of Dublin with schools, parks, commutes and Q2 2026 house rents by region.
articles.description: Moving to Dublin with children changes the question from "where is fun" to "where can we get a school place, a garden, a park and a commute that does not…
articles.previewHtml:
Moving to Dublin with children changes the question from "where is fun" to "where can we get a school place, a garden, a park and a commute that does not eat the evening". This guide walks through the suburbs that families in Dublin consistently choose, what each one offers, and what a family-sized home costs there right now. Rent figures come from the Daft.ie Rental Report for the second quarter of 2026 (published August 2026) and the RTB Rent Index for the first quarter of 2026, so treat them as a snapshot rather than a promise.

What to weigh up before you pick an area

Three things decide most family moves in Dublin. First, school places: primary schools in popular suburbs fill up, and many use catchment or "first come" enrolment policies, so you should check each school's admission policy on its website before signing a lease. Second, green space: Dublin is well served by large parks, but they are unevenly spread. Third, the commute: a house that looks affordable in the west of the county can cost you 90 minutes a day if it is not on the Luas, DART or a rail line. Read our commuter guide alongside this one.
articles.gatedHtml:
Also consider the type of school your family wants. Most primary schools are Catholic-patron national schools, but every area now has Educate Together (multi-denominational) and Gaelscoil (Irish-language) options, and secondary school choice is wider again. Citizens Information explains how enrolment works.

North side favourites

Clontarf and Raheny (Dublin 3 and Dublin 5) sit on Dublin Bay with the seafront promenade, Dollymount Strand and St Anne's Park, one of the largest parks in the city with playgrounds, a rose garden and weekend markets. Both are on the DART, about 10 to 15 minutes from Connolly. Rents are high but you get established schools and a real village feel.

Malahide and Portmarnock in north County Dublin are the classic family choice: a marina, the beach, Malahide Castle demesne with its playground and fairy trail, and a DART ride of roughly 25 minutes to Connolly. Expect to compete for houses here; supply is tight.

South Dublin City (Rathmines, Rathfarnham, Terenure)€2,779 (+4.8%)€3,464 (+2.2%)€4,531 (+8.7%)
North County (Malahide, Swords, Portmarnock)€2,353 (+8.0%)€2,803 (+7.5%)€3,717 (+13.4%)

Existing tenants pay noticeably less, which is why families who find a good house tend to stay put.

Practical tips for a family move

  • Apply to schools before you have an address if you can; many accept applications for the following September from early autumn.
  • Ask the letting agent whether the property is a "family let". Some landlords prefer families for longer tenancies, which can work in your favour.
  • Check the Dublin Bus, Luas and DART journey planner from the actual door of the house, not the suburb name.
  • Look for a home within walking distance of a primary school; the school run in Dublin traffic is a daily cost people underestimate.
  • Register your children with a GP as soon as you arrive. Children under 8 are entitled to a free GP visit card.

articles.appTitle: Best areas of Dublin for young professionals
articles.note: Docklands, Dublin 6, Stoneybatter and more, with Q2 2026 studio, one-bed and room rents by region.
articles.description: If you are moving to Dublin for work and do not have children in tow, your priorities are probably a short commute, somewhere to eat and meet people…
articles.previewHtml:
If you are moving to Dublin for work and do not have children in tow, your priorities are probably a short commute, somewhere to eat and meet people after work, and a rent that leaves something at the end of the month. Dublin is compact, so the trade-off is usually between paying more to live within walking distance of the office or paying less and relying on the Luas or DART. This guide covers the neighbourhoods that young professionals tend to pick, with current rents from the Daft.ie Rental Report for Q2 2026 (published August 2026).

How the numbers look in 2026

Dublin is expensive, and 2026 has not been kind to newcomers. The Daft.ie report puts the average rent for a two-bedroom apartment in Dublin at €2,551 in Q2 2026, and the RTB Rent Index for Q1 2026 shows new tenants in Dublin City paying a standardised average of €2,301 a month, 8.3% more than a year earlier. Most single professionals therefore either share a house or apartment, or rent a one-bed close to work. The table below gives you the Daft.ie figures by region for the property types you are most likely to look at.
articles.gatedHtml:
Dublin region (Daft.ie, Q2 2026)Studio1-bed apartment2-bed apartmentDouble room, no en suite
City Centre (Dublin 1, 2, 7, 8 core)€1,563€2,019€2,669€947
North Dublin City (Phibsborough, Drumcondra, Clontarf)€1,456€1,960€2,473€904
South Dublin City (Rathmines, Ranelagh, Portobello)€1,589€2,083€2,839€916
North County (Swords, Malahide)€1,360€1,930€2,443€845
South County (Sandyford, Dundrum, Blackrock)€1,579€2,150€2,654€945
West Dublin (Lucan, Tallaght, Blanchardstown)€1,355€1,869€2,353€842

Docklands and Grand Canal Dock

This is where most of the big tech, finance and law employers sit, and the modern apartment blocks around Grand Canal Dock, Spencer Dock and the Point are built for exactly this market. You get gyms, concierge desks, the Bord Gáis theatre and a five-minute cycle to the city centre. You also pay the highest rents in the city: expect one-beds at or above the City Centre average of €2,019. The Red Line Luas and the DART at Grand Canal Dock and Pearse cover the rest of the city.

Rathmines, Ranelagh and Portobello

South of the canal, Dublin 6 is the traditional home of house shares and first apartments. Ranelagh has the restaurants and a Green Line Luas stop a few minutes from St Stephen's Green; Rathmines has the supermarkets, the Swan Centre, a cinema and the largest choice of older red-brick conversions; Portobello puts you on the canal within a 15-minute walk of Grafton Street. Rents here are the highest outside the Docklands, but the choice of rooms in shared houses is also the widest, at around €916 for a double room in the South City region.

Smithfield, Stoneybatter and Phibsborough

The north-west of the inner city has become the most popular choice for people who want character rather than glass. Stoneybatter's small cottages and independent cafés, Smithfield's apartment blocks on the Red Line, and Phibsborough's Victorian terraces near the Royal Canal are all within a 20 to 30 minute walk of the city centre. The Green Line cross-city extension stops at Phibsborough, Grangegorman and Broadstone, which connects the area to the south side without changing trams. Rents are a step below Dublin 6.

Drumcondra and the north inner suburbs

Drumcondra (Dublin 9) sits between DCU, Croke Park and the city, with Griffith Park and the Tolka riverside walks. It is well served by buses on the Swords Road and is a 25-minute walk from O'Connell Street. Nearby Glasnevin adds the Botanic Gardens. If you work at the airport, at DCU or in the north Docklands, this is a sensible base at North City prices.

Sandyford, Dundrum and the south suburbs

If your job is in the Sandyford business district, Cherrywood or the tech campuses around Leopardstown, living along the Green Line saves you the reverse commute. Sandyford itself is a cluster of newer apartment blocks about 22 minutes by tram from St Stephen's Green; Dundrum adds the shopping centre and a village high street. Rents in South County are close to City Centre levels, so the saving is in time rather than money.

Tips for renting as a newcomer

  • Have your documents ready before viewings: passport, employment contract or offer letter, a landlord reference if you have one, and proof of income. Good properties go within a day.
  • A landlord can ask for at most one month's deposit plus one month's rent in advance. Anything more is not allowed.
  • Claim the Rent Tax Credit through Revenue myAccount: it is worth up to €1,000 a year for a single person in 2026.
  • Use a TFI Leap Card. The 90-minute fare of €2 covers bus, Luas and DART inside the city zone, with a daily cap of €6.
  • Room-only listings on Daft.ie and word of mouth in your new office are still the two most common ways people find their first place.

★ Useful links

  • Daft.ie Rental Report Q2 2026
  • Residential Tenancies Board
  • Revenue: Rent Tax Credit
  • Transport for Ireland fares
  • Citizens Information: renting a home

articles.title: Best Dublin suburbs for commuters
articles.note: DART, Luas and rail suburbs compared by journey time, Leap fare zone and 2026 rent.
articles.description: Dublin's rents fall quickly as you move away from the centre, but only some of the cheaper suburbs have a fast, reliable way in. The trick is to pick a…
articles.previewHtml:
Dublin's rents fall quickly as you move away from the centre, but only some of the cheaper suburbs have a fast, reliable way in. The trick is to pick a place on the DART, the Luas or one of the commuter rail lines, and then check the door-to-door time rather than the distance. This guide lists the suburbs and towns that commuters rate most highly, with typical journey times, the Leap Card fare zone and what rent you should expect. Rents are from the Daft.ie Rental Report for Q2 2026 (published August 2026); journey times are typical scheduled times and vary by service.

How Dublin's commuter network fits together

There are four systems and they meet in the city centre. The DART runs along the coast from Malahide and Howth in the north to Bray and Greystones in the south, every 10 minutes on weekdays. The Luas Green Line runs from Brides Glen through Sandyford, Dundrum and Ranelagh to St Stephen's Green and on to Broombridge; the Luas Red Line links Tallaght and Saggart with Heuston, Abbey Street, Connolly and the Point. Trams run every 3 to 4 minutes at peak. Commuter rail serves Maynooth, Kildare, Drogheda and the towns between, and the DART+ programme is extending electrified services to Maynooth and towards Drogheda over the coming years. Buses fill the gaps, but a bus into the city at 8am is the slowest option.
articles.gatedHtml:
Fares depend on zone. Inside Zone 1 (Dublin city and the DART area) the TFI 90-minute Leap fare is €2 with a daily cap of €6 and a weekly cap of €24. Leap rail singles to the city are €3.90 from Zone 2 (for example Skerries, Greystones, Naas), €6 from Zone 3 (Drogheda, Newbridge, Wicklow town) and €7.50 from Zone 4 (Kildare town, Navan). These are 2026 fares; the NTA has confirmed increases averaging 15% for adults from January 2027.

Commuter suburbs compared

Howth / SuttonDART to Connollyabout 26 min1North County €2,803
Dún LaoghaireDART to Pearseabout 20 min1South County €3,525
BrayDART to Pearseabout 45 min1Co. Wicklow €1,838 (all types)
GreystonesDART to Connollyabout 60 min2Co. Wicklow €1,838 (all types)

SandyfordLuas Green to St Stephen's Greenabout 22 min1South County €3,525

MaynoothRail to Connollyabout 30 to 42 min2Co. Kildare €2,155 (all types)

The county figures for Kildare, Wicklow and Louth are Daft.ie's overall average rent for the county across all property types, so a three-bed house there will usually cost more than the number shown, while an apartment will cost less.

Coastal DART suburbs

The DART is the most pleasant commute in Dublin: frequent, electric, and with a sea view for most of the route. Malahide, Portmarnock, Sutton and Howth on the north side and Blackrock, Dún Laoghaire, Dalkey and Killiney on the south side are all within half an hour of the centre. The catch is price. South County Dublin is the most expensive part of the country to rent in, and the north coast is not far behind. Bray in County Wicklow is the affordable end of the DART, with a long promenade, a busy main street and a 45-minute run into Pearse.

Luas suburbs

Along the Green Line, Dundrum, Stillorgan, Sandyford and Leopardstown give you tram access and large employers on your doorstep, while Cherrywood at the southern end is a new-build district with apartments priced a little below the older suburbs. On the Red Line, Tallaght, Citywest and Saggart are the cheapest tram-connected areas in the county, and Kilmainham and Inchicore are popular older choices closer in. Remember that trams are packed between 8am and 9am; if you board near a terminus you will get a seat.

Rail commuter towns

If you want a house with a garden for the price of a city apartment, look at the rail towns. Maynooth is a university town with a train every 30 minutes, Sallins and Naas and Newbridge have fast services into Heuston, and Balbriggan, Skerries and Drogheda serve the north. Drogheda is the standout value option: a Zone 3 Leap fare of €6 and Louth's average rent of €1,816 buy you a 56-minute train into Connolly. Check whether your employer is near Heuston or Connolly, because switching between the two adds 20 minutes by Luas.

Before you sign

  • Do the journey once at 8am on a weekday before you commit. Timetables and reality differ.
  • Check car parking at the station if you will drive to the train; many stations fill by 7.30am.
  • Ask if your employer offers the TaxSaver commuter ticket scheme, which takes the cost of an annual ticket out of your gross pay.
  • Consider the Bike to Work scheme for the last mile from the station.

  • Irish Rail timetables
  • Luas
  • Daft.ie Rental Report Q2 2026
  • TaxSaver commuter tickets

On the Red Line, Tallaght, Citywest and Saggart are the cheapest tram-connected areas in the county, and Kilmainham and Inchicore are popular older choices closer in. Remember that trams are packed between 8am and 9am; if you board near a terminus you will get a seat.

Rail commuter towns

If you want a house with a garden for the price of a city apartment, look at the rail towns. Maynooth is a university town with a train every 30 minutes, Sallins and Naas and Newbridge have fast services into Heuston, and Balbriggan, Skerries and Drogheda serve the north. Drogheda is the standout value option: a Zone 3 Leap fare of €6 and Louth's average rent of €1,816 buy you a 56-minute train into Connolly. Check whether your employer is near Heuston or Connolly, because switching between the two adds 20 minutes by Luas.

Do the journey once at 8am on a weekday before you commit. Timetables and reality differ.Check car parking at the station if you will drive to the train; many stations fill by 7.30am.Ask if your employer offers the TaxSaver commuter ticket scheme, which takes the cost of an annual ticket out of your gross pay.Consider the Bike to Work scheme for the last mile from the station.

1Dublin City CentreDublin 1, 2, Docklands, inner Dublin 7 and 8€2,801

3North County DublinMalahide, Swords, Portmarnock, Balbriggan€2,542

Ranked by RTB registered rent, Q1 2026

The RTB reports by local authority. These are standardised average rents for the first quarter of 2026 (index published September 2026), with the year-on-year change for new tenancies.

RankLocal authorityNew tenancies, Q1 2026Change on Q1 2025Existing tenancies, Q1 2026
1Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown€2,629+6.8%€2,301
2Dublin City€2,301+8.3%€1,901
3Fingal€2,269+10.4%€1,866
4South Dublin€2,267+6.9%€1,934

Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown is the most expensive local authority in the country on either measure. Fingal, in the north of the county, saw the fastest growth in new-tenancy rents in Dublin over the year.

Ranked by property type

If you already know what you want to rent, this table from the Daft.ie Q2 2026 report is more useful than the regional averages. Figures are monthly asking rents.

Property typeMost expensive regionCheapest region
StudioSouth Dublin City €1,589West Dublin €1,355

2-bed apartmentSouth Dublin City €2,839West Dublin €2,353
3-bed houseSouth County €3,525North County €2,803
4-bed houseSouth Dublin City €4,531West Dublin €3,436
Double room in a shared houseCity Centre €947West Dublin €842

Beyond the county boundary

The steepest drop in rent happens when you cross into the commuter counties. Daft.ie's Q2 2026 averages are €2,155 in Kildare, €1,838 in Wicklow, €1,816 in Louth and €1,569 in Meath, against €2,551 for a two-bed apartment in Dublin. If you can work from home part of the week, or your office is near Heuston or Connolly, a rail town can cut your rent by a third. See our guide to the best Dublin suburbs for commuters for journey times and fares.

How to use these figures

  • Treat them as averages. A modern apartment in a cheaper region can cost more than an old one in a dearer region.
  • Rents rose fastest in early 2026 because landlords can reset rent to market level between tenancies under the new rules. Once you are in, increases are capped at 2% a year or inflation, whichever is lower.
  • A deposit cannot exceed one month's rent, and advance rent cannot exceed one month.
  • Check that your tenancy is registered with the RTB; it is the landlord's legal duty and it protects you.

articles.title: Best areas to live in Cork
articles.appTitle: Best areas to live in Cork
articles.note: Cork neighbourhoods and commuter towns with 2026 rents, bus fares and rail times into the city.
articles.description: Cork is Ireland's second city and, for many people moving for jobs in pharma, tech or at the universities, it is a happier fit than Dublin: smaller…
articles.previewHtml:
Cork is Ireland's second city and, for many people moving for jobs in pharma, tech or at the universities, it is a happier fit than Dublin: smaller, walkable, close to the sea and the mountains, and cheaper to rent in, although not by as much as it used to be. This guide covers the neighbourhoods newcomers choose most often, how you get into the city from each, and what they cost. Rent figures come from the Daft.ie Rental Report for Q2 2026 (published August 2026) and the RTB Rent Index for Q1 2026.

The Cork rental market in 2026

Cork has had the second-fastest rent growth in the country this year. The RTB puts the standardised average rent for a new tenancy in Cork City at €1,903 in Q1 2026, up 16.3% on a year earlier, against €1,442 in the Cork County council area. Existing tenants in the city paid an average of €1,422. On the open market, Daft.ie's Q2 2026 average across all property types was €2,119 in Cork City and €1,700 in the county. Availability is tight, so start looking before you arrive and have your documents ready.
articles.gatedHtml:
Cork City (Daft.ie, Q2 2026)Average monthly rentChange on a year earlier
Studio€1,222+7.3%
1-bed apartment€1,781+17.6%
2-bed apartment€2,168+10.3%
3-bed apartment€2,428+7.4%
2-bed house€2,213+17.8%
3-bed house€2,511+10.9%
4-bed house€3,147+7.6%

City centre and the Victorian Quarter

Cork's centre is an island between two channels of the River Lee, and the apartments around the English Market, Oliver Plunkett Street and the docklands put you within walking distance of everything. North of the river, the Victorian Quarter around MacCurtain Street has become the city's food and nightlife hub and is a short walk from Kent Station. This is the best choice if you work in the centre or commute by train, and the obvious one if you do not have a car.

Douglas, Blackrock and Mahon

South-east of the centre, Douglas is the most sought-after suburb for families: two shopping centres, a large choice of primary and secondary schools, and buses into the city in around 20 minutes. Blackrock next door is a harbour village with the Marina Park and the Blackrock Castle observatory, and the walk or cycle along the old railway line into the city is one of Cork's nicest commutes. Mahon has newer housing and the Mahon Point shopping centre. Expect rents at or above the city averages here.

Ballincollig and Bishopstown

West of the city, Ballincollig has grown into a town of its own, with a regional park along the river, good schools and buses every 15 minutes taking around 16 to 25 minutes into the city. It is a favourite of people working at the pharma and tech campuses on the west side. Bishopstown and Wilton sit between Ballincollig and the centre, next to Cork University Hospital, University College Cork and Munster Technological University, and are the practical choice for hospital and university staff.

Glanmire, Carrigaline and the commuter rail towns

Glanmire, north-east of the city, has larger family houses and a 20 to 25 minute drive or bus to the centre; a car helps here. Carrigaline to the south is a big commuter town close to Ringaskiddy and the harbour employers. East of the city, the commuter rail line from Kent Station gives you Glounthaune, Carrigtwohill, Midleton and Cobh: Midleton is about 23 minutes and Cobh about 24 minutes by train, and both offer town life at county rents. The Daft.ie Q2 2026 county average was €1,700, well below the city.

Getting around Cork

Bus Éireann runs the city network. From 20 July 2026 Cork moved to a flat €1.70 adult Leap fare with free transfers within 90 minutes; young adult and student Leap fares are 85c and child fares 55c. The BusConnects redesign of the network is being rolled out route by route, so check the TFI journey planner for the current map. Cork is also small enough to cycle, and the TFI Bikes shared scheme covers the centre and the inner suburbs.

Tips for choosing

  • North side or south side matters less in Cork than in Dublin, but crossing the city at rush hour is slow, so live on the same side as your workplace.
  • Check flood history for ground-floor city-centre apartments; the centre has flooded in past winters.
  • Cork Airport is south of the city, 15 minutes from Douglas or Carrigaline.
  • Register with a GP early; lists in the suburbs fill quickly.

★ Useful links

  • Daft.ie Rental Report Q2 2026
  • RTB Rent Index Q1 2026
  • TFI journey planner
  • TFI Leap Card in Cork
  • Cork City Council

articles.title: Best areas to live in Galway
articles.appTitle: Best areas to live in Galway
articles.note: Salthill, Knocknacarra, Oranmore and other Galway areas with 2026 rents and how to get around.
articles.description: Galway is small, sociable and sits right on the Atlantic, which is why so many people who move there for the medtech companies, the university or the…
articles.previewHtml:
Galway is small, sociable and sits right on the Atlantic, which is why so many people who move there for the medtech companies, the university or the hospital never leave. It is also one of the tightest rental markets in the country, with far fewer homes to rent than Dublin or Cork. This guide explains how the city is laid out, which neighbourhoods suit which kind of newcomer, and what you should budget. Rents are from the Daft.ie Rental Report for Q2 2026 (published August 2026) and the RTB Rent Index for Q1 2026.

The Galway rental market in 2026

Galway City is now the second most expensive city in Ireland for new tenants. The RTB's standardised average rent for a new tenancy in Galway City was €2,004 in Q1 2026, up 13.3% in a year and €552 more than the €1,452 average in the Galway County council area. Sitting tenants in the city paid €1,445. Daft.ie's Q2 2026 average across all property types was €2,282 in Galway City and €1,559 in the county. The practical message: if you can live a few kilometres outside the city, you will pay a lot less.
articles.gatedHtml:
Galway City (Daft.ie, Q2 2026)Average monthly rentChange on a year earlier
Studio€1,157+3.0%
1-bed apartment€1,647+22.2%
2-bed apartment€2,336+13.0%
3-bed apartment€2,631+4.5%
2-bed house€2,274+21.0%
3-bed house€2,534+14.9%
4-bed house€3,121+16.0%

West side: Salthill, Knocknacarra and Barna

The west of the city is the most expensive and the most in demand. Salthill is the seaside suburb with the promenade, Blackrock diving tower, tennis and rugby clubs and a 25-minute walk into the centre; it has large family houses and a good spread of apartments. Knocknacarra behind it is the biggest residential suburb in the city, built mostly since the 1990s, with modern estates, schools, a retail park and the Cappagh Park playing fields. It is the default choice for families. Further out, Barna and Moycullen are villages with sea and lake views, but you will need a car and the coast road is slow at rush hour.

Near the university and hospital: Newcastle and Shantalla

Newcastle and Shantalla sit between University of Galway and University Hospital Galway, ten minutes' walk from Eyre Square. They are dominated by student rentals, which means plenty of shared houses and a lively atmosphere in term time, and are ideal if you work at the university or the hospital. Terryland and the Headford Road area to the north have newer apartments and the big supermarkets.

East side: Renmore, Mervue, Doughiska and Oranmore

Rents are lower east of the river, and this is where most of the jobs are. Renmore and Mervue are established suburbs beside Ballyloughane beach and a short bus ride from the centre. Doughiska and Roscam have the newest housing in the city, next to the Parkmore and Ballybrit business parks where the medtech firms are based. Oranmore, ten kilometres out, is a busy commuter village with its own train station: the train to Galway Ceannt takes about 9 minutes, and route 404 buses run every 30 minutes. It is the best balance of price, space and commute for many families.

City centre and the Claddagh

Living in the centre means Shop Street, the Latin Quarter, the Saturday market by St Nicholas' church and the pubs of Quay Street on your doorstep. Apartments are scarce and small, and the noise at weekends is real, but for a single professional or a couple it is the most fun place in the west of Ireland to live. The Claddagh and the Long Walk across the river offer terraced houses with harbour views and a five-minute walk to everything.

Getting around

Bus Éireann and City Direct run the city buses. With a TFI Leap Card the adult single fare is €1.35 for up to 11 stages and €1.55 beyond that; young adult, student and child fares are 65c to 80c. Route 401 links Salthill and Eyre Square every 20 minutes, and route 410 serves Knocknacarra. The new BusConnects Galway network, including a 24-hour cross-city route between Knocknacarra and Parkmore, is being introduced in stages, so check the TFI journey planner. Galway is flat and compact, and many residents cycle.

Tips for house hunting in Galway

  • Avoid the weeks before the university term starts in September; competition from students is at its peak.
  • The Galway Races in late July and the Arts Festival push short-let prices up, but they do not affect long-term rents.
  • Ask about heating and insulation: older houses near the coast can be cold and damp in winter.
  • If you have a car, factor in the city's traffic; the ring road has not yet been built.

★ Useful links

  • Daft.ie Rental Report Q2 2026
  • RTB Rent Index Q1 2026
  • TFI Leap Card in Galway
  • Galway city bus network maps
  • Galway City Council
