articles.previewHtml:
Electricity and gas are essential utilities for any household in Ireland. Whether you are moving into a new home or just looking to switch suppliers, it is important to understand the options available to you and make an informed decision. In this article, we will go over the different options for electricity and gas suppliers in Ireland, as well as some tips for reducing your energy consumption and lowering your bills.

Electricity Suppliers in Ireland

In Ireland, electricity is deregulated, which means that you have the freedom to choose your own supplier. There are several electricity suppliers operating in the market, each offering different plans, tariffs, and discounts. Some major players include:
articles.gatedHtml:
1. Electricity Supply Board (ESB)
  2. SSE Airtricity
  3. Bord Gáis Energy
  4. Energia
  5. Pinergy

When choosing an electricity supplier, it is important to consider factors such as price, customer service, and green energy options. Many suppliers offer online tariffs and discounts, so be sure to shop around and compare different options before deciding.

Gas Suppliers in Ireland

Gas is also deregulated in Ireland, which means that you have the freedom to decide your own supplier. Some major players in the gas market include:

  1. Gas Networks Ireland
  2. Bord Gáis Energy
  3. Flogas
  4. SSE Airtricity

Just like with electricity, it is important to consider factors such as price, customer service, and green energy options when choosing a gas supplier. You can compare different suppliers and plans using price comparison websites, or by contacting the suppliers directly.

★ Tip

Consider using price comparison websites to find the most cost-effective and suitable gas and electricity plans for your specific requirements:

  1. Bonkers.ie
  2. Switcher.ie

Reducing Energy Consumption and Lowering Bills

Regardless of which supplier you choose, there are several things you can do to reduce your energy consumption and lower your bills. Here are some tips:

Insulate your home: Insulating your home can reduce heat loss, lower your heating costs, and improve the overall energy efficiency of your home.

Switch off lights: Make sure to turn off lights when you leave a room, as well as appliances that are not in use.

Use energy-efficient appliances: Choose appliances that are energy-efficient, as they consume less energy and can lower your bills.

Reduce hot water usage: Take shorter showers, wash clothes in cold water, and reduce the temperature of your hot water tank.

In conclusion, understanding your options for electricity and gas suppliers in Ireland, as well as reducing your energy consumption, can help you make an informed decision and lower your bills. With a little effort, you can save money and help protect the environment at the same time.

articles.title: Water in Ireland
articles.description: Water is a precious resource that is essential to daily life. In Ireland, it is important to understand the regulations, providers, and payment options…
articles.previewHtml:
Water is a precious resource that is essential to daily life. In Ireland, it is important to understand the regulations, providers, and payment options for this commodity. In this article, we'll explore the basics of water supply and usage in Ireland.

Water Supply

Water supply in Ireland is managed by a network of local authorities known as Uisce Éireann (Irish Water, previously). This semi-state body is responsible for the provision of clean and safe drinking water to the population of Ireland. The water is sourced from rivers, lakes, and underground wells and is treated to ensure that it meets the standards set by the World Health Organization. Uisce Éireann operates and maintains the water supply infrastructure, including pipes, treatment plants, and storage reservoirs.
articles.gatedHtml:
Billing and Payment

At present, domestic customers in Ireland are not required to pay for water and wastewater services as long as they do not exceed their Annual Allowance. However, Uisce Éireann has plans to implement a household charge for excessive water usage in 2022, as per the Irish Water Charges Plan. The exact date for the Excess Use Charge has not been determined yet, but it is expected that households will not start receiving bills until at least January 2024.

The Excess Use Charge is a fee aimed at reducing water waste and will be levied on households that consume an excessive amount of water. Uisce Éireann has the authority to apply this charge once a household exceeds their Annual Allowance.

It is important to note that the threshold for the Excess Use Charge is set at over 1.7 times the average household usage. This means that households will only be charged if they consume more than 213,000 liters (213 m³) of water per year. Additionally, households with more than four people will have a higher allowance.

Conservation

In Ireland, water is a finite resource, and it is critical to conserve it for future generations. Irish Water provides a range of information and resources to help customers conserve water, including tips on reducing water usage, and information on water-saving devices. The company also encourages customers to report any leaks or water waste as soon as they become aware of them, to ensure that the water supply is managed efficiently.

articles.description: When it comes to entertainment and staying connected in Ireland, most households opt for Internet and TV subscription services. With a wide range of…
articles.previewHtml:
When it comes to entertainment and staying connected in Ireland, most households opt for Internet and TV subscription services. With a wide range of providers and packages to choose from, it can be a bit overwhelming to pick the right one. In this article, we will guide you through the process of deciding on an Internet and TV subscription in Ireland and what you need to know before making your final decision.

Internet providers in Ireland

Ireland has a number of reputable internet service providers that offer broadband and fiber optic connections.

Some popular providers include:
articles.gatedHtml:
1. Eir
  2. Virgin Media
  3. Sky
  4. Vodafone
  5. SIRO
  6. Pure Telecom
  7. Magnet+
  8. Digiweb
  9. Open Eir

These providers offer various plans and packages to choose from, based on your internet usage requirements, speed, and budget.

TV providers in Ireland

In addition to internet services, TV providers in Ireland also offer a range of packages that include television channels, on-demand content, and recording features. Similar to internet providers, you can decide from various TV packages offered by providers such as Virgin Media, Sky. Some providers even offer bundled packages that include both TV and internet services, which can be more cost-effective than purchasing the two services separately.

★ Tip

Providers offer various internet and TV packages based on your address.

Consider using price comparison websites to find the most cost-effective and suitable internet and TV plans for your specific requirements:

  1. Bonkers.ie
  2. Switcher.ie

Before you choose an Internet and TV provider

Here are a few things to consider before you choose an internet and TV provider in Ireland:

Cost: Make sure you compare the prices of different providers to see what works best for your budget. Don't just focus on the initial cost, consider any extra fees, charges, and contract lengths.

Speed: Consider the speed of the internet connection you need for your daily activities such as browsing, streaming, and gaming.

Availability: Make sure the provider you choose has coverage in your area. You can check this on their website or by calling them directly.

Packages and channels: Consider the channels you want to watch and make sure the provider you decide offers them. Some providers also offer additional features such as on-demand content, recording, and catch-up TV.

Contract length: Make sure you understand the contract length and any penalties for ending the contract early.

Conclusion

Deciding the right Internet and TV provider in Ireland can be a bit overwhelming, but by considering the above factors and comparing different providers, you can find a package that meets your needs and budget. Whether you're looking for high-speed internet for browsing and streaming, or a comprehensive TV package with a wide range of channels, you're sure to find something that works for you.

articles.title: TV license
articles.description: A television license is required for any household in Ireland that uses a television set to receive live broadcasts or recorded programs. The television…
articles.previewHtml: A television license is required for any household in Ireland that uses a television set to receive live broadcasts or recorded programs. The television license fee is the main source of funding for the Irish state broadcaster, RTE.
articles.gatedHtml:
In Ireland, the fee for a television license is €160 per year for a color television set and €58 for a black and white television set. The fee is due annually and is payable by direct debit or by post. A television license is also required for a television set used for recording live broadcasts for later viewing.

It is important to note that the fee must be paid even if the television set is only used for watching DVDs, streaming services, or other non-broadcast programming. This is because the law considers that the set is still capable of receiving live broadcasts.

Enforcement of the television license fee is carried out by the TV Licensing Authority, an independent body responsible for ensuring that all households in Ireland have the appropriate license. The Authority uses various methods, including regular address inspections, to monitor compliance. If a household is found to be without a valid television license, they could face a fine of up to €1,000.

In conclusion, a television license is a requirement for any household in Ireland that uses a television set to receive live broadcasts or recorded programs. The fee helps to support the Irish state broadcaster and ensures that the public can continue to receive high-quality programming. It is important to remember that the fee must be paid even if the television set is only used for watching non-broadcast programming.

articles.title: Household waste disposal
articles.description: Household waste disposal is an essential aspect of daily life in Ireland. The proper disposal of waste not only helps to maintain clean and hygienic…
articles.previewHtml:
Household waste disposal is an essential aspect of daily life in Ireland. The proper disposal of waste not only helps to maintain clean and hygienic surroundings, but also helps to protect the environment. In Ireland, local authorities are responsible for the collection of household waste and the management of landfill sites. In this article, we will discuss the various aspects of household waste disposal in Ireland.

Collection of Households Waste

The local authorities in Ireland provide a regular collection service for household waste. The frequency of collection depends on the area, but in most cases, it is once a week. Household waste is usually collected in the form of black bags or bins and should be placed outside the property on the day of collection. The local authorities have a list of items that are accepted for collection and items that are not accepted.
articles.gatedHtml:
Reduce Waste Expenses

To minimize your waste costs, sort your recyclable items from your non-recyclables and bring them to one of the many free public recycling facilities in your area. You can locate your nearest recycling center by searching online. These recycling centers do not typically charge a fee, however, the process of storing and transporting recyclables can be inconvenient, particularly if you do not have access to a vehicle. Landfills are also an option, but they incur fees.

Types of Household Waste

Household waste can be divided into two main categories: general waste and recyclable waste. General waste includes items that cannot be recycled and should be placed in black bags or bins. Recyclable waste includes items such as paper, cardboard, glass, plastic, and cans, and should be placed in separate containers for collection.

Recycling

Recycling is an important aspect of household waste disposal in Ireland. The local authorities provide a collection service for recyclable waste, and it is significant for households to follow the guidelines and place recyclable items in the correct containers. The recycling process helps to conserve natural resources and reduce the amount of waste that ends up in landfill sites.

Household Hazardous Waste

Household hazardous waste, such as batteries, light bulbs, and chemicals, should not be placed in the regular household waste collection. These items can cause harm to the environment and should be disposed of properly. The local authorities in Ireland provide a household hazardous waste collection service, and households can contact their local authority for more information.

Waste Reduction

Reducing the amount of waste generated in households is an important aspect of waste management in Ireland. Simple steps such as buying products with minimal packaging, composting kitchen waste, and reusing items can help to reduce the amount of waste that is generated.

In conclusion, household waste disposal is an essential aspect of daily life in Ireland, and the local authorities provide a regular collection service for household waste. The proper disposal of waste helps to maintain clean and hygienic surroundings and protects the environment. Households should follow the guidelines for waste collection and try to reduce the amount of waste generated in their homes.

articles.title: Public Transportation System of Ireland
articles.description: Ireland has a relatively efficient public transport system that includes buses, trains, trams, and taxis. While it may not be as extensive as some other…
articles.previewHtml:
Ireland has a relatively efficient public transport system that includes buses, trains, trams, and taxis. While it may not be as extensive as some other European countries, the network covers most major towns and cities, and getting around is generally affordable and straightforward.

Bus

Bus transport in Ireland is provided by both public and private companies. The national public bus company is Bus Éireann, which operates routes throughout the country. The larger cities, such as Dublin, Cork, Limerick, and Galway, have their local bus companies as well. Dublin Bus, for example, operates an extensive network of bus routes throughout the city and surrounding areas. Tickets can be purchased on board the bus or through various apps or top-up cards.
articles.gatedHtml:
Train

Ireland also has an extensive train network operated by Irish Rail, which covers most major towns and cities. Several types of trains are available, including commuter, intercity, and express trains. Commuter trains run frequently during peak hours and connect the suburbs to the city centers. Intercity trains run less frequently but connect major towns and cities across the country. Express trains are faster, and they provide a more luxurious experience. Tickets can be purchased at the station or online.

Tram

Trams, also known as Luas, are a popular form of transport in Dublin and serve the city center and surrounding suburbs. The Green Line runs from St. Stephen's Green in the city center to Bride’s Glen in the south, while the Red Line runs from The Point to Saggart in the west. The trams run every 10–15 minutes, and tickets can be purchased at ticket machines, on board the tram, or through various apps.

Taxis

Taxis are also readily available throughout Ireland, and they can be hailed on the street or booked through various apps. Taxis are metered, and fares vary depending on the time of day and distance traveled. It is important to note that some taxis only accept cash, so it's always a good idea to have some on hand.

Here are some taxi apps that operate in Ireland:

  1. FreeNow
  2. Uber
  3. Bolt
  4. Lynk

Bicycles

In addition to these modes of public transport, Ireland also has an extensive network of cycling and walking paths. Bicycles can be rented from various locations throughout the country, and walking is a popular way to explore the city centers.

Overall, Ireland's public transport system is reliable and affordable, and it is a great way to get around the country. Whether you're commuting to work, exploring the city, or traveling across the country, there are plenty of options available to suit your needs.

If you’re planning to use public transport in Ireland, you might have heard about the Leap Card. This rechargeable smart card is an essential item for anyone who wants to travel around Ireland’s major cities with ease. Here’s everything you need to know about the Leap Card.

What is the Leap Card?

The Leap Card is a smart card that can be used to pay for travel on public transport in Ireland. It can be used on Dublin Bus, Luas, DART, Commuter Rail, Bus Éireann, and Wexford Bus services. With the Leap Card, you can avoid the hassle of buying tickets and get access to discounted fares. The card is valid for five years, and you can top it up with credit as needed.
articles.gatedHtml:
Where can you get a Leap Card?

You can get a Leap Card from any Leap Card agent, which includes selected newsagents, post offices, and retail outlets (e.g., Spar). You can also buy a Leap Card online from the Leap Card website. The card costs €5, and you will need to top it up with credit before you can use it for travel.

How do you use the Leap Card?

Using the Leap Card is easy. Simply touch your card to the validator on the transport service you’re using, and the cost of your journey will be deducted from your card’s credit. You can also use the Leap Card to pay for multiple passengers at once, as long as they are travelling together. The card also has a daily and weekly cap, which means that you won’t be charged more than a certain amount each day or week, even if you take multiple journeys.

What are the benefits of using a Leap Card?

Using a Leap Card comes with several benefits, including:

Discounted fares – You can save up to 31% on fares compared to buying a cash ticket.

Convenience – You don’t have to worry about buying a ticket every time you travel, and you can easily top up your card online or at a Leap Card agent.

Daily and weekly caps – The card has a daily and weekly cap, which means you won’t be charged more than a certain amount each day or week.

Multi-operator – The card can be used on multiple transport services in Ireland, including Dublin Bus, Luas, DART, Commuter Rail, Bus Éireann, and Wexford Bus.

Better for the environment – Using the Leap Card helps reduce the amount of paper waste from tickets, making it a more eco-friendly option.

In summary, the Leap Card is an essential item for anyone planning to use public transport in Ireland. It’s easy to use, convenient, and offers discounted fares, making it a smart choice for regular commuters and visitors alike. Get your Leap Card today and enjoy hassle-free travel around Ireland.

articles.title: Driver's license in Ireland
articles.description: Getting a driving license in Ireland is a relatively straightforward process, but it does require some time, effort, and preparation. In this article…
articles.previewHtml:
Getting a driving license in Ireland is a relatively straightforward process, but it does require some time, effort, and preparation. In this article, we'll walk you through the various steps involved in obtaining a driving license in Ireland.

Types of Driving Licenses in Ireland

Before we dive into the process of obtaining a driving license in Ireland, it's important to understand the different types of licenses available. There are four types of driving licenses in Ireland, namely:

Learner Permit: This is a provisional license that allows you to drive under certain conditions. It's valid for two years and can be renewed for a further two years.
articles.gatedHtml:
Full License: This is a standard driving license that allows you to drive without any restrictions.

International Driving Permit (IDP): An IDP is a document that allows you to drive in other countries that recognize the IDP. It's valid for one year and can be used with your Irish driving license.

Professional License: This is a license for drivers of certain vehicles, including buses, taxis, and heavy goods vehicles.

Step-by-Step Guide to Getting a Driving License in Ireland

Step 1: Obtain a Learner Permit

The first step in getting a driving license in Ireland is to obtain a Learner Permit. To achieve this, you need to:

  • Be at least 17 years old
  • Pass a theory test
  • Pass an eyesight test
  • Submit a completed application form
  • Pay the relevant fee

Step 2: Take Driving Lessons

Once you have your Learner Permit, you can start taking driving lessons from a qualified instructor. You'll need to complete at least 12 lessons with an approved driving instructor before you can take your driving test.

Step 3: Practice Driving

In addition to taking driving lessons, you'll also need to practice driving with a qualified driver. You must display L-plates on the front and rear of the vehicle and be accompanied by a fully licensed driver at all times.

Step 4: Take the Driving Test

Once you have completed the required driving lessons and practice, you can apply to take the driving test. The driving test consists of a 40-minute driving test and an eyesight test. You'll need to bring your Learner Permit, your logbook, and a roadworthy vehicle to the test.

Step 5: Obtain your Full License

If you pass your driving test, you'll be issued a full driving license. Your new license will be valid for ten years and will need to be renewed after this period.

Conclusion

Obtaining a driving license in Ireland is a process that requires time, effort, and preparation. By following the steps outlined in this article, you can ensure that you have the best chance of success. Remember to practice safe driving habits and to always respect the rules of the road. Good luck and safe driving!

articles.title: Exchange a driving licence from a non-recognised state
articles.note: Special content for non recognized driving license holders
articles.description: As you may have a valid driving license from a non recognized country, you can drive in Ireland for up to 12 months. Thereafter, you will need to obtain…
articles.previewHtml:
As you may have a valid driving license from a non recognized country, you can drive in Ireland for up to 12 months. Thereafter, you will need to obtain an Irish driving license to continue driving legally. The process for obtaining an Irish driving license varies depending on the country that issued your current driving license.

As your current driving license is not from a recognized country, you will need to take the Irish driving test. The test has two parts: a theory test and a practical test. Before taking the tests, you must apply for a learner permit and have it for at least six months. During this time, you must take a course of driving lessons with an approved driving instructor. Once you have completed the required driving lessons, you can apply to take the tests.
articles.gatedHtml:
The theory test consists of multiple-choice questions about the rules of the road, road signs, and driving regulations. You must pass the theory test before you can take the practical test. The practical test involves driving with an examiner who will assess your driving skills and ability to respect the rules of the road. If you pass both tests, you will be issued an Irish driving license.

Reduced EDT course

In Ireland, the EDT (Essential Driver Training) course is a mandatory training program for all new drivers who obtained their first driving license on or after April 4, 2011. The EDT course consists of 12 one-hour lessons that cover a range of driving skills, including driving in different road and traffic conditions, maneuvering, and driving safely at night.

A reduced EDT course is an option for drivers who hold a full driving license from another country, and who wish to obtain an Irish driving license. The reduced EDT course includes 6 one-hour lessons, rather than the full 12 lessons, as it is assumed that drivers who hold a full driving license already have some experience and knowledge of driving.

The reduced EDT course is designed to help foreign drivers understand the rules of the road and driving practices in Ireland, and to ensure that they are familiar with the local driving conditions before taking the practical driving test. After completing the reduced EDT course, foreign drivers can then apply for an Irish driving license and take the practical driving test.

It is important to note that driving in Ireland can be challenging, especially for those who are not used to driving on the left side of the road. It is recommended that you take driving lessons and practice driving on quiet roads before attempting to drive in busier areas.

In conclusion, if you have a driving license from a non recognized country, you will need to take the Irish driving test. It is significant to prepare and practice for the tests to increase your chances of passing, and to familiarize yourself with the rules of the road and driving conditions in Ireland.

articles.previewHtml: As you may have a driving license is from a country that is recognized by the Irish government, you can exchange it for an Irish driving license. To exchange your driving license, you must provide the following documentation:
articles.gatedHtml:
• Your current driving license.
  • A completed D401 application form, which can be obtained from the NDLS (National Driver Licensing Service) website.
  • Evidence of your residency in Ireland, such as a utility bill or a letter from your employer.
  • A passport-sized photograph.
  • The appropriate fee (€55 as of 2023).

Not all categories of license can be exchanged in every case. You can read more about the specific exchange rules governing each country and territory listed above on the NDLS website.

You must exchange your license within 1 year of its expiration date.

It is important to note that driving in Ireland can be challenging, especially for those who are not used to driving on the left side of the road. It is recommended that you take driving lessons and practice driving on quiet roads before attempting to drive in busier areas.

articles.title: Cycling in Ireland
articles.description: Biking is a great way to explore and travel in Ireland, and renting a bike is a convenient and affordable option for visitors and residents alike. There…
articles.previewHtml:
Biking is a great way to explore and travel in Ireland, and renting a bike is a convenient and affordable option for visitors and residents alike. There are several bike renting companies in Ireland that offer different options and services to their customers.

  1. DublinBikes
  2. TFI Bikes
  3. Bleeper
  4. Zip
  5. Moby Bikes
  6. ESB
  7. Tier

Ireland's City Bike Schemes

Dublinbikes

One of the most popular bike renting companies in Ireland is Dublinbikes, which operates in Dublin city. Dublinbikes offers an affordable and convenient bike rental service for short-term use. With more than 100 stations across the city, Dublinbikes offers a great way to get around and explore the city at your pace. Users can register online, and once registered, can rent bikes from any station using their Leap card or credit card.
articles.gatedHtml:
Dublinbikes offers two types of subscription plans for users:

Annual subscription: This plan costs €25 per year and allows unlimited rentals of up to 30 minutes per ride. If the bike is not returned within 30 minutes, an additional charge is applied.

Three-day ticket: This plan costs €5 for three consecutive days and allows unlimited rentals of up to 30 minutes per ride. As with the annual subscription, additional charges are applied for rides exceeding 30 minutes.

Both plans provide users with access to over 100 bike stations across Dublin, which are open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Users can use the Dublinbikes app to locate available bikes and docking stations, as well as to track their usage and receive notifications about their subscription.

TFI Bikes

A DublinBikes similar scheme is operated by Transport for Ireland (TFI) and offers users access to a fleet of shared bicycles across several locations in the country, including Waterford, Cork, Limerick, and Galway.

To use TFI Bikes, users need to first register online or through the TFI Go app. Once registered, they can choose a plan that best suits their needs. The options available include a 3-day pass, a 30-day pass, and an annual membership. Payment for the plans can be made using a credit or debit card.

Private bike sharing companies

There are several private bike-sharing companies operating in Ireland. Here are a few examples:

Bleeper: Bleeper is a private bike-sharing service that operates in Dublin. Users can rent bikes via the Bleeper app and pay per ride or decide a subscription plan.

Moby: Moby is a private bike-sharing company that operates in Dublin. Users can rent bikes via the Moby app and pay per ride or choose a subscription plan.

Zipp: Zipp is a private bike-sharing company that operates in South Dublin. Users can rent bikes via the Zipp app and pay per ride.

These private bike-sharing companies offer an alternative to the public bike-sharing schemes, like Dublinbikes and TFI Bikes, and provide users with more flexibility in terms of rental times and locations.

In addition to these large-scale bike rental companies, there are also smaller, independent bike rental shops located throughout Ireland. These shops offer various bikes for rent, including road bikes, mountain bikes, and electric bikes. Some of these shops offer guided tours as well, which can be a great way to explore the countryside and other areas of interest.

Regardless of the company you choose, renting a bike in Ireland can be an excellent way to get around and see the sights. With so many options available, there is sure to be a bike rental company that meets your needs and budget. So, whether you're a resident or a visitor, consider renting a bike for a day or more and explore all that Ireland has to offer.

articles.title: Bike to Work Scheme
articles.description: The Bike-2-Work scheme is a government initiative designed to encourage people to cycle to work, by offering tax incentives on the purchase of bicycles…
articles.previewHtml:
The Bike-2-Work scheme is a government initiative designed to encourage people to cycle to work, by offering tax incentives on the purchase of bicycles and cycling equipment. It is a win-win situation for both employees and employers, as it promotes a healthy lifestyle while reducing carbon emissions.

How does the scheme work?

Under the scheme, employers can purchase bicycles and cycling equipment up to the value of €3,000 for their employees. The employee then pays for the bicycle through salary sacrifice, meaning they can spread the cost of the bicycle over a 12-month period, effectively making the purchase tax-free.

The scheme has been in operation since 2009, and it has proven to be a great success. More and more people are using bikes to commute to work, and the scheme has played a significant role in promoting this trend.
articles.gatedHtml:
How much can I spend on the Bike to Work Scheme, and how often can I use it?

There are 3 limits depending on the type of bike you bought. The limit (including related safety equipment) is:

  • €3,000 for cargo and ecargo bikes.
  • €1,500 for pedelecs and e-bikes.
  • €1,250 for other bicycles.

As an employee, you can use the scheme once every 4 years. The four-year span between tax breaks is counted by tax year. If you bought a bike in 2023, regardless of the month, you could buy a new bike and avail of the next tax relief in January 2027.

What equipment does the Bike to Work Scheme cover?

The scheme covers the following items, which must be purchased as new (not second-hand):

  • New bikes and pedelecs (electrically assisted bikes that require some effort to propel)
  • Cycle helmets
  • Bells and bulb horns
  • Lights (including dynamo packs)
  • Mirrors
  • Mudguards and skirt guards
  • Cycle clips
  • Panniers, luggage carriers and straps
  • Locks and chains
  • Pumps
  • Puncture repair kits, cycle tool kits and tire sealant
  • Reflective clothing
  • Bike reflectors

The scheme does not include motorbikes, mopeds, scooters or second-hand bicycles or equipment or bicycle parts or associated equipment.

Benefits of the scheme

The Bike-2-Work scheme is a great way to save money on the purchase of a new bicycle, as it is effectively tax-free. This means that you can save up to 52% on the cost of a new bike, depending on your income tax bracket.

The scheme also provides significant health benefits. Cycling to work is an excellent form of exercise, and it can help to reduce stress, improve fitness levels and boost your overall wellbeing. Regular cycling can also help to reduce the risk of developing health conditions such as heart disease, diabetes, and obesity.

Additionally, cycling to work is an eco-friendly and sustainable mode of transport that can help to reduce your carbon footprint. By reducing your reliance on fossil fuels, you can help to protect the environment and reduce air pollution.

How to apply for the scheme

To avail of the Bike-2-Work scheme, you must be employed and pay tax in Ireland. Your employer must also be registered with Revenue as an employer and be able to provide you with a salary sacrifice arrangement.

To apply for the scheme, you must first select a bike from an approved bike retailer. You can then apply to your employer to purchase the bike on your behalf. Your employer will purchase the bike and cycling equipment and deduct the cost from your gross salary over a 12-month period.

Conclusion

The Bike-2-Work scheme is a great initiative that promotes cycling as a sustainable, healthy, and cost-effective way of commuting to work. By taking advantage of this scheme, you can save money on the purchase of a new bike, improve your health, and help to protect the environment.

articles.title: Which countries' driving licences can be exchanged in Ireland
articles.appTitle: Which countries' driving licences can be exchanged in Ireland
articles.note: Full NDLS list of exchangeable licences, the €65 process, and the route for non-recognised countries.
articles.description: Whether you can swap your existing driving licence for an Irish one, or must start again with a learner permit, depends entirely on where your licence…
articles.previewHtml:
Whether you can swap your existing driving licence for an Irish one, or must start again with a learner permit, depends entirely on where your licence was issued. Ireland exchanges licences from every EU and EEA state and from a short list of "recognised states" with which it has a bilateral agreement. Everyone else, including holders of US, Indian, Brazilian and Chinese licences, goes through the full Irish licensing process, with one concession. This guide sets out the full list published by the NDLS and Citizens Information in 2026, the process and fee, and what to do if your country is not on it.

The full list of exchangeable licences

GroupCountries and territoriesNotes
EU member statesAustria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, SwedenYou may drive on your EU licence while it is valid; exchange within 10 years of its expiry
EEA statesIceland, Liechtenstein, NorwaySame rules as EU licences
United Kingdom and Crown dependenciesUnited Kingdom (including Northern Ireland), Gibraltar, Isle of Man, Jersey, GuernseyUK visitors can drive on a UK licence; UK residents of Ireland must exchange
Recognised states: Europe and AsiaSwitzerland, Georgia, Moldova, Japan, Republic of Korea (South Korea), TaiwanExchange within 1 year of the licence's expiry date
Recognised states: rest of worldAustralia, New Zealand, South AfricaExchange within 1 year of the licence's expiry date
Canada (listed provinces only)Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Ontario, SaskatchewanLicences from Quebec, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and the territories cannot be exchanged
articles.gatedHtml:
Two important limits apply. Not every category transfers in every case: some agreements cover car (category B) licences only, and truck, bus or motorcycle categories may not carry over, so check the country-specific rules on the NDLS site. And if your first licence came from a country Ireland does not recognise and you later exchanged it for one from a recognised state, the NDLS will still refuse the exchange; the original issuing country is what counts. Ukrainian licence holders under temporary protection can drive on their Ukrainian licence in Ireland, but the exchange arrangement for Ukrainian licences has ended.

How long you can drive before exchanging

Holders of EU and EEA licences can keep driving on them for as long as they remain valid. If your licence is from a recognised state you can drive as a visitor for up to 12 months, but once you become normally resident, meaning you live here at least 185 days a year, you should exchange it. Holders of licences from non-recognised countries can also drive for up to 12 months as visitors if they hold an international driving permit, but if they plan to stay longer than a year they must apply for an Irish licence through the full process. Only full licences can be exchanged; a foreign learner permit is not valid for driving in Ireland.

The exchange process and fee

The fee is €65, and free if you are aged 70 or over. You can apply online or in person at an NDLS centre by appointment.

  • Online: you need a Public Services Card and a verified MyGovID. Complete the form on ndls.ie and then post your foreign licence to the NDLS; it is sent to the issuing authority or retained, so keep a photocopy.
  • In person: book an appointment at an NDLS centre and bring your current licence, proof of your PPS number, photo ID, proof of address dated within six months, and proof that you are normally resident in Ireland if you are not an EU/EEA citizen.
  • Eyesight report: if you are exchanging a recognised-state (non-EU) licence you must bring a completed eyesight report form signed by an optician or doctor.
  • Medical report: needed if you are over 70, have certain medical conditions or are applying for truck or bus categories.
  • Professional drivers: bring your Certificate of Professional Competence if you hold one.

The NDLS sometimes has to confirm details with the issuing country, and when that happens the exchange takes longer. Your foreign licence is surrendered, so if you need it for another country ask about the return arrangement before you apply.

If your country is not on the list

You cannot exchange, and you go through the same steps as a new Irish driver, with one shortcut. The steps are:

  1. Pass the driver theory test (book online at theorytest.ie).
  2. Apply to the NDLS for a learner permit; you will need your PPS number, proof of address and an eyesight report.
  3. Complete Essential Driver Training. New drivers must do 12 lessons, but if you hold a full licence from a non-recognised country you need only 6 EDT lessons.
  4. Drive accompanied by a fully licensed driver, display L plates, and wait for your test date. First-time learner permit holders must normally hold the permit for six months before sitting the test.
  5. Pass the driving test and apply for your full licence.

Driving test waiting times are published by the Road Safety Authority and have run to several months in the Dublin area, so book as early as you are allowed. Insurers will price you as an inexperienced driver until you pass, so shop around.

Practical points

  • Get your PPS number first; the NDLS will not process any application without it.
  • Your address must match your Public Services Card record or be proven with a document dated within six months.
  • An Irish licence is valid for 10 years for most drivers under 70.
  • An Irish licence lets you drive throughout the EU.

  • Citizens Information: foreign driving licences in Ireland
  • RSA: exchanging a foreign licence
  • Driver Theory Test
  • National Driver Licence Service

articles.title: Leap card fares 2026
articles.note: Dublin 90-minute fare, daily and weekly caps, commuter zones, city fares, Local Link and 2027 changes.
articles.description: The TFI Leap Card is the pay-as-you-go smart card for public transport across Ireland, and in Dublin it is the difference between a cheap commute and an…
articles.previewHtml:
The TFI Leap Card is the pay-as-you-go smart card for public transport across Ireland, and in Dublin it is the difference between a cheap commute and an expensive one: Leap fares are typically 30% below cash, transfers within 90 minutes are free, and daily and weekly caps mean you never pay more than a set amount. This guide lists the 2026 fares for Dublin bus, Luas, DART and commuter rail, the caps, the fares in the other cities and on TFI Local Link, and the discounted cards for students and young adults. All figures are from Transport for Ireland and Leap Card as of September 2026; a fare increase has been announced for January 2027, which is covered at the end.

Getting a card

An adult Leap Card costs a €5 refundable deposit plus a minimum €5 top-up, and you can buy one at newsagents and shops showing the Leap sign, at Luas and rail ticket machines, or online. You top up in shops, at machines, on the Leap Top-Up app (which also lets you check your balance on your phone) or online. Tap on when you board a bus or enter a Luas or rail platform; on rail and Luas you must also tap off, or you will be charged the maximum fare.
articles.gatedHtml:
Dublin: the 90-minute fare

Inside Zone 1 (TFI Dublin City), one Leap fare covers all the journeys you make on Dublin Bus, Go-Ahead Ireland city routes, Luas, DART and commuter rail within 90 minutes of your first tap. The fare is taken on the first tap and every transfer within the window is free.

FareAdultYoung Adult (19 to 25) and StudentChild (5 to 18)
TFI 90-minute Leap fare (bus, Luas, DART, commuter rail in Zone 1)€2.00€1.00€0.65
Dublin Bus cash fare, short journey€2.00n/a€0.90
Dublin Bus cash fare, long journey€2.60n/a€0.90
Daily Leap cap, Zone 1€6.00€3.00€1.95
Weekly Leap cap, Zone 1 (Monday to Sunday)€24.00€12.00€7.80

The daily cap runs from 4.30am to 4.29am the next day and the weekly cap from 4.30am Monday to 4.29am the following Monday; once you hit the cap, further journeys that day or week are free. Caps cover Dublin city buses, Luas, DART and commuter rail within Zone 1, but not Nitelink, tours, Bus Éireann or Go-Ahead commuter routes. Children under 5 travel free, and children aged 5 to 8 travel free with a Child Leap Card.

Dublin commuter zones 2 to 4

Beyond the city zone, fares are set by four concentric zones stretching about 50 km from the centre. These are the Leap single fares to the city centre.

ZoneExample placesRail Leap single, adultRail Leap single, young adult or childCommuter bus Leap single, adult
Zone 2Skerries, Greystones, Kilcoole, Naas, Sallins, Kilcock, Blessington€3.90€1.95€3.70
Zone 3Drogheda, Newbridge, Enfield, Trim, Wicklow town€6.00€3.00€5.30
Zone 4Kildare town, Navan, Rathdrum€7.50€3.75€6.30

Commuter zone daily tickets range from €6 for Zone 1 to €14.80 for Zones 1 to 4, and monthly tickets are available up to €206.85 for the full four zones; if you commute daily, ask your employer about the TaxSaver scheme, which pays for a monthly or annual ticket from gross salary.

Cork, Galway and other cities

Each regional city has its own Leap fares. From 20 July 2026, Cork city buses moved to a flat adult Leap fare of €1.70 with free transfers within 90 minutes (cash €2.40; young adult and student 85c; child 55c). In Galway, the adult Leap single is €1.35 for up to 11 fare stages and €1.55 beyond, with young adult, student and child fares between 65c and 80c. Limerick and Waterford use similar stage-based Leap fares; check the Leap Card page for each city.

TFI Local Link

TFI Local Link runs the rural and regional routes. Fares are distance-based and set locally, so there is no single national figure, but paying by Leap Card, the TFI Go app or contactless card is up to 30% cheaper than cash, and Young Adult and Student Leap Cards get 50% off. From 17 August 2026 several Local Link services stopped selling return, 7-day and young adult tickets for cash, so a Leap Card or the app is now the practical way to pay. Free Travel Pass holders and children under 9 travel free.

Young Adult and Student Leap Cards

If you are aged 19 to 25 you qualify for the Young Adult Leap Card whether or not you are a student, which halves most fares (the Dublin 90-minute fare drops to €1 and the weekly cap to €12). Apply online at leapcard.ie with a passport, driving licence or learner permit and a live selfie; the card is posted within about five working days and costs the same €5 deposit. The Student Leap Card gives the same fares to students of any age at participating colleges and is arranged through your college. Children aged 5 to 18 use the Child Leap Card, and adults over 66 travel free with the Free Travel Pass.

What changes in January 2027

On 3 September 2026 the National Transport Authority published its 2026 Fares Determination, the first broad fare review since 2018. From January 2027 adult fares rise by an average of 15%: the Dublin 90-minute Leap fare goes from €2.00 to €2.30, the adult daily cap from €6.00 to €6.90 and the weekly cap from €24.00 to €27.60. Young adult and student fares stay at half the adult fare, many child fares fall, and free travel for under 9s and over 66s is unchanged. The exact date depends on each operator, so check TFI before the new year.

★ Useful links

  • TFI: Dublin bus fares and caps
  • Leap Card: fare capping
  • TFI: Dublin fare zones
  • Leap Card: Young Adult and Student cards
  • National Transport Authority

articles.title: Irish Healthcare System
articles.description: The healthcare system in Ireland is a complex mix of public and private services, with the government providing the majority of funding. Ireland's…
articles.previewHtml:
The healthcare system in Ireland is a complex mix of public and private services, with the government providing the majority of funding. Ireland's healthcare system is ranked 16th in the world in terms of overall performance, according to the World Health Organization.

Public healthcare in Ireland is provided through the Health Service Executive (HSE), which is responsible for delivering health and personal social services to the population. The HSE provides a range of services, including hospitals, community care, mental health services, and primary care services such as GPs and public health nurses. These services are available to all residents of Ireland, regardless of their ability to pay.
articles.gatedHtml:
While the HSE is the primary healthcare provider in Ireland, private healthcare is also available for those who wish to pay for it. Private healthcare is provided by numerous private hospitals, clinics, and other healthcare providers throughout the country. These services are generally pricier than public healthcare, but may offer shorter waiting times and more personalized care.

The Irish government has introduced some initiatives aimed at improving the country's healthcare system. The Sláintecare report, published in 2017, recommended some changes to the system, including a shift towards community-based care, the establishment of a single-tier health service, and increased investment in primary care services. The government has also pledged to increase healthcare spending in the coming years, with a focus on improving mental health services and reducing waiting times for elective procedures.

Despite these initiatives, Ireland's healthcare system still faces some challenges. Waiting times for some services can be lengthy, and there are concerns about a shortage of healthcare professionals in certain areas. The high cost of healthcare is also a concern, with many people struggling to afford private health insurance.

In conclusion, Ireland's healthcare system is a mix of public and private services, with the government providing the majority of funding. The system is generally well-regarded, but faces several challenges, including waiting times for certain services and the high cost of healthcare. The government has introduced numerous initiatives aimed at improving the system, and has pledged to increase healthcare spending in the coming years.

articles.title: Find a GP
articles.description: General Practitioners (GPs) are the primary healthcare providers in Ireland. They are usually the first point of contact for individuals seeking medical…
articles.previewHtml: General Practitioners (GPs) are the primary healthcare providers in Ireland. They are usually the first point of contact for individuals seeking medical advice and treatment for non-emergency health issues. GPs provide a wide range of services, including general health check-ups, treatment of minor illnesses and injuries, referral to specialist services, and management of chronic diseases. They also offer preventive services such as immunizations and screening for health conditions.
articles.gatedHtml:
Register with your local GP

To access general practitioners (GPs) in Ireland, individuals need to register with a GP of their choice. This is necessary as GPs operate on a patient list system and are only allowed to provide services to registered patients.

Once an individual registers with a GP, they will receive a medical card or a GP visit card.

In Ireland, most GPs work in private practices, and patients must pay a fee for their services. The fee for a GP visit varies depending on the practice, but it usually ranges from €50 to €70 for a standard consultation. However, medical cardholders and individuals with a GP visit card are entitled to free or reduced-cost GP services.

Medical cardholders are people who meet certain eligibility criteria, such as low-income or chronic illness, and are entitled to free healthcare services, including GP visits, prescription medications, and hospital care. GP visit cardholders are people who have a higher income than medical cardholders but still qualify for reduced-cost healthcare services, including free or heavily subsidized GP visits.

In addition to private practices, GPs also work in community health centers, which are publicly funded and offer primary healthcare services to individuals who cannot afford private care. These centers provide services on a sliding scale based on income, and some services may be free or heavily subsidized.

GPs in Ireland are regulated by the Irish Medical Council, which sets standards for medical education, ethics, and practice. To become a GP in Ireland, medical graduates must complete a three-year postgraduate training program in general practice, which includes supervised clinical practice, training in specialist areas such as pediatrics and geriatrics, and assessments of clinical competence.

Overall, GPs play a vital role in the Irish healthcare system, providing accessible and affordable primary healthcare services to individuals and families throughout the country.

articles.description: In Ireland, emergency health services are operated by the Health Service Executive (HSE). If you require urgent medical attention, there are several…

In Ireland, emergency health services are operated by the Health Service Executive (HSE). If you require urgent medical attention, there are several services available that can be accessed at any time, day or night.

Ambulance Service

The ambulance service provides emergency medical assistance to those in need. It is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and can be accessed by dialing 999 or 112 from any phone.

The fee for ambulance services varies depending on the circumstances. If a person has a medical card, they will not be charged for emergency ambulance services. However, if they do not have a medical card, they may be charged for the use of an ambulance.
articles.gatedHtml:
If you attend an emergency department without being referred there by a GP, there is a charge of €100. There is no charge if you are referred by a GP (bring your referral letter with you).

In non-emergency situations, such as for transport to a hospital for a scheduled medical appointment, a fee will always be charged. Patients are responsible for paying these fees themselves, although some private health insurance policies may cover the cost of non-emergency ambulance services.

Emergency Departments

Emergency Departments (ED) are located in hospitals and are designed to treat patients with serious and life-threatening injuries or illnesses. EDs operate on a triage system, where patients are seen according to the severity of their condition. The most serious cases are treated first. While the service is free to everyone, it is important to note that waiting times in EDs can be long, especially for less serious cases.

GP Out-of-Hours Service

The GP out-of-hours service provides medical assistance when GP surgeries are closed, such as evenings and weekends. This service can be accessed by calling your local GP surgery and following the instructions on the message. If your GP surgery is closed, your call will be diverted to the GP out-of-hours service.

Pharmacies

Pharmacies are an essential part of the emergency health services in Ireland. They provide a range of over-the-counter medications, advice, and support to patients in need. Some pharmacies operate extended hours or out-of-hours services, so it is important to check with your local pharmacy to see if they offer this service.

In conclusion, Ireland offers a range of emergency health services that are free of charge to all residents. If you require urgent medical attention, it is critical to access these services as quickly as possible.

articles.title: Medical Insurances
articles.description: Health insurance in Ireland is an important consideration for those looking to protect themselves and their families against unexpected medical expenses…
articles.previewHtml:
Health insurance in Ireland is an important consideration for those looking to protect themselves and their families against unexpected medical expenses. While the Irish public health system, known as the Health Service Executive (HSE), provides some level of free healthcare, many people choose to purchase private health insurance to supplement their coverage and gain access to additional benefits and services.

There are some health insurance providers in Ireland, each offering different plans with varying levels of coverage and premiums. The major providers include VHI, Laya Healthcare, and Irish Life Health, as well as several smaller companies and specialist insurers.
articles.gatedHtml:
When considering a health insurance plan, it is important to determine the level of coverage needed, including the specific services and treatments that are important to the individual and their family. Plans can cover everything from hospital stays and surgeries to preventative care, mental health services, and dental treatment.

Premiums for health insurance plans in Ireland can vary widely depending on the level of coverage and other factors such as age, medical history, and location. It is essential to shop around and compare plans from different providers to find the best fit for your needs and budget.

In addition to private health insurance, many employers in Ireland offer health insurance as a benefit to employees. This can be a cost-effective way to access private healthcare, as employers may negotiate discounted rates or contribute to the cost of the premium.

The Irish government also offers a range of health-related benefits and schemes for eligible individuals, including the Medical Card and the GP Visit Card, which provide free or subsidized healthcare to those with low incomes or certain medical conditions. Those aged 70 and over may also be eligible for the Seniors' Alert Scheme, which provides support and assistance for living independently at home.

Overall, health insurance is an important consideration for those living in Ireland, whether through private providers or the public health system. By carefully considering your needs and options, you can find a plan that provides the coverage and peace of mind you need to protect your health and wellbeing.

articles.title: Children's health
articles.note: Special content for parents
articles.description: Children in Ireland have access to a range of healthcare services. Many of these services are free, while some require payment.
articles.previewHtml:
Children in Ireland have access to a range of healthcare services. Many of these services are free, while some require payment.

General Practitioners (GPs) provide medical care to children and adults. Children are usually brought to a GP by their parents or guardians. Children under 6 years of age are entitled to free GP care under the General Medical Services (GMS) Scheme. All other children are entitled to free GP care under the GP Visit Card Scheme. The GP Visit Card Scheme covers the cost of GP consultations for children under 16 years of age. There are no income restrictions for children.
articles.gatedHtml:
Public health nursing services are available to all children. Public health nurses provide a range of services, including health screening, health promotion, and advice and support on child health and parenting issues. Services are provided free of charge.

Child health clinics provide a range of services to children under 6 years of age, including developmental assessments, health screening, immunizations, and advice and support on child health and parenting issues. Services are provided free of charge.

Children are entitled to a range of hospital services, including inpatient care, outpatient care, and diagnostic services. Hospital services are provided free of charge to children under 6 years of age. Children aged 6–16 years of age are entitled to free hospital care, but there may be charges for some services. Children over 16 years of age are treated as adults in the hospital system.

Children with disabilities are entitled to a range of services, including assessment, therapy, and support services. These services are provided by the Health Service Executive (HSE) and are free of charge.

Dental care is not free for children in Ireland. Children are entitled to a dental examination once a year, free of charge, under the HSE Dental Treatment Service Scheme. Some other services, such as fillings and extractions, are also available under the scheme, but charges apply.

Overall, children in Ireland have access to a range of healthcare services, many of which are free. Parents or guardians should ensure that their children are registered with a GP and attend regular check-ups and appointments to help ensure that they receive the best possible care.

articles.title: How to find a GP in Dublin that is taking new patients
articles.appTitle: How to find a GP in Dublin that is taking new patients
articles.note: Where to search, what to say, private fees, GP visit card limits and D-Doc and Dubdoc out of hours.
articles.description: In Ireland your GP (general practitioner, or family doctor) is the front door to the health system: prescriptions, referrals to hospital consultants…
articles.previewHtml:
In Ireland your GP (general practitioner, or family doctor) is the front door to the health system: prescriptions, referrals to hospital consultants, sick certificates and children's vaccinations all go through them. The problem in Dublin is that many practices have closed their lists. The Irish College of GPs says the country has about 4,600 GPs in practice against a need for more than 6,000, and its 2026 workforce data flags particular pressure in the Dublin commuter belt and parts of the north side. Start looking in your first weeks, not when you are sick. This guide explains where to look, what it costs and what to do out of hours. Figures are correct as of September 2026.

Where to search

SourceWhat it gives you
HSE Find a GP (www2.hse.ie/services/find-a-gp)The official directory of around 2,500 practices that hold a GMS contract (they take medical card and GP visit card patients). Search by place or use your location; each entry has an address, phone number and often email
HSE Live, 1800 700 700Free helpline, Monday to Friday 8am to 8pm, Saturday 9am to 5pm. If you hold a medical card and cannot find a GP willing to take you, the HSE can assign you to one
Google Maps and practice websitesMost Dublin practices state on their website whether they are "accepting new patients", and many let you register online
Your employer or collegeLarge employers and universities often have arrangements with a nearby practice
Neighbours and local community groupsWord of mouth is still how most people in Dublin find a GP with an open list
articles.gatedHtml:
How to approach a practice

Phone rather than email, mid-morning after the early rush. Say you have just moved to the area, give your Eircode (many practices only take patients within a catchment), and ask whether they are taking new private patients, or new GMS patients if you hold a medical card or GP visit card. Expect several calls before one says yes. If a practice is closed, ask whether they keep a waiting list and whether they know a nearby practice that is open. Once accepted, you will usually fill in a registration form with your PPS number, address, medical history and any regular medication, and be asked for a summary from your previous doctor.

What a GP visit costs

GP fees for private patients are not regulated. In Dublin, a standard consultation typically costs between €50 and €80, with city-centre practices at the upper end and evening or same-day appointments sometimes carrying a premium. Blood tests, vaccinations and minor procedures are charged separately unless covered by a public scheme. Some insurance plans refund part of the fee, and you can claim 20% tax relief on medical expenses through Revenue myAccount.

GP visit cards and medical cards

Two HSE cards make GP visits free. The GP visit card covers visits to a participating GP and the GP out-of-hours service, but not prescriptions or hospital charges. It is automatic, with no means test, for children under 8, everyone aged 70 and over, and people receiving Carer's Allowance or Carer's Benefit. For everyone else it is means-tested on net weekly income after tax, PRSI and USC; the basic rates set on 13 November 2023 are €418 for a single person living alone, €373 for a single person living with family and €607 for a couple or a lone parent, with allowances for children, rent, childcare and travel-to-work costs. The medical card has lower income limits but also covers prescriptions and hospital charges. Both are applied for with the same form at medicalcard.ie, and the HSE assesses you for the medical card first. You must be ordinarily resident, meaning living in Ireland and intending to stay at least a year. Note that a GP must have a GMS contract to accept these cards, so ask when you register.

Out of hours: D-Doc, Dubdoc and the rest

GP surgeries open Monday to Friday in office hours. Outside those hours, urgent problems that are not emergencies go to the GP out-of-hours co-operatives. You must phone first; a nurse triages you and books an appointment, a home visit or advice. Which service you use depends on where your registered GP is, so ask your practice which one covers you.

ServiceAreaPhoneHoursCost without a card
D-Doc (NorthDoc)North Dublin city and county0818 22 44 766pm to 8am weekdays, 24 hours weekends and bank holidays€75 at a centre for patients of member GPs, €90 for others; home visits €110 to €120
DubdocSouth inner city, based at the Meath Primary Care Centre, Heytesbury Street01 454 56076pm to 10pm weekdays, 10am to 6pm weekends and public holidaysFee charged; free with a medical or GP visit card
Other co-ops (for example EastDoc, LukeDoc, SouthDoc in Cork and Kerry)Varies by areaSee the HSE list of out-of-hours servicesEvenings, nights and weekendsSet by each service

All out-of-hours services are free if you show a valid medical card or GP visit card. For a life-threatening emergency, call 112 or 999 or go to an emergency department; the HSE also runs injury units for minor injuries that are faster than an emergency department.

If you cannot find anyone

  • Widen the radius: practices in the next suburb along a bus route are often open when your own is closed.
  • Ask HSE Live to help if you have a medical card; they cannot assign a GP to private patients, but they keep track of which practices are open.
  • Use an online GP service for prescriptions and certificates in the meantime, but keep looking for a local practice.
  • Register the whole household at once; practices often prefer taking a family.

★ Useful links

  • HSE: find a GP
  • HSE: GP visit cards
  • Citizens Information: GP visit cards
  • Citizens Information: GP out-of-hours service
  • D-Doc (NorthDoc)

articles.title: An overview of Irish Education System
articles.appTitle: An Overview of Irish Education System
articles.description: Education is a fundamental right and a cornerstone of a healthy society, and Ireland has a strong education system that is highly regarded around the…
articles.previewHtml:
Education is a fundamental right and a cornerstone of a healthy society, and Ireland has a strong education system that is highly regarded around the world. In this article, we will explore the education system in Ireland, including the different levels of schooling, the qualifications that can be obtained, and how to enroll in schools.

Primary Schooling

Primary education is compulsory in Ireland, and all children between the ages of six and 16 are required to attend school. Primary schools are publicly funded and follow the national curriculum. Students generally begin primary school at the age of four or five and complete it at the age of 12.

In primary school, students learn subjects such as English, Irish, mathematics, social, environmental and scientific education (SESE), and physical education. They also learn about art, music, and drama. Primary schools in Ireland often have a strong focus on extracurricular activities, such as sports and music.
articles.gatedHtml:
Secondary Schooling

After completing primary school, students move on to secondary school. Secondary education is not compulsory in Ireland, but the vast majority of students continue their education at this level. Secondary schools can be either publicly funded or fee-paying.

At secondary school, students study a wide range of subjects, including English, Irish, mathematics, science, business studies, history, geography, and modern languages. They also have the opportunity to specialize in certain subjects. Students take their Leaving Certificate examinations at the end of secondary school, which determine which college or university they can attend.

Post-Secondary Education

Post-secondary education in Ireland is provided by universities, institutes of technology, and colleges of education. The most prestigious universities in Ireland include Trinity College Dublin, University College Dublin, and the National University of Ireland, Galway.

Students can obtain various qualifications at the post-secondary level, including certificates, diplomas, and degrees. There are also opportunities to obtain professional qualifications in areas such as law, medicine, and teaching.

Enrolling in School

Enrolling in a school in Ireland is generally straightforward. Parents of school-age children can apply to their local school, and the school will usually ask for proof of the child's age and address.

For international students, enrolling in an Irish school can be a bit more complicated. Non-Irish nationals are entitled to free primary and secondary education if they are legally resident in Ireland. To enroll in school, parents will need to provide proof of their child's age and residency status.

In Conclusion

The education system in Ireland is comprehensive and well-respected. All children are entitled to a primary education, and the vast majority continue on to secondary school. There are also numerous opportunities for post-secondary education, with a wide range of qualifications available.

Enrolling in an Irish school is generally straightforward, and international students are entitled to free primary and secondary education if they are legally resident in Ireland. Whether you are a parent or a student, Ireland's education system offers many opportunities for learning and growth.

articles.title: Pre-school education and childcare
articles.description: Preschool education and childcare are crucial in a child's early development. In Ireland, the government has numerous initiatives to support families in…
articles.previewHtml:
Preschool education and childcare are crucial in a child's early development. In Ireland, the government has numerous initiatives to support families in accessing affordable preschool education and childcare services.

Preschool Education

Preschool education is available to children aged between 3 and 5 years. The government provides a free preschool education scheme called the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) program. This program is available to all children, regardless of their family's income, and covers the cost of three hours of preschool education per day, five days a week, for 38 weeks of the year.
articles.gatedHtml:
Parents have the option to extend the ECCE programme to a full day or to continue the child's education in a private preschool facility. The government also provides funding to parents who cannot afford private preschool education for their children.

Childcare Services

Childcare services are available for children aged up to 15 years. There are a range of childcare services available in Ireland, including crèches, nurseries, and childminding services.

Crèches are group childcare facilities that provide full-day care for children up to the age of six. They are typically open from early in the morning until late in the evening to accommodate working parents.

Nurseries provide childcare and early education for children up to the age of six. They are usually open for shorter hours than crèches, typically from 9am to 1pm or 2pm.

Childminding services are provided by individual childminders who care for children in the childminder's own home. This service is typically less expensive than crèches and nurseries.

The government provides numerous financial supports for parents to help them pay for childcare. These supports include the National Childcare Scheme, which provides subsidies to families who meet certain income criteria. Parents may also be eligible for the Universal Childcare Subsidy, which provides financial assistance for parents who are not eligible for other childcare support.

Conclusion

In summary, preschool education and childcare are essential for a child's development, and the Irish government provides a range of initiatives to support families in accessing these services. Whether it's through the free ECCE program or through financial support for private preschool education and childcare services, parents in Ireland have a range of options to choose from.

Whether it's through the free ECCE program or through financial support for private preschool education and childcare services, parents in Ireland have a range of options to choose from.

articles.title: Primary and post-primary education
articles.description: Education is an important aspect of Irish society, with a strong emphasis placed on providing quality education to all students. Ireland's education…
articles.previewHtml:
Education is an important aspect of Irish society, with a strong emphasis placed on providing quality education to all students. Ireland's education system is divided into primary, post-primary, and higher education, with all children having access to free primary and post-primary education.

Primary Education

Primary education in Ireland is mandatory for all children aged 6 to 12 years. It is typically completed over an 8-year period and provides students with a solid foundation in literacy, numeracy, and social skills. The primary curriculum covers a broad range of subjects, including English, mathematics, science, history, geography, art, music, and physical education.
articles.gatedHtml:
Post-Primary Education

Post-primary education is for students aged between 12 and 18 years. It is divided into junior cycle (first three years) and senior cycle (final two or three years). Students generally take a range of subjects during the junior cycle, including English, Irish, mathematics, science, history, geography, and physical education.

In the senior cycle, students have more flexibility in the subjects they study. They must take a minimum of five subjects, including English and Irish, and can choose from a range of options including mathematics, science, languages, social studies, and creative arts. At the end of senior cycle, students can sit for the Leaving Certificate examination, which is the main qualification for entry to higher education in Ireland.

Higher Education

Higher education in Ireland is provided by a range of institutions, including universities, institutes of technology, and colleges of education. Higher education qualifications range from certificates and diplomas to bachelor's, master's, and doctoral degrees.

Admission to higher education is based on a student's academic performance, with places awarded because of Leaving Certificate results, and sometimes based on an interview or portfolio submission. Irish universities are highly respected worldwide, with many ranked among the top universities globally.

Special Education

Ireland has a strong commitment to providing quality education for all students, including those with special educational needs. Children with special educational needs can receive additional support in mainstream schools, with extra resources provided for students with physical or intellectual disabilities, learning difficulties, or sensory impairments. Special schools and classes are also available for children with more complex needs.

In conclusion, Ireland's education system is designed to provide quality education to all students, from early childhood education to higher education. The system is accessible and comprehensive, with a range of support available for students with special educational needs.

articles.title: State examinations
articles.description: In Ireland, the State Examinations are a vital part of the education system. These exams are taken by students at the end of their secondary school…
articles.previewHtml:
In Ireland, the State Examinations are a vital part of the education system. These exams are taken by students at the end of their secondary school education and are used to determine eligibility for higher education courses and other opportunities.

The State Examinations include a range of different exams, including the Leaving Certificate, the Junior Certificate, and the Leaving Certificate Applied. Each of these exams has a different structure and purpose, but all are important for students' future prospects.
articles.gatedHtml:
The Leaving Certificate is the most important of the State Examinations, and it is usually taken by students in their final year of secondary school. This exam consists of a range of subjects, including English, Irish, Maths, and a number of optional subjects. Students take written exams in each of these subjects, and their results are used to determine their eligibility for higher education courses.

The Junior Certificate is taken by students in their third year of secondary school, and it is used to provide a comprehensive assessment of students' abilities across a range of subjects. This exam covers a range of subjects, including English, Irish, Math, and some optional subjects. Students take written exams in each of these subjects, and their results are used to help them plan their future studies.

The Leaving Certificate Applied is a less academic exam, and it is taken by students who prefer a more practical approach to education. This exam includes a range of practical subjects, including business, engineering, and art. Students take written exams in each of these subjects, and their results are used to determine their eligibility for further vocational education and training.

Overall, the State Examinations are a vital part of the Irish education system, and they play an important role in determining students' future prospects. By providing a comprehensive assessment of students' abilities across a range of subjects, these exams help to ensure that students are well-prepared for higher education and other opportunities.
